speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Rt. Hon. Sir GEORGE FOSTER (Acting Prime Minister) moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 37 respecting copyright.

maintopic: ACT RESPECTING COPYRIGHT.
speechtext: Explain.

maintopic: ACT RESPECTING COPYRIGHT.
speechtext:
This Bill is intended to bring the Copyright Law of Canada into conformity with the Berne Con-

vention. It establishes a uniform period of copyright protection, and also extends copyright protection to records, perforated rolls, cinematograph films, and so forth, and is intended to secure Canadian authors full copyright protection from all parts of His Majesty's Dominions as well as in Canada.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Hon. NEWTON W. ROWELL (President of the Privy Council): With the consent of the House I move that the following members be added to the Committee on Pensions: Messrs. Calder, Chisholm, Cooper, Copp, Edwards, McGregor, McLean (Royal), Morphy, Ross, Tweedie, White; and that the committee be authorized to continue the inquiries instituted by the committee on civil re-establishment last session into such matters as may call for further investigation, and to report its recommendations to the. House.
The work of the Pensions Committee this year, as I pointed out in moving for the committee, will not be nearly so onerous as that of last year, nor would a committee on re-establishment have the onerous work that the committee had last year, in view of the extent and character of the investigation carried on by that committee. Furthermore, a number of the members of the House were on both committees, and it is thought that it would not meet with the convenience of the members to have 'two committees at work which might well be centred in one committee. I am therefore moving to add to the Pensions Committee the names of all the members of the Reestablishment Committee who are not already on the Pensions Committee, and to give the Pensions Committee the power to continue any investigations that may be found necessary.
Motion agreed to.
[Fir George Foster.]

speakeroldname: Sir GEORGE FOSTER (Acting Prime Minister) moved:
maintopic: EASTER ADJOURNMENT.
speechtext: That this House adjourn on Thursday, the first April next, at 6 p.m., and that when the House so adjourns it stand adjourned until Tuesday, the sixth April next.

maintopic: EASTER ADJOURNMENT.
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I lequest the right hon. the leader of the House to amend his motion so that the adjournment may commence on Wednesday evening. Thursday is a holiday of great importance to us who belong to the religious minority in this House, and I really think that it would be only proper, in view of that fact, that the adjournment should start from Wednesday night.

maintopic: EASTER ADJOURNMENT.
speechtext:
There is no sitting on
Wednesday night either.

maintopic: EASTER ADJOURNMENT.
speechtext: I do not desire to encroach on the sacred holiday privileges of my hon. friends. At the same time, however, the object was to devote as much time >as we possibly could to the business of the House. It is not at all difficult for those hon. membeais who reside in proximity to the seat of Government to take holidays, because they can go home or go to their friends and enjoy themselves. But those who come from a distance and have to remain here have that much longer time on their hands, and unless my hon. friend strongly presses hie suggestion I think it would be the opinion of the House that we should pursue our business, as moderately as possible, of course, and with as good demeanour als should befit the day. Thereby we should save that much time.

maintopic: EASTER ADJOURNMENT.
speechtext: I may say that I have been a member of this House for over sixteen years, and it has always been the custom to have the Easter adjournment from Wednesday night. I really do not see why there should be a change this year.

maintopic: EASTER ADJOURNMENT.
speechtext: I had not paid any particular attention to the matter, but as my hon. friend assures me that the custom is as he states, perhaps it would be rather out of place to break it on this occasion. Under the circumstances I have no objection to amending the motion in accordance with the suggestion of the hon. member.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: EASTER ADJOURNMENT.
speechtext:
The motion as amended now reads:
That this House adjourn on Wednesday, the thirty-first day of March, at 6 p.m.. and that

when the House so adjourns It stands adjourned until Tuesday, the sixth day of April next.

speakerposition: topic
maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERIM VOTE.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: On motion of Sir Henry Drayton the House went into Committee of Supply, Mr. Boivin in the Chair.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERIM VOTE.
speechtext: Resolved, That a sum not exceeding $62,900,986.09, being one-sixth of the amount of each item set forth in the Main Estimates for the year ending March 31. 1921. laid on the table of the House on the 22nd instant, be granted to His Majesty for the year ending March 31. 1921.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERIM VOTE.
speechtext: May I ask if it is one-sixth of the whole Estimates?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERIM VOTE.
speechtext: It is understood that we are consenting to one-sixth of the total appropriation but we reserve our right to criticise every individual item.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERIM VOTE.
speechtext: Absolutely so.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERIM VOTE.
speechtext: But we cannot move to throw out any item if we vote one-sixth of it?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERIM VOTE.
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERIM VOTE.
speechtext:
We have already voted
one-sixth of it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERIM VOTE.
speechtext: I am told that this is the ordinary way of arriving at it.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERIM VOTE.
speechtext: During the war.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERIM VOTE.
speechtext: The whole object is to get something with which to carry on the public service. The hon. member is not committing himself upon any item that he may wish to discuss.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERIM VOTE.
speechtext:
While the practice is
to take one-sixth of the whole I would suggest that the power should only be used in urgent cases, such as to pay the Civil 'Service and such like matters-. Of course, in regard to debatable items, we cannot withdraw the vote for the one sixth, but I do not anticipate any trouble. The power is generally used to pay for urgent matters such as the Civil Service and I take it that the Government will apply it in that spirit and not apply it to other items which can just as well wait.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERIM VOTE.
speechtext: Does this include one-sixth of the $20,000,000 that we were asked to vote for government ships two or three days ago?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERIM VOTE.
speechtext: It includes one-sixth of everything but the effect is that the hon. member or any other hon. member will not be bound in any way with regard to any particular vote.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERIM VOTE.
speechtext:
We are bound by the
fact that we have voted one-sixth.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERIM VOTE.
speechtext:
Yes, but the
vote is not a vote of endorsation in so far as any particular item is concerned. As I understand it it is the ordinary vote which enables public business to be carried on.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERIM VOTE.
speechtext: I have great confidence in the minister's explanation but on the other hand I very often clash with the chairman of the committee and I would like to have his interpretation of the rule.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERIM VOTE.
speechtext:
The resolution which is now before the House provides for a vote of one-sixth of the entire Estimates which were laid on the Table on the 22nd of March. There is absolutely no doubt that this vote gives the Government the power to expend

one-sixth of every item in the Estimates if it desires to exercise that right. This is the customary blanket vote, but every item in the Estimates must once more come before this Committee in order that the other five-sixths be approved. Rule 17c remains in force the same as though this resolution were not adopted, and hon. members will have the absolute right to fully discuss any item when it comes before this Committee as a separate resolution.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERIM VOTE.
speechtext: Suppose an hon. member, when the House is in Committee later on in the session, should move that an item be struck out altogether?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERIM VOTE.
SUPPLY-INTERIM VOTE.
speechtext: Heretofore it has always been customary to grant one-sixth of the amount required for the salaries of the civil servants and other public employees who are dependent upon those salaries for the maintenance of themselves and families, but how can we vote one-sixth of the sums necessary for the payment of contracts that we know nothing about? If we make the vote we are committed to the principle and we cannot escape from it. If we admit the principle that the 'Government has the right to spend one-sixth of the sum of $1,000,000 involved in the contract, it would be ridiculous for us to intervene later and say that the remaining five-sixths should not be spent. I cannot then move to strike the item out because I have already acquiesced in the principle of the vote.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERIM VOTE.
speechtext: My hon. friend is, I think, unduly exercised over this matter.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERIM VOTE.
speechtext: I am not exercised at all.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERIM VOTE.
speechtext:
It has been the practice ever since I have been in Parliament that when the end of the fiscal year draws near the Government shall secure the sums of money necessary in order to carry on the business of the country. The votes for this purpose have always been 48J
granted, and cheerfully granted. I am not sure that my hon. friend himself has not passed through two or three crises like the present in past years.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERIM VOTE.
speechtext: Yes, fortunately I did pass through them.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERIM VOTE.
speechtext:
It has always
been considered proper to grant the votes and no opposition has been made to that course.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERIM VOTE.
speechtext: It is a wrong principle to ask us to vote fifty or one hundred million ~ dollars out of perhaps a total of $300,000,000, when there is absolutely no explanation of the proposed expenditure. That is what I object to. A vote for the salaries of civil servants is something we are familiar with, something that we know is necessary. But when you ask us to vote en bloc large amounts for other things that we know absolutely nothing about, and have had no opportunity to look into, that is an entirely different matter.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERIM VOTE.
speechtext: I would like to assure the hon. gentleman that the motion which has been moved is the customary motion, and it was furnished to me by officers of the House. So far as I have been able to learn, the course which is now proposed, is the one which has always been followed. We must remember that salaries and other commitments have to be provided for, business must be carried on, obligations must be fulfilled, and interest must be met. However, I would meet the views of my hon. friend absolutely to the fullest extent that we can. For example, I do not think that the present vote of one-sixth would be any authority to the Government to undertake new obligations in the meantime. That, I think, is the only point about which my hon. friend is very much concerned.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERIM VOTE.
speechtext: I am not so much concerned except that I think that the principle which is proposed here is wrong, and I desire to protest against it.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERIM VOTE.
speechtext:
I have looked up Hansard to ascertain the form in which previous requests have been made and the nature of the replies by the Opposition to those requests. I observe that in each case the Opposition has taken care to state that while granting one.-sixth of the total appropriation it was to be distinctly understood they were not thereby sanctioning any individual item, but reserved the right to pass upon every item appearing in the Estimates. It is in that spirit that we are pre-

pared to meet the Government at the present time. That is, the understanding shall be that while voting one-sixth of the total appropriation necessary to enable the business of the country to be carried on until such time as the Estimates may be passed, we are in no wise prejudicing the right of any hon. member to discuss any individual item on its merits.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERIM VOTE.
speechtext: My understanding agrees absolutely with that of my hon. friend.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERIM VOTE.
speechtext: If it is desired to get at the root of the trouble the Government must be reminded that they should not have allowed so much time to elapse before seeking Supply. This House should have been called at a much earlier period. In the olden times when the fiscal year terminated on the 30th of June Parliament met in January or February. However it was thought that that time was too late and for business convenience it was deemed desirable that the session should begin earlier and end earlier. Accordingly the fiscal year was changed so as to terminate on March 31. Parliament was then summoned to meet in November or December and in the intervening time from the 31st of March, it was considered that ample opportunity was afforded to prepare the necessary public documents for the proper despatch of business. The present Government, however, for reasons of their own, have allowed months to pass without taking action. Now they find themselves at the end of the fiscal year with no money voted. The explanation of this trouble is that they should have called Parliament several months ago.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERIM VOTE.
speechtext: That should have been done on numerous other occasions by my hon. friends on the other side.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERIM VOTE.
speechtext: Quite possibly, but let us take each case in its turn. I would like to know what reason the Government can give, in view of the fact that we changed the fiscal year in order to have an early meeting of Parliament, why Parliament was not summoned before the 26th of February.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERIM VOTE.
speechtext:
I invite the attention of the Government to the point as to how an item that has once been dealt with should be considered when it comes up a second time. Are we not debarred from taking action in the future with respect to an item which has been already considered?
[Mr Mackenzie King.]
It should be distinctly understood that although we are passing one-sixth of every item in the Estimates on the present occasion we shall not be precluded from discussing such items when they again come before the House for consideration.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERIM VOTE.
speechtext:
I entirely agree with my hon. friend.
Resolution reported, read a first and second time and concurred in.

speakeroldname: Hon. ARTHUR MEIGHEN (Minister of the Interior):
speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
subsubtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON SECOND READING OF BILE NO. 12.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the only purpose I have in intervening in the debate is to refer to a phase of it that developed

yesterday afternoon and evening with regard to a certain section of the Bill. It is a phase that ordinarily might well he left to discussion in committee, as it really concerns a particular item of the measure. The only reason that I desire to speak upon it now is that the Acting Solicitor General, who has charge of the measure in the House, has already spoken and, consequently, cannot address the House a second time.
Certain hon. members on both sides of the House called attention yesterday to what appears to be the effect of a reading together of the Naturalization Act as passed a year ago and section 29 of this Bill. The Naturalization Act passed in the -first session of 1919 was an Act to determine Canadian naturalization in such a manner that a person naturalized in Canada would thereby become naturalized for all purposes of the British Empire, that wherever he might be he would be deemed a British subject. The Act as then passed was drawn and enacted in conformity with British legislation, part 2 of which was submitted to and adopted, I believe, by all of the Dominions of the Empire, thereby having the effect of establishing what might be termed Empire Naturalization.
By the terms of section 8 of that Act it was provided that no subject of a then enemy state could obtain naturalization in Canada until a period of ten years had elapsed after the expiration of the war. There were three exceptions to that general provision. The disabling clause contained in sub-subsection (b) of subsection 4 of that section was made not to apply to: First, those who though born in an enemy country were of a race or community known to be opposed to the enemy governments; secondly, those who had taken part in the war on behalf of the Allies; and, thirdly, those who, though enemy subjects, were British born, having thereafter become naturalized in enemy states. Those were the three exceptions to the general rule as embodied in the British legislation and as virtually transcribed into our legislation.
It will become manifest at once that the purpose of the legislation of 1919 was to impede, for a period of ten years, the admission into citizenship in the British Empire of those who were enemy subjects. Consequently nothing can be more apparent than that there was no thought that those who were British subjects at that time should be affected in any way whatsoever by section 8 of the Naturalization Act. Its
purpose was only to delay, to impede for a fixed period, the admission to the privileges of British citizenship of those who theretofore had been subjects of enemy states.
Section 29 of our own Act provides that those who have become British subjects not by birth but by naturalization,-naturalization not based on the personal merit or qualification of the subject, but resulting from the operation of law alone-those subjects, though naturalized by the operation of law, must show the same qualification that British subjects should have before being admitted to the franchise. The intent of the section was that such examination, such investigation into the qualifications of those who would seek to vote by reason of naturalization by construction of law, should take place as would determine that they were qualified just in the same way as those who secured naturalization by personal application for same. The form of the certificate appended to section 29 is such that no one would be entitled to that certificate who, though not a British subject, could nevertheless become a British subject at that time. Well, it requires only a little reflection to see that the result is this: That the subject of an enemy state who became a British subject by construction or by operation of law would, if he or she had not so become a British subject, still be a subject of an enemy state. In this case the provisions of the Naturalization Act would at once tabs effect, and a judge hearing the application of such person for naturalization would be compelled to say: Yes, you are a British subject, but if you never had become such by construction of law I could not now make you such because-you would be a subject of an enemy state and consequently disabled under the provisions of the 1919 Naturalization Act. This is the way section 29 comes to read the way it does. It is, I believe, word for word the same section as appears in the Act of 1918 which first of all gave the franchise to women and then determine what should be the extent of woman's voting privilege as a result of that franchise. The 1918 Act effected the purpose that it was intended to effect, because there was at that time no Naturalization Act to read with it. Subsequently the 1919 Naturalization Act was passed, and in the By-election Act of last year, just as in the Act of 1918, a similar clause to clause 29 of this Bill appeared. That was carried forward into the legislation that is now presented to the House, and from the discussion of yesterday it appeared that reading the Naturalization Act

with this section, a consequence not intended by the Government resulted. That that consequence does result there can be, in my judgment, no doubt; indeed, the Acting Solicitor General (Hon. Mr. Guthrie) in answer to an inquiry last night, clearly indicated that it did result. Now, I firmly adhere to the principle that no one in this country naturalized merely by operation of law should acquire rights to the franchise until he or she shows that in point of actual qualification he or she lives up to the general provisions of the legislation applicable to all naturalized subjects; lives up to all the qualifications that others applying for naturalization must have. No reason in the world could be advanced why, .for example, a married woman who becomes a British subject, perhaps two or three days or weeks after she comes to Canada from an enemy country, by the mere act of marriage with a former alien enemy who had previously been naturalized, should be entitled to the franchise, whereas a man coming from an enemy country must, before he may be naturalized, show that he has an adequate knowledge of French and of English; that he possesses a character such as we desire in citizens of this country and the other qualifications called for in general by the provisions of the Naturalization Act. Those requirements that are demanded from all who come from all countries and ask for citizenship here should be found to exist in all persons who desire the franchise in Canada before that franchise should be granted. But I do not think, and I am sure that on reflection hon. gentlemen will see that it could not be logically argued, that any special disability should be put upon a person which was intended to apply to non-British subjects but which, taking into account the Naturalization Act and reading in connection with it the Act of this year, has the effect of applying to British subjects to whom it was never intended to apply at all. If that were to result, an alien enemy or one who formerly had been an alien enemy, who came to Canada in 1910 or 1911, took a homestead, and, to fulfil the requirements of the homestead law, took out naturalization in 1913 and became a British subject,-that alien enemy, according to the Act now presented, is entitled to the right to vote. Such a man under the provisions of the previous law which operated only for the duration of the war would not have had the right to vote, whereas a person who came to this country say forty years ago, and shortly after coming, say at the age of eighteen, became a naturalized British subject by reason of the naturalization of his 
father and had remained a British subject and had voted as such throughout all the elections since and even in the election of 1918-that person would find himself disentitled to the franchise. Well, there could be no justification, it clearly appears to me, for disfranchising that person and enfranchising the other. A much stronger argument could have been made for the retention of the disability on the recent arrival than could possibly be applied to a person who had been a British subject and a resident of Canada for perhaps forty years. That was not the intention of section 29, and the Government will propose in committee an amendment to the effect that no disability read out of paragraph (B) of subclause 4 of section 8 of the Naturalization Act should disentitle a person on that ground alone to the certificate required under section 29 of the present legislation. I feel that I have made clear our position as it is assumed by the Government. Of course, hon. members understand, without any explanation from file, that this Bill, in all its provisions and with all its principles, because as regards principles there are a dozen or twenty-four principles in legislation of this kind, as merely a declaration first of all that provision should be made for a general manhood suffrage and then that provision should be made for machinery for taking the vote In Canada for purposes of the election of members to this House. Hon. gentlemen will agree, without any explanation from me, that this Bill, presented in this way to the House of Commons, comes before the House open to amendment, discussion and suggestion. In respect of section 29 as I now explain it to the House, and in respect of every other section, as regards every feature whether embodied in the Bill or believed ought to embodied in the Bill, the Bill comes before the House, for suggestions as to amendment and for improvement if, in the wisdom of the House, improvement can be made. I simply present this feature of the legislation as it was intended to be constructed, with the effect it was intended to have, and in that way the Bill will be laid before the House in committee for full discussion and debate.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is not my purpose to pursue the discussion along the lines of the debate of last evening, nor to make any review whatever of the remarks made by the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Meighen) to-day. The discussion of last evening dealt with very interesting aspects of the question. The discussion respecting a clause disfranchising certain persons, not aliens, but British subjects, and the kindred legislation concerning the naturalization law, was certainly deeply interesting, much more interesting, I am sure, than anything I can hope to present to-day. In several of the speeches, and notably in the most impressive and very calm and effective speech of the hon. member for Waterloo North (Mr. Euler), we had presented what I may call the anomalies, injustices, and even absurdities which would arise under ,the operation of this franchise measure if it were to remain in the condition in which it now stands. I hope that the suggestion made to-day by the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Meighen) will remove some of those difficulties, and that when we have the Bill in its final shape, there will not be so much room for the criticism which was so effectively offered by the hon. member for Waterloo North. It is, however, not with these subjects, but rather with the more prosaic and matter of fact features of the Bill in one or two particulars that I desire to deal. There are many aspects of this measure which can most conveniently be discussed in committee, but there are some leading features which we may well discuss, as we have been discussing them, at this stage, the second reading of the Bill.
I accept, in unreserved manner, the assurance of the Acting Solicitor General (Mr. Guthrie) that the desire of the Government is to make this a fair and sound Bill which can be accepted by all parties. Believing that he has that object in view, and having in mind his invitation that suggestions are desired from all classes, I want to call the attention of the minister and the Government to one or two features of the Bill which I think are capable of amendment in order that the purposes which the Government say they have in view may be carried out.
In the operation of our electoral machinery, there are two stages at which there arise very strong temptations for the Government of the day to exercise an undue influence. The first of these is with regard to the preparation of the electoral lists. The second of the occasions when they have a strong temptation to act otherwise than fairly is with regard to the appointment of returning officers. If the 4 p.m. Government may obtain, wholly or partly, control over the pre-partion of the electoral lists, and if after that preliminary step in connection with the electoral machinery has been taken, .they can proceed to go out into the highways and byways and select any partisans they please to fill the places of returning officers, then we shall not have a fair Franchise Act; we shall have a measure designed to bring about the purposes of the Government and not to guard, as they should do, the franchise as a sacred trust. In both these respects, the Government are taking to themselves unnecessary, dangerous power, power that they should not seek, power which the House ought not to grant. I shall not occupy the attention of the House more than a few minutes; but first, let us give a thought to the question of the returning officers. After the Acting Solicitor General had discussed the question for some time, some hon. member, it appears, had suggested that the judges might appoint returning officers. The Acting Solicitor General at once took exception to that, and I heartily agree with him on that point. I
A

do not think judges should be called upon to appoint returning officers. We are all interested in keeping our judges out of politics, and I agree with the Acting Solicitor General that if we were to give judges power to appoint returning officers, that would be getting them dangerously near the political field. But it does not follow that because it is not wise to have judges make the appointments, we should give an unreserved hand to the Government to make the appointments themselves. It is true they have that power now; and that it has been exercised improperly is easily capable of proof. Every hon. member probably has within his own experience some knowledge of appointments made of returning officers which were not made for the highest purposes of a Franchise Act. But should the Government have an unlimited power? In my province of Nova Scotia, the Government exercises the power to appoint returning officers. The Acting Solicitor General says that this is a power which the Government should nob abdicate, and I agree with him on that; the Government should take the power. But in Nova Scotia, when the Government appoint returning officers, they aie not free to appoint whom they please; they must appoint the sheriffs of the province, who are judicial officers, so that there the Government, while they exercise the power of appointing returning officers, are not free to go out and appoint partisans for that important function, but they must take important public judicial officers for that duty.

speechtext:
I expected that my hon. friend or somebody else would raise that question. But if the appointment of a sheriff by a Government makes him the partisan of that Government, does the appointment of a judge by the Dominion Government make him a partisan of that Government? What is the difference between an officer appointed by the Dominion Government to perform a judicial duty and an officer appointed by a provincial government to perform what is also a judicial duty? If we regard it as a crime for the Government of a province to appoint a sheriff to perform such a duty, what shall we say of the Dominion Government which calls upon the judges of the country whom they appoint to

discharge judicial functions in connection with the administration of this law? Partisans they are and naturally always will be. I am not finding fault with the appointment of judges; I am not making complaint. But when exception is taken to a sheriff because he is an appointee of a provincial government, I say that with equal force one could take exception to deputing to one of the judges the duties in connection with this Bill, because the judge is appointed by the Dominion Government.
Let us consider the province of Quebec, from which there are some things that we can very well learn. The Government of the province of Quebec undertake the function of appointing returning officers, but they do not claim for themselves an unlimited right to choose. They cannot go out on the highways and byways and pick up the first man who will serve their purpose. They have the right to appoint the returning officer, but they must appoint him from the prescribed list of permanent public officials. If I am correct in the opinion, I think these officers are the sheriff, the pro-thonotary, and the registrar. At all events, there are three permanent stated officers and the Government must appoint one or other of them. Why cannot we have a similar provision in this Bill? If objection be taken that these three officers are provincial officers, then, as I have already said, the fact that they are provincial officers is no more a disqualification than the appointment by the Dominion Goverftment is a disqualification in respect of a judge. In both cases you have men discharging, with a sense of responsibility, a judicial function, or what is to some extent a judicial function. But if there is anything in the point that because officers are appointed by the provincial government they are disqualified, then let us enlarge the list and say that the Dominion Government shall select as returning officer a person from a class on a prescribed list; and if the three officials named in the province of Quebec, or the sheriff named in Nova Scotia, are not enough, then put on the list, if you like, one or two responsible officers appointed by the Dominion. My point is this: I do not think that the Government should have the power, as they now have, to go out on the street and select any partisan and appoint him as a returning officer. I want them to exercise their power, but I desire to see them exercise it with the limitation that they shall appoint to this high and important office some man who has already a fixed status in the country, a man who

holds a responsible office, either local or Dominion, and who can therefore be held accountable for his acts. I submit in all sincerity to the Government of the day that in seeking the continuation of the present system,, whereby they can take any partisan they choose and appoint him to the position of returning officer, they are exercising a dangerous power; and if the Government desire to make this Bill as fair and equitable as it is their avowed intention to make it- I am accepting their assurance in that regard-I ask them very earnestly to give careful consideration to what I have said touching the selection of returning officers.
Let us turn to the question of provincial lists. My hon. friend the Acting Solicitor General (Mr. Guthrie) argued at considerable length to prove that this Parliament has the power to enact a Dominion Franchise law. Well, Mr. Speaker, I really do not know why the hon. gentleman devoted so much time to that point. I do not think that any one ever disputed the power of Parliament to pass a Dominion Franchise Law. I am quite sure that Edward Blake and the other great men to whom reference was made never for one moment set up the contention that the passing of a Dominion Franchise Act was beyond the jurisdiction of the Parliament of Canada. It was not a question of constitutional power or of constitutional jurisdiction; it was a question of public convenience and public advantage; it was a question of public economy. I think it is a great pity we could not have in every province provincial lists adopted for Dominion purposes. I can see great advantages in that if it were possible. The preparation of these lists is a matter of great trouble and expense, sometimes of worry and annoyance, to men interested in politics. It is a pity we have to have trouble of that kind in the preparation of one list, and it is doubly a pity that we should have to go to the same trouble and expense a second time for a Dominion list. I repeat that the question is one of public convenience and not of constitutional power. I have had such strong views on that question that a great many years ago, in the early days of my political experience in Nova Scotia-more years ago than I care to confess-I remember sending a telegram to Sir John Macdonald offering the suggestion-for the franchise question was then up at Ottawa-that instead of quarreling about lists a conference should be called of the Dominion and provincial governments with a view to agreeing upon some basis of lists that both could accept. Unfortunately that view
was not taken. My hon. friend, the Acting Solicitor General yesterday read an extract from a speech delivered by Sir John Thompson who said that there was so little difference between the Dominion and provincial franchise that there was no reason for maintaining the separation. I quite agree. But if the difference was so slight that there was no need for two law's, what need should there be for two lists? For obvious reasons, we should favour the adoption of provincial lists generally, if it rwere (possible, but we know that it is not possible because the Mists of the several provinces differ so widely. In Quebec the women are not on the list, and clearly, if we are to carry out the purpose of this House, so far as that province is concerned, there must be some machinery for enrolling the women of Quebec. In that case you cannot adopt the provincial list as it stands. In the case of Prince Edward Island, there are no lists at all. A man comes to the poll and swears that he has the right to vote, and he votes. Speaking generally, I think that is a dangerous practice. Prince Edward Island is a happy, prosperous community where everyone knows everyone else, and there is no room for dispute regarding any one's qualifications down there. That province is the most prosperous part of the Dominion of Canada. There are none who are very rich and none very poor; everyone knows his neighbour, and there are no possibilities of dispute. But when you adopt generally the principle in vogue in that province you will have men coming up to the poll at the last moment and getting on the list by simply Swearing that they have the right to he placed on it. As I say, that is a dangerous principle. I am afraid that you cannot adopt the provincial lists generally. Let me say, however, that the provincial lists ought to be encouraged wherever they exist and are fair and reasonable. What I am about .to say by way of illustration concerns Nova Scotia, but it may, I think, be said as well concerning New Brunswick. I think that conditions are much the same in these two provinces, hut my hon. friends from New Brunswick will speak for themselves. There is no reason why the lists of .the province of Nova Scotia made up under the existing law should not he accepted as a* finality, and When the Government proposes to appoint A, B, and C, possibly their own partisans, to get out and add to that list or take from it, I think they are making a grave mistake. Whatever may be said about the other provinces, the lists are made up in Nova Scotia in a way which

I believe leaves no room for dispute. What is the method? The foundation of the electoral list in Nova Scotia is the assessment roll. The property qualification in Nova Scotia is so small that I agree with the statement that it is virtually manhood suffrage. The revisors are' not appointed by the Government of Nova Scotia but by the municipal councils. They take the first assessment roll as a basis. That assessment roll indicates the names of all persons who are assessed as owners of property, to a very modest extent, as tenants of property, also to a moderate degree, as sons of tenants, sons of owners, sons of farmers. Practically speaking, it gets down almost to a basis of manhood suffrage. A public notice is given of a day when the revisers will meet for the purpose of making further inquiry. The lists as prepared by the officers are posted up, the officers hold a meeting, and those concerned add to the list or take from it as the case may be. The lists are then made up. Is there no appeal? Yee, there is an appeal to the sheriff. I suppose my hon. friend from Annapolis (Mr. Davidson) from his interruption a moment ago, considers that that is no appeal at all. The sheriffs of Nova Scotia are as much a judicial body, lacking only in volume of dignity, as the judges of our country. They hold their offices by a tenure almost as secure as that of the judges. There was a time many years ago when the sheriffs held their offices from year to year. That has passed away and the sheriff is now appointed not for life, but during good behaviour, and he can only be removed for cause. Let me illustrate the character of these men from my own experience. There are two counties -Queen's and Shelburne-

I want to illustrate the character of these sheriffs to show that they are a body deserving of respect. It is a fact that they are appointed during good behaviour. I want to give an illustration from my own constituency. I happen to represent two counties. In these counties there are two sheriffs and the junior of these two sheriffs is the senior in the mat-

ter of the years of his official life of all the judges in the province of Nova Scotia. He is a man of longer experience in official life than any member of the bench of Nova Scotia. The junior of these two men has been in office for thirty-six years. He is the sheriff of the county of Queens. The sheriff of the county of Shelburne has been in office for forty-three years. The sheriff of the county of Shelburne, Mr. George Maclean, a most respected Conservative, was appointed many, many years ago by a Conservative Government. He was in office when I and my friends came into power in 1882. He was continued as a capable and respected official and he has been there for forty-three years, a man who has performed the duties of his office, as sheriff and returning officer, in a manner that has won the respect and confidence of the people at large. These happen to be the older sheriffs in the province. Other hon. gentlemen who are familiar with the sheriffs in other counties will be able to testify that the sheriffs of Nova Scotia are a body well qualified to act as a court of appeal in the revising of the lists and although there may be some party strife I think we all agree that the manner in which the sheriffs of Nova Scotia discharge their duties is satisfactory to all political parties. Therefore I want to suggest now in regard to the provincial lists, whatever may happen with other provinces, because in Canada conditions vary, that the Government consider the manner in which the lists in each province are made up and that, unless they have some reason to believe that the lists are made up in a partisan and unfair manner, they accept the lists as a finality and do not appoint any parties of their own to go out and put names on, or take them off and make up whole new lists for themselves. In the interest of fair play I ask it; in the interest of economy I ask it. It means a waste of time and money to get out a second list under conditions of that character. I think the situation is much the same in New Brunswick but again I say I must not speak too positively as to that.
My only purpose at present is to offer the Government in all good faith two suggestions., The first is that you amend your present system of appointing returning officers. If it is necessary to show how that system has been abused I shall be prepared to do so but I do not want to raise that question now. As I am not dealing with individual cases; I am only dealing with principles. I would suggest that the Gov-

ernment adopt a prescribed list of officials from whom they shall select their returning officers and if there is any fear that the provincial officers are prejudiced then put on your prescribed list some Dominion official who can be called upon to act as a returning officer and who would be a responsible citizen known to everybody. Let that be done instead of appointing a man particularly for the occasion.
The second point is that inasmuch as I believe the lists of Nova Scotia are fairly made and there is no reason why they should not be accepted, I want to suggest to the Government that as respects that province unless somebody can show that the lists are not fairly made, these lists be accepted as a finality and that this Government shall not send out men to disturb lists of that kind.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think the hon. Minister of Militia and Defence (Mr. Guthrie) should be congratulated upon the very able address with which he favoured this House in introducing the Franchise Bill. Although we have had in this Parliament such great men as Macdonald, Blake, Mackenzie, Aylesworth and others and although a review of the history of Parliament presents many notable figures, I think we will come to the conclusion that we have a degree of talent in the House to-day equal to that at any period in its history. It seems to me that while honouring the memory of the able men of those early days we should not be unmindful of the quality of the men that we have in this House to-day. If I chose, I think I could name many members who are sitting in the House to-day who could be truly compared with the great men of former years.
The hon. the leader of the Opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King), in replying to the speech of the hon. the Minister of Militia and Defence laboured very strenuously in his criticism of the Franchise Bill. His attempt was a complete failure. His particular effort seemed to be to inform the House that while he was offering a criticism of the Bill, at a later period, when it came before the committee, he would reserve the right to further criticize it and possibly suggest many amendments. I feel, Mr. Speaker, that he has need to make a greater effort if he wishes to be more successful than he did yesterday.
The Minister of Militia and other members of" the Government, with the ability which they possess, have prepared what
may be a fair Bill but there possibly will be some amendments to be made to it. In fact there are some amendments that they have consented to make. But I think there should be other amendments. I think the Government should consider the disfranchising of slackers, deserters, evaders and alien enemies. When I speak of this class of citizens I might remind the House that we have had some experience. We need only go back a few months and recall what took place in the great city of Winnipeg. There we found a class of people who were creating a great deal of trouble and who undertook to cause a rebellion that might have spread throughout the Dominion and become a very serious matter for the country at large. However, it was checked. These people were principally foreigners but amongst them were a few Canadians who had held prominent positions including some clergymen who had associated themselves with these foreigners and aliens in the effort to create a rebellion in this country. That being so there is still danger to be feared from the actions of the "Reds" or Bolshevists of whom we have many thousands in Canada. There should be some check on this class of people and they should not be permitted to dictate, or to voice their views, as to how the country should be governed, or offer themselves for public positions, neither should they be permitted to participate in the enactment of legislation. In my opinion this class should be disfranchised and the present Bill should be amended so as to bring about that result. In order to retain control over these people either the War-time Elections Act should be continued or the present Bill should be amended in the desired direction.
We must consider the sentiments of the people of Ontario and of Manitoba and the other Western Provinces with respect to slackers, deserters and evaders. We should heed the desire expressed in regard to these persons not only by returned soldiers, but by. the mothers, wives and sisters of men who fought at the front, and who say that these undesirable individuals should not enjoy the rights of free citizenship. I think I am safe in saying that hundreds of thousands of worthy citizens throughout the Dominion have given utterance to that sentiment. In my travels throughout the Dominion, from the Atlantic to the Pacific, I have found that a general feeling exists in favour of the disfranchisement of these undesirable characters, and that the aliens

especially should be deprived of the franchise for some years to come. During the war we had to intern many thousands of these aliens in order to prevent them from destroying the property and probably even going further and destroying life, and the adoption of the necessary safeguards involved the Dominion in millions of dollars of expense. I do not think that these people have changed materially in their sentiments since the war was brought to a close, and therefore the Government would be well advised to enact such amendments to the present Bill as will disfranchise them until they have demonstrated themselves to be suitable citizens. They should not be allowed to be candidates for office or register a vote at any election in this country. It is not asking too much to insist upon that course. All slackers, deserters and evaders should be disfranchised for at least ten years. 1 have heard it even suggested that the period of disfranchisement be extended to twenty or twenty-five years, but the shorter time proposed will give us a chance to judge as to their qualifications for citizenship. It is not fair to those gallant men who freely volunteered their services to defend this country and the rest of the British Empire that slackers and men of a similar type should have as free a voice in the making of the country's laws as should be enjoyed by those who underwent such great sacrifices. To any such proposition as that I say No.
When it became necessary to reinforce the ranks of our gallant men who were fighting overseas and the Military Service Act was called into operation, many young men who should have been in the ranks of the defenders of this country fled to the backwoods and even crossed to the United States to avoid military service. Perhaps if these young men had been left alone they would have accepted conscription and would not have been characterized so unworthily as evaders. Unfortunately they were badly advised, by certain of the Liberal press. Doubtless if good counsel had been extended to them many of these men would have gone overseas without any compulsion. But the advice given to them was bad, perhaps even pressure was brought to bear upon them. They acted upon that advice and failed to rally to the defence of this country. Why then should the same treatment be extended to these young men as is enjoyed by those who fought and bled for their country and the Empire?
It would almost appear as though the underlying motive with some persons in

their antagonism to our war efforts was to sacrifice the English and preserve the young Frenchmen of Quebec. Doubtless many hon. gentlemen opposite will dispute the existence of any such motive; but I have heard it stated by many citizens throughout Canada that there appeared to be in the province of Quebec a desire to conserve the lives of the young French-Canadians and to sacrifice men of British birth so that those who had thus been preserved to the detriment of the British-born might be free to engage in a policy of expansion having for its object the securing of control in the other provinces of the Dominion.
We have been told by the hon. member for Red Deer that we should get rid of "the war mind." How is it possible to get rid of the war mind when we recall the numerous slackers, deserters and evaders who have shirked their duty in Canada? It is all very well to talk of getting rid of the war feeling, but that feeling has been so strongly impressed upon the minds of people in the majority of homes in this country by the actions of those individuals to whom I have referred that it is very hard to eradicate.
, The hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Clark) asks us to help , heal the wounds of war. Who created 'the wounds of war? The slackers, the deserters, the draft evaders- men who refused to do their duty in their country's hour of need. How can we heal the wounds of war, Mr. Speaker, when those wounds are so impressed on the minds of our people? It is all very well for the hon. member for Red Deer, who, as well as his brave sons, did their duty nobly and well, to preach reconciliation, but he must remember that all minds do not think alike, ,and he must permit those who lost their loved ones at the front to express their opinions as to how soon they will be prepared to forget iand forgive. I venture to say that it will take a lifetime to erase from their minds the impressions created by the war.
In some parts of the Dominion we had the experience of practically no response from young men to do their duty, notwithstanding the efforts of the Government by voluntary pnlistment and, that having failed, by conscription, to bring those young men to a sense of their obligations to fight for their country. Indeed, the attempt to enforce the Military Service Act led to riots in some parts of the Dominion, and we heard the threat made that rather than obey the law those men would create a revolution. I submit, Sir, that it was not creditable to en-

courage that condition of affairs, and it seems to me that a great deal of the responsibility for this revolutionary sentiment is upon the shoulders of many of the priests and bishops and public men of this Dominion. It has been said by bon. members that there should be no ill-feeling amongst th'e people of the various provinces, but when we remember such instances of disloyalty it forces us to the conclusion that it will take many years to restore the oldtime harmony that existed in this country. Had those who were so anxious to give advice attended to their own business I believe conditions would have been entirely different. I do not blame those young men, but I do blame their advisers. I firmly be-Jieve that we shall not be able to overcome the lack of harmony created by such improper advice for perhaps another forty years.

The matter has been pretty well discussed, particularly by the hon. member for North Waterloo (Mr. Euler), who has pointed out the great injustice that is about to be done to a large proportion of our population. 1 may say that it is not in any spirit of selfinterest that I am taking part in the debate, because, owing to the Military Service Act, those who were inclined to support me did not get an opportunity to do so.
I may also say that I was not, as was charged by the hon. member for Frontenac (Mr. Edwards) against another hon. member (Mr. Pardee) elected by reason of the Military Service Act. I submit, Mr. Speaker, there must have been a tremendous difficulty in the Unionist party when of two members elected on the same ticket one cannot withdraw from that party without the other taunting him that he could never have been elected had it not been for that Adt.

speechtext:
I find the following passage in the unrevised Hansard report of the hon. gentleman's speech:
The hon. gentleman is very bold and very courageous in stating to this House and to the country that he does not care a button whether his course is popular or unpopular. Just a short time ago he was perfectly willing, when he was seeking election in 1917. to avail himself of the measure disfranchising some people whom to-day he says it would be a crying shame to disfranchise.
A little later in the course of his speech the hon. gentleman (Mr. Edwards) said:
The hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat (Mr. Pardee) in the election of 1917 was not only perfectly willing, but anxious to avail himself of the Act which was passed enabling him to get his seat in the House.
Is that clear? Will the hon. gentleman accept Hansard?

speechtext: I said that he was willing to take advantage of the Act which gave him the soldier votes.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
