speechtext: "To get his seat in the House."

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
subsubtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON SECOND READING OF BILE NO. 12.
speechtext: That does not say that the soldier vote elected him. That is what my hon. friend said; I did not say that.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
subsubtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON SECOND READING OF BILE NO. 12.
speechtext:
"Enabling him to get his seat in the House " and " being elected ''-there may be some distinction between those two statements, but there is very little difference. With regard to the Bill itself and the promise that has been made by the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Meighen) that some changes will be made in the most contentious clause-clause 29- I may say that certain hon. members from the eastern part of Canada, judging from their remarks regarding the people affected by this Bill, would lead one to believe that there is something wrong with those people,-that they are so wild and unprogressive that we would he better rid of them. I think the member for Frontenac (Mr. Edwards) said: We do not want them; let us get rid of them, or words to that effect. But let us go outside of this Parliament and take the statement of a man to whom frequent reference is made in this House, the man who is able to, handle the largest spending department of the Government. I refer to Mr. D. B. Hanna. I remember his appearing before a committee of some members of this House and pointing out that some of the most productive districts in the North-west Territories were settled by Austrians. He pointed to a certain line along which these people had located and said that more was being produced along that line than in any other part of Canada. These people, he said, are our hope for the West; some day they will be our best citizens.

I ask hon. gentlemen what is the matter with these people? What is the charge against them? What have they ever done that they should be discriminated against or singled out for special treatment? Let us take the history of these people. They came to this country at the invitation of the Government of the day; they settled on land that was not cleared; in many cases they took sections en bloc in order that they anight be together, and often they got the very worst kind of land. But they were encouraged to settle on it, and to-day wherever they are, they are producing more per acre than any other class in the whole of the Western territory. What have they done? Have they not been as progressive as others? Do they not produce as much? What was their attitude when the war broke out? An hon. gentleman on the other side of the House has said that thousands of them left his district and enlisted in our Forces. In some cases they changed their nationality in order to be able to enlist. They wanted to become Canadians; they wanted to serve Canada. I may say in passing that they are a people who bring no national pride with them; you never hear them boast of their country, as the Americans and the Old Country people do. The Austrian never says anything about the country that he came from, though after he learns English he may tell you what part of Ontario he had been in. He wants to be a Canadian citizen. He does not want to be an Austrian all his life; he never intended such a thing. But apparently we do not want to let him become a Canadian. If the member for St. Antoine (Sir Herbert Ames) were here he would bear me out when I say that the provincial constituency of Whitford in Alberta, largely peopled by Ukrainians, was the first constituency in that province, or perhaps, in any province, to make a voluntary assessment upon themselves of $5 each per month for the Patriotic Fund. Afterwards they went further and subscribed another $5, making the contribution $10 per month from every homesteader in that district. So that from that point of view they appear to be good citizens. The very fact that the 218th Regiment was made up of ninety per cent of that class of the people shows that they were willing to serve their country.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
subsubtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON SECOND READING OF BILE NO. 12.
speechtext: What was the other name of the 218th Regiment?

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
subsubtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON SECOND READING OF BILE NO. 12.
speechtext: I believe it was called the " Cornwall Cossacks."

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
subsubtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON SECOND READING OF BILE NO. 12.
speechtext: It was the "Irish Guards," was it not?

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
subsubtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON SECOND READING OF BILE NO. 12.
speechtext:
They were called the Irish Guards first and afterwards the Cornwall Cossacks. But that only goes to support my statement that the majority of them were of that class. That nickname was applied to them because most of the men were of Austrian birth, but they did good service.
Now, it appears that these people have been willing both to assist patriotic movements and to serve their country in the military forces. Moreover, hundreds of them got past the recruiting officers and went to the war; yet under the provisions of an Act similar to this the wives, mothers, sisters and brothers of these people were cheated out of their vote in the election of 1917-that is, if you like to call it an election. I never considered it an election; in my opinion it was a revolution. A revolution is usually organized and carried out for the purpose of removing from office a Government that cannot be dislodged by constitutional means, but this revolution was organized and carried out for the purpose of continuing in office a Government which could not remain in office by constitutional means. This revolution has had no parallel on this continent, unless it be in Mexico and some of the other Latin republics.
While on this subject I wish to read from a local paper to show what is the spirit of the Ukrainians in the Western country. A body of Ukrainian farmers, about the time the Soldiers' Land Settlement scheme was inaugurated, held a meeting and adopted the following resolution:
We, the Ukrainian farmers assembled at this meeting, hereby volunteer and promise to gratuitously help any returned soldiers settling In my district on the land by offering to do all the required improvements on their farms, such as hauling lumber, erecting buildings and fences, clearing, breaking and discing the land, and will also arrange to do all necessary work with our teams and machinery during the seeding and harvesting operations, free of charge.
Yet some people say they are against the soldier. The resolution continues:
We also wish to solemnly assure such newcomers that friendly help will be at their disposition, and they will not suffer any want or hardships of a beginner. And we will greatly appreciate the presence of the returned man in our communities who would be able, willing and anxious to teach us the great British ideals, to promote our loyalty and to help us to attain the standard of British citizenship.
Knowing that the soldiers who would take up land would have difficulties to meet, these people determined to make it as easy for the soldiers as possible and solemnly pledged themselves to give them assistance.

Governments, like people, sometimes have suspicions that are not well founded. Shortly after the war broke out the Government called from their duties certain members of the Royal Northwest Mounted Police. I was for many years a member of that body. It is an organization that has a splendid record for efficiency; no organization of its kind has had so few failures recorded against it. Well, these men moved about among the Austrians and people of that class in the West, not in uniform but in civilian clothes, putting forward one pretext or another-the pretext of buying cattle or of looking for land; and during four years of this ferret work they never found one man in Victoria district guilty of uttering a word of sedition. Why be suspicious about a class of people like this? * If you go into some other sections among the Scotch, you will find somebody who is dissatisfied and making criticisms in connection with the conduct of the war. I do not know whether or not you can find any such people amongst the Irish. There is, however, no reason at all for these suspicions, because those people have never done anything to warrant them.
Let me take another class of people with whom this measure is going to deal harshly. I know of a man of the nationality to which I refer who comes under this Act, who sent his boy to the war, and his boy is still over there and will remain there. Under this measure, if it passes, that man, now that his son does not give him a vote, is disfranchised and he cannot vote in the next election. Another case which I know is that of an Englishman, British-born, married to a German girl, and there is a good deal of intermarriage of that kind in this country. They had three children, one boy being nine years old, and although that man made the supreme sacrifice, his wife is not entitled to vote under this legislation. That may be justice; it may be freedom ; it may be the way to build up national unity, but it does not look like that to me. I am sorry the Acting Prime Minister (Sir George Foster) is not in the House, for two reasons, one being that I wished to compliment him on the splendid speech he made the other day when he said that we should have more tolerance; that we should get closer together; that while it was very easy, sitting in private, side by side, to agree, when we got into the House, differences arose. I should like to submit to him the case of two neighbours of mine who came to this country possibly thirty years ago, farmed side by side; who paid the
same taxes, who went through this period of development, suffering hardships side by side, each man doing his part to develop and make a great country of Canada. Then, when an election comes along, although they pay the same share in taxes and every thing else, one man is disfranchised while the other is permitted to exercise his franchise. iSuch a condition of things is unfair whatever way you view it.
Another case which I should like to mention is that of a man, honest and good enough to pay an income tax on $11,000 of his profits, paying it cheerfully. This man sent his eldest son to France and he is still overseas and will remain there, but his father is disfranchised under this measure. We know that this present Government and'the Conservative Government before it have at least the reputation of dividing the Canadian people into two classes. It is chai'ged to them, and I think everybody who knows anything about the matter will say, that they are to blame for whatever disunion there exists at the present day. If the Acting Prime Minister were in his seat, I should like to appeal to him, because judging by the speech he made the other day I do not believe that this Bill suits him very well. Although he is only Acting Prime Minister for a short period of time, let it not be said that under his regime he is creating another unnecessary division. These people of whom I speak and who are disfranchised will, as long as they live, be called alien Canadians; they cannot get away from that. We have the French Canadian and the English Canadian, but these people will be distinguished by being called alien Canadians, and there is not much chance of building up, and it is a waste of time and energy for any one to speak of unity in Canada when 5 p.m. every session, one after another, the Government brings down legislation that divides people further and further apart. I do not expect that there will be any fairness in this Bill. I feel somewhat as the hon. member for Edmonton East (Mr. H. A. Mackie) does about the Bill. He said: We shall have another Act that will win our elections by disfranchising. He suggested to the Government that they should go further and do the thing right and disfranchise all but those who voted for Union Government last time. I will go one better than my hon. friend; I will raise the " ante " and say that there is no need at this time to go to the expense of a general election. Money is very hard to get, and this measure is framed in such a way

that you can have out of it pretty nearly any result you wish. My suggestion is that there should be one man appointed by the Government to decide the political complexion of each district and that the Government should be allowed to appoint that man.
Mr. H. A. MACKIiE: My hon. friend agrees with me that we ought to disfranchise every one who voted against the Government?

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
subsubtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON SECOND READING OF BILE NO. 12.
speechtext: No, I was supporting the suggestion of my hon. friend by going him one better. The suggestion was yours and 'I made it better. My hon. friend thought- that would be a good idea.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
subsubtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON SECOND READING OF BILE NO. 12.
speechtext: Even at that the Government would not be safe.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
subsubtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON SECOND READING OF BILE NO. 12.
speechtext: ll do not think I have anything to add, but ll am sorry I cannot hope for any success, because the policy of the Government seems to be "safety first." That is the game they are playing. This Bill is, for this side of the House, a little worse than the other election law, a lid for hon. members opposite, a little better. They are exercising their privilege of making laws with majorities, and I suppose they will continue to do so as long as the people permit them. I wanted to do my duty, in fairness to many citizens although they will never have an opportunity to support me or, for that matter, to vote against me, in bringing this matter to the attention of the House and in endeavouring to find out what reasons the Government have for so unfairly discriminating against these people.

speakeroldname: Mr. S. W. JACOBS (Georges Etienne Cartier):
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
subsubtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON SECOND READING OF BILE NO. 12.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, representing one of the most cosmopolitan constituencies in the Dominion of Canada, I feel that I cannot allow this debate to conclude without offering a few observations, reserving any extended remarks which I may have to make when the. Bill reaches the committee stage. I have not had the time to peruse with -care the Bill as it is before the House; but I have read several sections of it, and in my remarks I wish particularly to deal with those. Perhaps, inasmuch as I have not read this measure, I may be considered to be in the same position as the famous Sydney Smith who said that he never read a book before he reviewed it, because it prejudiced him so. The origin of some of the principles embodied in this Bill will be found in the Act which was passed in

the session of 1919; that is, in the By-elections Act, and the part of it to which I wish to refer particularly is that which deals with the naturalization of married women. The House will remember that when that Bill came before the House in July, 1919, I made a somewhat vigorous attack on the principle enunciated and in the clause of that Bill to which I am about to refer. Notwithstanding anything that we on this side of the House had to say, the Bill went through, and probably the Government find that it has worked so well that they want to perpetuate it in the Bill now before us.
I should like to know from the Acting Solicitor General or from the Government, why a distinction is made in the matter of naturalization and in the matter of voting, between women born on the North American continent and women born on the continent of Europe. Is it because women on this continent are more intelligent? Ts it because they are more refined? Or is it because they understand the advantages of voting for Union Government? What is the reason that women born on the continent of North America are placed in a category by themselves and in a higher class than are women born in Europe? Under this law, if it passes, you will find a full-blooded negress of San Domingo; a daughter of a Mexican greaser; a Mulatto from the State of Georgia, having greater rights in this country as voters, than the most refined and cultured womanhood of France, Belguim or any other continental Euiopean country. This is not a matter which affects enemy alien countries at all; it is not a matter that appertains only to Germany and Austria. It declares in so many words that any woman who comes from the continent of Europe is obliged to obtain personal naturalization from a judge of the district in which she lives before she can exercise the right to vote, while this negress from San Domingo will have the right to vote simply upon going to the poll and declaring that she is the wife of so-and-so, who happens to be a British subject. Is not that grotesque; is it not ridiculous; is it not something that brings the laws of this country into disrepute? Why, under this law the late respected Duchess of Connaught, if she were alive, and living in this country, would have no vote whatever; hut her cook or housemaid, or some person who happened to be imported from Alabama, would have the right to vote. I leave that thought with our super-patriots on the other side of the House.

I should like to. say a word or two with regard to the naturalization of alien enemies and the postponing of their naturalization and concomitant right to vote until the expiry of ten years after the' close of the war. There seems to be an idea among the members of this House, and *qven outside of this House, that we are excluding from naturalization the whole of Austria and Germany; that is to say, that every one who comes to this country from what were Austria and Germany will not be able to secure naturalization until the expiry of the ten-year period. That is not the fact. We are excluding from naturalization only those people from the portions of these countries that are still named, Austria, Germany, Bulgaria and Turkey. Austria to-day is dismembered. There is in that country a population of something like five or six milloins, in Vienna and the surrounding neighbourhood. Piactically the whole of Austria, or fifty-five millions of people, now comprises Jugo-Slavia, Czechoslovakia, Roumania and other countries surrounding Austria. The man in Canada from Vienna will not be allowed to exercise the franchise, but the man from Prague will have that right because he comes from Bohemia. The citizen from Cracow will be given the right to vote because he comes from what is now Poland, while citizens from any of the other places ll have mentioned will also be accorded the privilege by reason of the fact that they hail from countries that no longer form a part of the new Austria. I ask hon. members, is that a protection to this country? Are we protected when we give the right to vote to fifty-five millions cif former alien enemies, and deprive of this right a paltry five or six millions living in what is now Austria? Take Alsace, which to-day is as much German as is Saxony. If Alsace had the right to declare by plebiscite whether it would elect to remain a part of Germany or be a part of France, it would no doubt choose to remain with Germany. But citizens of Alsace to-day will have the right to come here and in the ordinary course be naturalized after five years. Any man living in Danzig to-day-and no one can conceive of any place more German than that- has the right to come and be naturalized in the same way, as if he did not come from an enemy country. But the man from Berlin will have no right to vote. These are some of the anomalies in the Act which naturally attract the attention of even the . most superficial observer, and it seems to 49
me that the Government must give some good and valid reason why it should declare in the Act that some people of enemy alien origin have not the right to vote while others have. Let us be logical first.
I desire to say a few words regarding the Naturalization Act which was passed last year, and which is intimately associated with this Act. We have bQasted in this House for the last year or two, at least since the Peace Treaty was signed,-and no one was louder in his paeans of praise of our nationhood than the President of the Privy Council (Hon. Mr. Rowell)-that Canada has achieved k national status and is now in a position which it has never occupied before. Mr. Speaker, we have not re-written one line nor changed one tittle of the British North America Act, but it seems that by some unseen force the whole position of Canada has changed, and we have now an entirely new status. That being so, do you not think that it would be only right and just that we should have onr own Naturalization Act?. Why was it that, simultaneously with our achievement of this national status, we tore our Naturalization Act into a thousand pieces and threw it into the waste paper basket, and accepted the British Naturalization Law? Surely we should be able to declare who is a British subject in Canada and who is not. Yet, when I ask the Acting Solicitor General why he did not allow these two Acts, the Imperial Naturalization Act and the Dominion Act, to function side by side, so that we could take our choice either of the Act conferring the right of British citizenship in Canada after three years, or the other extending the period to five years, the hon. member informed me:	"We have
only the Imperial Naturalization Act; we have not the right to draw up a different Naturalization Act and place it on the statute book, we must take the Naturalization Act dictated and written by Downing street and sent to us, and if we do not taKc it we shall get nothing." And we took it; we swallowed the dose, nauseous though it may have been.
I do not wish at this stage of the debate to go into the question of the advisability or justice of having in this country three different classes of citizens, first, the British citizen who has the right to vote; secondly the potential British citizen who will have the right to vote ten years after the expiration of the war; and, thirdly, the citizen who does not intend to become naturalized at all. Under the ancient system in England-and in Russia it continued, I think, down to 1862,-there were three classes of



citizens, first the free man; second, the serf; and third, the slave. We are making serfs Mr. Speaker, of these people to whom we deny the vote in the regular way. Here are people who come to- Canada, having selected this country from among all the countries in the world as that m which they should like to live and bring up their families, and where they expect to die. they have left their native country because they are dissatisfied with conditions at home, they are dissatisfied with the life lived there and with the class distinctions that prevail in their society. We admit them to this country, and mark you, Mr.' Speaker, before they are admitted they are examined through a microscope by the Immigration Department. The Department of Immigration have page after page of rules in regard to the admission of foreigners into this country. One who reads that list of rules would imagine that people thus selected are too good for this world, that they are as white as the driven snow and that they have to be 100 per cent perfect before they come into this country and are received by the immigration officers. They must be mentally perfect, they must be perfect physically, and they must never have declared any views in regard to constituted government-they must never have said that they wished to forcibly remove the autocrat of Russia or the Kaiser at Berlin When it is found that they have complied with all these requirements we permit them in the goodness of our hearts, to come into Canada. They are perfect, in so far as respectability is concerned when they enter. But they do not know about our naturalization law and they find that they have to wait ten years before they can be permitted to make the declaration: Civis Britannicus sum.
Why should they want to come to this country? They can go to the United States, reside there for five years and have conferred upon them the rights of American Citizenship, land those rights they hold against the world. If a man i.s a respectable citizen and if he is qualified in regard to the immigration rules, he is permitted to enter the United States and the test is one of character and not geography. But for some reason known only to the Government, hon. gentlemen fear that people who come from these countries may vote against [DOT] the Unionist Government. Judging from the lurid picture painted last night by the. hon. member for Frontenac (Mr. Edwards) who said that they aTe the worst people in the world and that the door should be closed 
to them for all time, that they are traitors, and so on, one would imagine that these were a very bad lot, but all I have to say is that if 'they are only half as Prussian as the member for Frontenac they would qualify as voters on the Unionist side.
When these people can go to the United States and be received as citizens after five years' residence, why should they want to come to Canada; why should a German want to come to Canada? We are not offering any advantages to him; we * are declaring in our laws that he is to be put in a class 'by himself, that he is to be a pariah among our people, that he must breathe the free atmosphere of Canada for ten years before he is entitled to the rights of citizenship and that at the expiration of that time we, in the goodness of our hearts, may take him in. The hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Clark) yesterday said something that I consider a truism. He said that people may chew together, or they may smoke together or perchance they may drink together, but when they go to the polls they cannot vote together. Do you think that makes for harmony in this country;-does it not rather make tor intolerance? The rank and file of our own people are the proper judges of these things, and it is the rank and file of our own people that the alien comes in contact with. What will be the impression of the Canadian citizen bom in humble circumstances who happens to fraternize with an alien in the village or on the farm, whom he finds to be quite a respectable person and fit to associate with his wife and family when he discovers that that alien is denied the privileges which, he himself possesses and for a reason which he cannot understand? The fact is that when this Bill becomes la-w it is going to prove a boomerang to those who are its authors. The Government will find that every man who is now denied the right to vote, when he does get that right after a period of ten years, will have his reckoning with the party and the Government.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to point out the anomalies, the absurdities, the grotesqueness of this Bill. It is practically impossible to discuss this Bill, in its ref-

*erences to naturalization, without referring to the Naturalization Act. I am attacking the Government not only because of the terms of the Bill now before the House, but the provisions in that measure with respect-to naturalization. They deprive us of the Naturalization Act under which we worked successfully for so many years. I charge that upon the Government and I say it is because of the fact that these people who are affected not only suffer the loss of their vote,.but will be unable to obtain the most elementary rights of citizenship.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I have concluded what I desired to say on that phase of the subject but I shall have something further to say when the Bill goes into committee. I was not in the House yesterday when the Acting Solicitor General stated that he understood some one had made the remark that there was a joker in the Bill but that for himself he wished to say that he knew of no such joker. There may be no joker in the Bill but there are in it a few jokes which I have endeavoured to point out to the House. I trust that before the Bill emerges from committee we will have full opportunity of dealing further with it, and that after the anvil pounding which we may have to bring to bear upon the measure it will be something less objectionable than it is in its present shape.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
subsubtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON SECOND READING OF BILE NO. 12.
speechtext:
I do not intend to occupy the time of the House at any length upon the present occasion. I purpose making such remarks as I deem to be necessary, when the House is in committee and we can review the respective claiises. However the Acting Solicitor General was kind enough'when he presented the Bill to say that if anybody could discover grave difficulties in its application he would be prepared to accept amendments and remedy the defects so discovered. Well, Sir, taking that statement in conjunction with the one just made by the hon. gentleman who preceded me as to there being a joker in the Bill, I would like to call the minister's attention to what might possibly be the joker in question. To-day we have heard a number of hon. gentlemen speak about the rights of different nationalities in connection with this Bill and the Naturalization Act. I had hoped that I would see some hon. gentleman opposite rise and speak in the name of the Democracy of England, and show how the poor Englishman is being treated under this Bill. So far, however, no one has taken that point, and therefore it falls to my lot to draw the minister's attention to the fact that under this Bill harsh treatment is 
meted out to residents in Englond. If the minister will kindly read section 38 of the Bill he will find the following clause:	-
Except as in this Act otherwise provided any British subject, male or female, who is of the full age of twenty-one years, may be a candidate at a Dominion election.
That means that any gentleman living, say, in England, may be a candidate in our Federal elections-there is absolutely nothing to prevent him. But if that gentleman living in England should take it into his head to come over to this country and offer himself for election and ask the electors to refrain from voting for him or to vote for him, or should he have the hardihood to advance reasons why the electors should vote for him, then he falls immediately under the provisions of section 11 which the Government apparently overlooked when they drafted the Bill and commits an indictable offence, which seems hardly fair. Let us read section 11:
Any person, not being an elector, who resides without Canada and who. to secure the election of any candidate, canvasses for votes or in any way endeavours to induce voters to vote for any candidate at an election, or to refrain from voting, is guilty of an indictable offence against this Act punishable as in this Act provided.
The Minister of the Interior being a shrewd and very capable lawyer, will see right away, or I am a very dull lawyer, that any gentleman residing, say in the city of London or in any part of England, may under section 38 become a candidate for this House, tout if he attempts to say a word as to why he should be elected, then anybody in the country who wishes to bring a charge against him for so doing, can land him in jail. Now, hon. gentlemen have spoken about the Austrians, about the Germans, and about men of different nationalities. I do not claim any great intimacy with the Germans or with the Austrians, which may be my great misfortune, but I do know something about England and about Englishmen, and I am a great admirer of the democracy of England. I am a greater admirer of the democracy of England than I am of the laws of England, and I believe this to be a case in which the Englishman should get fair play. I bring this point to the attention of the Government and I say further that whereas I have found in the perusal of this Bill innumerable clauses that are jokes, and mean when the House resolves itself into Committee to move to amend some of them; in the meantime the Acting Solicitor 'General

should see to it that the Englishman is properly treated by this Bill.

The second omission, Mr. Speaker, which I noticed in the remarks of the hon. Acting Solicitor General was that of a spirit of high statesmanship when he came to discuss the amendments to the electoral law of Canada introduced by the Laurier Government in 1908. The hon. gentleman told us that in 1908 he had supported amendments to the then Franchise Bill, and he gave us the reason why those amendments had been brought in. The way I wish to answer that part of my hon. friend's remarks is as follows: Either the vote given by the Acting Solicitor General in 1908 was a thoroughly honest vote

and I have no doubt that it was-and if such was the case I do not think that the Acting Solicitor General of Canada, speaking as such in the House of Commons, when introducing a Bill of such great moment as the Bill he introduced yesterday, should try to ridicule the Government of 1908 and their motives for

having afforded him the opportunity of giving a good vote. Or, Mr. Speaker, the ease may be the opposite, and the vote given by the hon. Acting Solicitor General in 1908 might not have been as good as I think it was. In such a case I think my hon. friend should not boast about it, because if he does we might have our doubts as to whether he is sincere-he must be- but we might have our doubts as to his sincerity on the present occasion.
The hon. Acting Solicitor General told us yesterday: "If there are any vices that can be remedied, if there is any flaw that can be removed, just point them out and I will be pleased to consider your suggestions." It is my intention to study most carefully and seriously the Bill when it comes in Committee of this House. And why so? Because the idea that the Acting Solicitor General may have of a vice or of a flaw may not be exactly the idea that I myself hold. When I consider the Votes and Proceedings of the Seventh Session of the Twelfth Parliament, that is, the session of 1917, I notice to my great surprise, although the hon. Acting Solicitor General yesterday afternoon told us that he had always fought in the fore ranks of the Liberal party, that during' that session he left his party and voted in favour of the War-times Election Act.
