maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext: We will go through the Bill and when we come to another clause Vhere notice is to be given, we can provide the mode by which notice shall be given.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext:
In all involved acts there is usually inserted a general clause to cover anything that might be unforeseen.
Mr.,TRAHAN: These general clauses are always dangerous.
Mr. GUTHRIE': It is more dangerous to have no general clause.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext: I would like to impress upon the minister the fact that for any public notice, especially if it is a general one, a handbill is a very dangerous proceeding. The whole principle of giving notice in important affairs of a public character imquestionably is to post something in the public office of the municipality wherever that may be. Every city, every township, has a place where certain noticeb for the public benefit must be posted, and really I think the least the returning officer, or any other election officer, can do, is to post up there within a certain specified time the notice which he desires the public to take cognizance of. Because, to leave it to a handbill simply means that the handbill may be thrown away, and that be the end of it.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext: IE my hon. friend (Mr. Burnham) would examine the Act he would not make suggestions of that kind. As I say, so far as I know, and I think I know the Bill pretty well, every case where notice is necessary is specially provided for. With respect to anything the returning officer. the deputy returning officer, the registrar, or the judge has to do there is an express -way of giving notice by posting, by registration, by publication in the newspapers. For every single case there is a specific provision. But it may be that same notice will be required that has not been provided for, and if so, rather than have no provision, we have a general clause. Take any important Act in the country, take the Municipal Act, and it is declared that in all other cases not otherwise provided for the advertisement shall be so-and-so. Under any general legislation occasion may arise when notice has to be given and there is nothing in the law which provides for it. This is intended only for cases not otherwise provided for. [DOT]

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext:
With all due deference to the minister and his reasoning I do not see why the analogy in the Bill itself should not be followed in a case not provided for. It is quite possible that something or other of an important nature may arise, not provided for by Parliament, which the election officer would treat as if it were of no importance whatever. He could give notice where it suited him, by handbill or othei* wise. It might be extremely bad whether and nobody would know where to go to find out about these things. Above everything else in the world in the matter of an election it is most important that a candidate or his agent should know what is going on by simply visiting a certain office-going
[.Mr. Guthrie.)
to a certain place and looking at the notice board to see if any new notice has been posted up. That is a precaution it is very easy to take. I am not at all convinced by the minister that because there may be some things unprovided, therefore the analogy in the very Bill itself should not be followed.
Mr. H. A. MAlCKIE: I agree with the clause and will give the committee an example of where it will be useful. Supposing you wanted to get a notice from Edmonton to Fort McMurray. There is no way in which notice can be given to a place three hundred miles away except by wire. Now supposing you wanted to give a notice to say to Fort Vermilion. There is no way in wdiich you can cover the distance of three hundred miles except by sending a telegram to Peace River, and from there you will have to go in three hundred miles on horseback. If there is not a general clause by which you may use some discretion to get over those distances in our country publication will be of no use. This clause provides for a method and gives the returning officer discretion to do what he thinks best under all these circumstances. The clause is quite an important one and should stand as it is because of the great distances we have to contend with in the western country.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext:
I would say in reply
to that, it is very easy for the man who has authority to send the telegram to say " Please post this telegram in the- usual place for the municipality."

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext: There is no such place.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext:
If there is no such
place then all I have to say is that whilst the principle would be violated there is no question it is not of much importance. I can assure the hon. gentleman however that in more thickly settled places, in cases that are not so extreme as the hon. member has just spoken of, it would be an exceedingly dangerous thing, if a candidate had a hostile returning officer or election agents who were unfavourably disposed to him or were themselves unscrupulous.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext:
In the case of Fort McMurray the only places we have for posting of notices are' the Hudson Bay Company's store and the office of the North Bay Transportation Company. The same at Fort Vermilion and also at Wabasca. The only places there are the Hudson Bay Agency and the Roman Catholic church. There" is no use in talking about Sending

out notices in the western country, we have not got the facilities for it.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext:
I am talking about
municipalities.
Section stands.
On section 5-printed documents to bear name, etc., of printer:

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext: This clause is the same as the one in the old Act, is it not?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext:
Under the old Act the
penalty for non-compliance with the provision was $200 and costs or six months.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext:
What is the
penalty for violation of the provision in this case?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext: It is much more serious.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext:
Would printing
cover typewriting?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext:
I do not know. It has been held in the province of Ontario that typewriting is printing. The clauses in regard to penalty will be found on page 67 commencing at section 84:
Any person who is guilty of any indictable offence against this Act is liable on indictment or on summary conviction to a fine not exceeding two thousand dollars and costs of prosecution or to imprisonment for a term not exceeding two years, with or without hard labour, or to both such fine and costs and such imprisonment, and if the fine and costs imposed are not paid forthwith (in case only a fine and costs are imposed) or are not paid before the expiration of the term of imprisonment imposed (in case imprisonment as well as fine and costs is imposed) to imprisonment with or without hard labour for such term (or such further term) as such fine and costs or either of them remain unpaid, not exceeding three months.
With respect to non-indictable offences the fines are less. They are dealt with by section 85.
On section 6-Removing notices forbidden.-Copy of subsection 1 to be printed on documents posted up.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext: If memory serves me right that is the old clause unchanged.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext: Is there any reason for repeating the penalty, of this section? It is all set out in section 84.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext: I would think that the provisions of section 84 applied to any offence under section 6. The latter section was taken bodily from the former election law, section 250A.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext: It seems to be needlessly encumbering the Statute.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext: But this section must be published.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext: Yes, there is some necessity for it. It has to be printed as a notice, and the notice would have to include the penalty. That is the object in view, I suppose.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext: Otherwise there would be no offence.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 7-Oaths, how administered.- Gratuitous Administration.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext: I suggest that " police magistrate " be added there. I have an unpleasant recollection of an election that I lost in Manitoba because those words were not in the Act.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext: The section now includes " a judge of any court, a notary public, a justice of the peace or a commissioner for taking affidavits having authority or jurisdiction within the place where the oath or affirmation is administered." Personally, I see no objection to including " police magistrate." If the words are to be included I would insert them after " justice of the peace " in line 33.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext: While we are adding a few words to this section I would suggest that we also add " stipendiary magistrate." He is not a justice qf the peace.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext: I think a stipendiary magistrate is a judge, but I see no objection to adding the words, " stipendiary magistrate, police magistrate," after the word " peace " in the thirty-third line.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext: I think it is worth while to have the French version before us while we are reading that section. The English version reads, " having authority or jurisdiction." Why is it that in the French version it is, " ayant autorite et jurisdiction." That is not a correct translation.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext: I can hardly be held responsible for the translation into French -I wish I could be. I am glad my hon. friend has mentioned that point. I think both versions should be the same.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext:
In the interpretation
clause, Air. Chairman, the word " judge " is defined. The definition is, ' judge ' includes chief justice." I would have less doubt about a chief justice being a judge

than I would about a stipendiary magistrate being one. If a chief justice is a judge, the puisne judges have not got much judgeship about th,em.	.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext: It is sometimes difficult to get-a justice of the peace in a polling booth when a deputy returning officer requires to be sworn in. Can the oath be administered by the poll clerk?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext: I am not sure on that point, Mr. Chairman. I will look it up.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext: I see no reason why it should not be done It would be a great convenience if the statute provided for it.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext: It is only for the swearing in of officers that you want power given to the poll clerk to administer oaths?

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext: The deputy returning officer is sworn in by the returning officer.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext: The returning officer, we will say, is the sheriff of the county and resides in the county town. The county may be a hundred miles long. My hon. friend surely does not mean that all the deputy returning officers must come before the returning officer to be sworn in? At any rate, it has not been the practice in the past.	[DOT]

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext:
I do not think that the Act as drawn states before whom ' the deputy shall be sworn. Section 25 provides:
Every deputy returning officer shall before acting1 as such take the oath in form H.
I assume that would be an oath taken before any person authorized by this Act to administer oath.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext:
Suppose a returning officer residing in Edmonton appoints deputies at Peace River, Colling River, Me-Murray, Mackay, Fort Oliipewyan and Fort Smith. These points cover a distance oi several hundred miles, and at none of these places is there a notary public or justice of the peace. If you happen to'find a member of the Mounted Police at his post you may get him to swear somebody as commissioner. But at the last election I endeavoured to get the Provincial Government to appoint a man a commissioner and send him along with the ballot boxes to swear the deputies as he went along the route. The Provincial Government was not favourable or kind to me and at first I was not able to succeed. However I took the matter up with Mr. O'Connor

by wire and he got in touch with the provincial authorities and they finally yielded and had a man appointed who could go about and do this. It would be impossible for the returning officer to do the work himself. I would like to see some provision in the Act under'which it would be possible for the authorities at Ottawa to appoint someone a commissioner to swear in deputies or other officers in these far away places.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext: Section 25 does not provide that the deputy returning officer shall be sworn in before any particular person; consequently he can he sworn in under the provisions of section 7. The returning officer can swear in the poll clerk, and the poll clerk, when sworn in, can swear in the deputy returning officer. Would that remove the difficulty?

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext: No. In this stretch of country five hundred miles long there is no person to administer an oath, although there are six or eight ballot boxes and, consequently, six polls. The returning [DOT]officer cannot accompany the men with the boxes and swear the deputies, so we have to gelt a commissioner, and that commissioner must be appointed by the local authorities. If the local authorities are not well disposed toward you, you may not get one at all, and the returning officer will be forced to take a trip of perhaps three hundred miles in order to administer this oath.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext:
As the Bill is drawn,
. every deputy returning officer before acting as such must take the oath. The question .raised by my hon. friend is:	How is the
deputy returning officer himself to be sworn? He cannot act until he is sworn; I see the difficulty where very great distances have to be covered and there are very few commissioners. When we come to section 25 I shall be glad if my hon. friend will remind me of that point.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext:
What does the
Acting Solicitor General say to my suggestion that the poll clerk be authorized to administer the oath to the deputy returning
officer?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext: The poll clerk is appointed under section 26, but before he can act he must be sworn. We all assume that the first man sworn is the deputy returning .officer; the deputy himself cannot appoint a poll clerk until he is sworn.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext:
Then the deputy
.must go before a justice of the peace to be sworn.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext: He must go before someone authorized by this Act to administer an oath; then he can swear his poll clerk.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext:
Is there any provision in
the Act imposing a penalty upon any person with jurisdiction who refuses to administer an oath? We have had numerous cases in Nova Scotia where magistrates have refused to swear in a man, even for the voters' list.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext:
Yes, there is a provision in that regard somewhere between sections 80 and 90.
Section, as amended, agreed to.
On section 8-penalty for inducing persons to make false oath:

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext: The former sections covering this subject were 273 and 274; they have been combined in one. The former section read, " Every candidate who," and so on; this section says, " Every person ,who " does so-and-so.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 9-executory contracts void:

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext:
Would this clause cover,
for instance, a contract made toy a. candidate with a newspaper or an advertising concern for advertising?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext:
I think it would. An
executory contract is a future contract uncompleted by payment, delivery or execution. The purpose of the section is to void promises made before an election to be implemented after.' It has been the law of the land for many years.
Mr. .POWER:	There have been things
in the law.of the land for many years that I think are wrong. We have laid down as crimes things which are not crimes. Why force a man to commit a crime?! I suppose every member of the House has at one time or another made a contract with a newspaper or an advertising agency for advertising-

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext: That is not an executory contract. An executory contract is for something to be performed and paid for in the future.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext:
What about the terms o'
the undertaking?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext:
If it be an executory
contract, the amount cannot be recovered. There are in this law provisions for the recovery of debts incurred during an election; there is a time within which an account must be rendered, and the like Those provisions
will be found towards the end of the Bill. There is a general provision to make void every promise of an executory nature which is not to be performed before the election, promises which used to be made for the purpose of securing political influence here, there and the other place. I think there is a strong moral ground for retaining this section.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext: It is a promise or undertaking to pay, after the election, if one be elected. I maintain that we should not void it; there is nothing wrong in promising that you will pay a newspaper only if you be elected.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext: The case of a newspaper is, an executory contract, so that it is a contract completed by execution. It may be postponed.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 10-contributions for political purposes:

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext:
Is not subsection 2 going too far? It reads:
Any company or association violating the provisions of this section.
Some shareholders might not know that the directors were making contributions. The word "wilfully" or the word "knowingly" should be inserted.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext: This is a good old section passed after careful consideration. I think, in the year 1908, and possibly it was in the old Act of 1898. It is considered a very salutary proviso in our law. I would not open the door in this respect if I could avoid doing so.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext: But do companies contribute towards election expenses?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext: They cannot under this clause.	*

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext:
Why limit the clause to
companies? Why not extend it to persons? It might be easy for a man connected with a big company to make a large contribution, and that would be just as wrong as if the contribution were made by the company.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext: No.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext: Why not?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext:
An individual has a
heart and soul and mind of his own, and he has a right to vote and can lawfully exercise political influence. The case is different with a company. An incorporated company is not a person within the meaning of

this legislation. The (purpose of the section, [DOT]as my hon. friend probably knows, was to get rid o-f a system that was growing up in the * United States and in Canada, which was very objectionable in its results. The great .corporations were exercising a large amount of influence on the political situation in this country and in the United States, heavy contributions being given by the corporations as such. Individuals might think twice before they would spend their own money; but when it was looked on as a matter of corporate funds and the result of .the election might possibly help the general financial standing of the company; and ultimately favourable legislation might, be passed by the successful party, huge contributions began to flow, not so much in this country as in the United States. But the time came in Canada when, in the wisdom of .this Parliament, it became necessary to check that evil, and I think it has been fairly well checked in this country.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext: Oh, oh.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext: Oh, oil. I do -not think so.	,

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext: The hon. member for Quebec East (Mr. Lapointe) seems to smile at that.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext: He is doubtful about it.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext: I do not, know the system that prevails in the province of Quebec, but in Ontario and elsewhere the evil has been pretty well checked; and if it has not been checked in Quebec, let us devise legislation that will check it.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext: Was that, what my ihon. friend told us after the election of 1911 when he came back to the House?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext: I do not remember ever discussing the question of contributions by corporations in this House, and I did not tell any one anything about it. I think this is the first time in twenty years that I have ever opened my mouth on the subject. But if there be any doubt as to what is going^on in this respect, let us have a law broad enough to stop i't, and if the present enactment be not broad enough, let us improve it. I would not suggest weakening it in any way, 1 would suggest strengthening it.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext:
I was suggesting to my hon. friend that the law should be broadened by adding the word "person." He mentioned Quebec. Naturally I am more familiar with conditions existing in Quebec than with conditions existing in the
(Mr. Guthrie.]
other provinces, but in Quebec, and probably in all the other provinces, individuals doing very large business now do not do their business under their individual names any more, but under corporate names. Most people do that. Therefore, individuals who have in reality the greatest interest and sometimes all the interest in the companies are doing business under corporate names in our province-and I think the same is true of most of the provinces. These gentlemen naturally will not, according to this clause,
9 p.m. contribute as a corporation, but they may well do so individually under their personal names, and that is not supposed to be an indictable offence, although the result is exactly the same in the end.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext: They cannot use corporate money for the purpose.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext:
But the corporate money is their own money.
Mr. [DOT] GUTHRIE: I never before heard that it was considered as wrong in this or in any other country for a man, out of his private means, to contribute to cause which is desired to succeed in an election. I never heard it suggested before that such a thing was an offence or wrong in principle or morals or in any other respect. But it has always been considered, to say the least, as a matter of doubtful propriety, to use corporate funds in an election. Under this clause an individual cannot, as a shareholder, or officer, or attorney, or agent of a company., contribute any corporate money. The company itself cannot contribute. But I have never yet heard it suggested that an individual should not be permitted, out of his private money, to contribute some of his money for the success of the cause which he happens to have at heart.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext: Is this clause exactly the same as the clause in the old Act?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext: With the exception of two or three words, it is. '

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext: Would the minister mind giving us those exceptions?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext: The clause in the old Act read as follows:

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext: Is the minister referring to the Act of 1911?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext:
No, I am referring to the Act of 1908. If I recollect the matter

properly, the only change in the clause is in the first words. Tire first words of the old section read:
Any company or association.
And the first words in the present clause read:
No unincorporated company or association and no incorporated company or association.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext: Does this mean that no group of individuals, whether large or small, can contribute to or secure funds in any way for the .purpose of the election campaign of a candidate?	[DOT]

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext: I think that is practically the effect of the section. No business men can group themselves together as a company or association, whether incorporated or not, to contribute funds towards an election campaign.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext:
According to the section no group of labour men, returned soldiers or others-
Some hen. MEMBERS:	Farmers.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext: -can group themselves together, unless they get incorporated, to assist financially in the election of a candidate. Could this be done under the old Act?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext: The object aimed at is to prevent men from grouping together and using their joint contribution for the purpose of assisting in an election campaign.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext: What about their individual contributions? -

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext: An individual contribution would not be viewed as unlawful, but if a number of men joined together in the form of an association for the purpose of using their joint contributions towards a campaign it would be unlawful under this Act.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext:
I think the same
purpose was accomplished with the section as it stood in the old Act. Why make people suspicious that this section has been drafted in a different way with the object of reaching them? What is tRe object of changing the words of the two first lines?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext:
The only reason I know for the change was that it would prevent men from grouping themselves together for the purpose of influencing an election by financial contributions.
It seems that this is one of the clauses that may be regarded as contentious, and
in view of my statement this afternoon perhaps it might be as well for us to postpone its further consideration for the time being. I would therefore move to let the section stand.	'

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext:
Does the minister
think that individuals could group together under the old Act?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext: I think they could. The only groups prohibited under the former Act were those who incorporated.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext:
They could not group
together under the old Act.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext: It has been pointed out to me that my interpretation of the former law was incorrect. The former Act provided that " no company or association other than one incorporated for political purposes .alone shall " etc. That would cover a group of association just as under the present Act. The draughsinan of the present Bill, Mr. W. F. O'Connor is, I may say, an experienced man, and he changed the language into " no unincorporated company or association " etci

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext: There is a provision. I have not the exact section, but it is the same provision as in the former law, which requires that a detailed statement of all contributions, payments, loans, advances, deposits or promises of money made on behalf of the candidate, shall be given to the agent or returning officer for publication.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext:
I think this section might very well stand. But before leaving it I would say that, it being mainly intended, as I interpret it, to prevent business corporations from contributing to campaign funds, it has my hearty approval.' I feel that it cannot be made too exacting. In order to make perfectly clear the purpose of the section, I think it would be an improvement if one or two words were added to subsection 2. This subsection reads:

Every director, shareholder, officer, attorney or agent of any company or association violating the provisions of this section
*
is guilty of an indictable offence, etc.
I should like to see inserted, after the word " agent," the words " or any person on behalf of any company or association."

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext: In law the term "agent" includes any person acting on behalf of another. However, I note the suggestion of the hon. member.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext:
My desire is to have it made perfectly clear that the law prohibits business corporations from contributing to political funds, and I should like to see the section amended to that extent.
Section stands.
On section 11-Persons not electors and not residents of Canada forbidden to canvas:

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext: The change here is in reference to the penalty. Under the former Act the penalty was from $100 to $200, or six months' imprisonment. Now it will be an indictable offence punishable by fine up to $2,000.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext: What is the reason for this clause?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext:
It is fairly explicit; it is a clause adopted by Parliament in 1908. I do not know that I can give any better reason than the language in the section. I do not think I could give the reason for it better than it is given in the language of the section:
Any person, not being an elector, who resides without Canada and who, to secure the election of any candidate, canvasses for votes or in any way endeavours to induce voters to vote for any candidate at an election, or to refrain from ' voting, is guilty of an indictable offence against this Act punishable as in this Act provided.
The object was to prevent eonvassing by the foreigner who has no right or business in this country, who is not a native of Can. ada, and who only takes part in an election as a paid agent. A man who has no stake in the country will take a desperate chance that a citizen of the country would not take, and then skips over the border when the election is over so that he cannot be reached by our criminal law.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext: Take an election in which we would have imperial preference discussed in Canada, would a person from Great Britain be debarred?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext:
That is not a foreign
country.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext:
It says anybody who
resides outside of Canada.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext: People of that class will be debarred from taking part in an election. Suppose we should discuss at a future election the question of reciprocity and a prominent man from the United States would like to address a meeting in Montreal and tell the people there what his views were upon that question; this section would bar him out of our country.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext:
No, it is to be " at an election," and " at an election " is defined in section 2 as including:
The period after the issue of the writ for an election, or after the dissolution of Parliament or the occurrence of a vacancy in consequence of v-hich a writ for an election is eventually issued, until the elected candidate is returned as elected.
People who came out from Great Britain or other parts of the world to discuss public questions could not be very well be said to be coming here for the purpose of securing the election of any candidate. They would not be canvassing for votes at an election.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext: Certainly they would.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext:
I can only say to my
hon. friend that I do not know the exact origin of this section but my hon. friends across the way who then sat in the Government when this Act was put upon the statute book can probably give the reason for it better than I can. I admit the propriety of it, I see good reason for it and I do not think it is open to the narrow interpretation that the hon. member for Dorchester (Mr. Cannon) seeks to put upon it.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext: I am perfectly willing to accept any interpretation that the minister can give, but that is how I interpret the clause, and I think my interpretation is right.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext:
I think my hon.
friend's interpretation is absolutely wrong. The Act says that the person must be here canvassing and that he must be here at an election.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext: "endeavours to induce"-

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext:
Yes, I grant that. The object was to keep out a person who had not a vote in this country and who/had no interest in the election. The real object that the section was intended to achieve was to keep out stragglers from the other side who came in here, hired by some political party or other and who, after having done their nefarious work, quit the coun-

try, went to the other side and we were not able to catch them.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext: If the section were wider than the Minister of Militia (Mr. Guthrie) says it would not do any harm, because the words are " in any way endeavour to induce voters to vote for any candidate at an election." That means during the period intervening between th% issue of the writ and the polling day,. I do not see why persons from outside should come into Canada anyway.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext:
I called the attention of
the House to this section this afternoon. The hon. Minister of Militia not having been here at the time, the hon. Minister of the Interior (Mr. Meighen) took note of' the objection, but apparently the Minister of Militia has not received any intimation of it. I will repeat in substance, very shortly, the objection I have to this clause. By section 11 it is provided that:
Any person, not being an elector, who resides without Canada and who, to secure the election of any candidate, canvasses for votes or in any *way endeavours to induce voters to vote for any candidate at an election, or to reflain from voting, is guilty of an indictable offence against this Act punishable as in this Act provided.
That means that any citizen of England -I used the. words " citizen of England " this afternoon to call attention to the absurdity of the matter; I might have included any citizen of Ireland, or any citizen of Scotland, or anybody residing in the Isle of Man, or any other place that I might mention-would not have the right to come over here and try to influence-I want the minister's attention because this is a serious point-or induce any voter to vote for any candidate. By section 38 of the act any one of these gentlemen may be a candidate himself. The result is that of any man in -England, or Ireland, or Scotland, or the Isle of Man, or Newfoundland, wants to be a candidate for this House, he may be one.
#Mr. POWER: He would go to jail.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext: No, he could be a candidate. But if he undertook to come over and hold meetings and say to the electors: " You should vote for me " for the reasons I have given, he would find himself landed in jail. Now that is very absurd and I would like to ask the minister if he can offer any other interpretation of the clause to the House.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext:
It would be a very easy matter .to change section 38 by saying that all candidates for seats in this House shall 50
be residents of Canada. I think they should be. I quite approve of the section as it is drawn, but it is not of very great consequence. I would not like to see it changed unless there is some good reason for it. My hon. friend and myself were in the House when the section was put in and we supported the Government that had put it there. I thought it was a good section.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext: That was section 69.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext: No, both sections,-certainly section 11.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext:
I do not wish to interrupt the minister but if he will allow me, I have under my hand section 69 of the Act which my hon. friend refers to and which corresponds to section 38. Section 38 of this Bill reads:
Except as in this Act otherwise provided any British subject, male or female; who is of the full age of twenty-one years, may be a candidate at a Dominion election.
The clause to which the minister refers in section 69 of the Dominion Elections Act which reads:
Except as in this Act otherwise provided any British subject may be a candidate in an election for a seat in the House of Commons. No qualification in real estate shall be required of any candidate.
That is really more favourable to the British subject.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext: I do not see how. I may be obtuse but I cannot see the difference.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext: Well, I did make the remark to the Minister of the Interior that I might be dull but I could not help seeing it.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext: I see the anomaly that might arise if we permit section 38 to remain as it is in the Bill. What I suggested was that we could very easily cure the difficulty by inserting a few words in section 38 to provide<that a person who offers himself as a candidate for election to this Parliament should be a resident of Canada.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext: If the minister is going to undertake to debar any British subject from being a candidate for this House then I cannot offer any further objection.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext: Unless he is a resident of Canada.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext: I cannot offer any further objection.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext: I personally would be prepared to go that far.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext: If the clause were amended so as to read that any. person who canvasses for votes or who, by personal solicitation, endeavours to induce voters to vote for any candidate other than himself -at an election, that will fix the whole matter.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext:
It has been suggested to me that we could meet the point raised by my hon. friends opposite very simply by amending the first line of section 11 to make it read thus:
Aliy person, not being an elector or a candidate-
And so on. Then my hon. friend would be able to carry out his wish that at some time or other in the future, residents of the British Isles might sit in this House. I do not agree with the proposal, but if the Committee is willing I am perfectly content that after the words "not being an elector" we shall add "or a candidate."

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext: Shall the amendment carry?

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext: I do not take the responsibility for it; it is the Act of the Government.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext: Notwithstanding the very lucid explanation of the Acting Solicitor General I am still opposed to this clause. I expect we will very shortly have in this country a strong Labour party. The Labour party are about to organize and will perhaps need in their organization the help and assistance of some members of their body in the United States.	^

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext: Oh, oh.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext: I see no reason why they should not be allowed to come in-

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext: Keep them out.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext: -to help in an election by speeches. More than that we shall also have, I think-

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext: We have got enough Socialists here now.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext: . -a . strong Prohibition party. I see no reason, for instance, why "Pussyfoot" Johnson, who is now in England, should not come here, and yet if "Pussyfoot" Johnson were to come here he might be put in jail, and then the President of the Privy Council -would be in trouble.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext:
Even Billy Sunday might come here.
	*

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext: In any of these cases it might be pleaded that intervention on the part of strangers would be perfectly legitimate. Lord Jellicoe could even come here and explain his naval proposals] I would not like to see Lord Jellicoe put in jail.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext: I would not like to see him here engaged .in an election either.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext:
It would not be a good thing for tire Tory party. However, if the clause must remain let the hon. gentleman make it a proper one. The clause provides:
Any person, not being an elector, who resides-
And so on. Well, residence is a very difficult term to define. A man who remains here over night might be deemed to "reside" in Canada. If the Acting Solicitor General adopted the phrase "who is domiciled in the country," then I think perhaps the clause might suit his purpose. In the province of Quebec we have discussed the question of "residence" and "domicile" in making up electoral lists time and again, and I would ask. the minister to substitute "domicile" for "residence."

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext:
As a representative of
another province than that of my hon. friend opposite, I should like to say that personally I am convinced that the Canadian people can very well run their own elections without assistance from either English or Americans.
Section as amended agreed to.
On section 12-conveyance of electors to polls, etc., for hire, forbidden.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext: These are the time-honoured clauses 270 and 271 which have been for a long time in our law.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext: Honoured more in the breach than in the observance.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext: They have been combined in these proposals and the language has been changed to some extent but the change does not affect the meaning. There are the same old sections, and as my hon. friend (Mr. Fielding) said a moment ago perhaps more honoured in the breach than in the observance. It has not been my experience, but I have heard of it in other cases.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext: I think we ought to be candid -and fair and strike this out.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext: Let us be honest.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext: I endorse that view, only I support it (more strongly than the hon. gentleman has done. In the last election when I heard my opponent was hiring everything in the city I engaged more men to go and hire the remaining conveyances. 1 make this statement without any reservation. If any gentleman wants to prosecute me under the Act for .what I have done he can do so, but I will institute prosecution against every other member of the House if anything is started on me. As a matter of fact, however, that is the practice that is followed. I will give you a good reason for it. In the city of Edmonton there is a pretty large territory, as much as would accommodate the cities of Chicago and New York. They have two or three mills there and the men cannot go to the polls in the morning; the operator will not allow them out at noon except for an hour. If you are to get these men to the polls between five and seven o'clock you must do something else than merely send invitations to them. It is well known that we have been hiring conveyances for election purposes, and I endorse the statement of the hon. member for Muskoka (Mr. McGibbon) that it is time for us to stop being hypocrites.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext:
Just before the motion for the adoption of this clause is put let me say that I agree entirely with the Bill as it stands only it does not go quite far enough. I think it would be well if the Acting Solicitor General would add to the prohibited conveyances:
Dirigibles, hydroplanes, submarines, submarine chasers, and all other chasers.
Same hon. MEMBERS: Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, all that
my hon. friend has suggested is covered by the clause as it now stands in these words "or other means of conveyance." I think, though, this clause might stand. As we have made fair progress on the Bill I now move that the Committee .rise, report progress and ask leave to sit again.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext:
Before you leave the
Chair-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext: The motion is not debatable.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext: I do not want to debate the motion, but-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext: If the minister wishes to withdraw his motion it will be in order for the hon. member to continue the debate.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext: I withdraw my motion.

speakerposition: subtopic
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext: I wish to ask ii the Government has any information to give the House in regard to the election in 'St. James, Montreal? Is it to be postponed on account of the notices being sent out too late?

speakeroldname: Rt. Hon. C. J. DOHERTY (Minister of Justice) :
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext: I have no knowledge of any postponement of the election. I have seen it stated that there has been some irregularity in connection with the lists, but I have not definite infonnation as to what the particular irregularity is. If I may be permitted to give an impression that I do not want to be bound by, I would say that it does not seem clear to me that there is any authority in any one to decide that there is any irregularity and to postpone the election. If there be any gross irregularity, I can see that it would be for the courts to deal with it when properly seized of the particulars. However, I am speaking without accurate knowledge of what is the difficulty that is-said to exist.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext:
I move that the Committee rise, report progiess and beg leave to sit again.
Progress reported.

speechtext: Do I understand that the Bill is made to empower the Governor in Council to carry out agreements which may be the result of the report of the commission to settle Indian affairs in British Columbia?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
subsubtopic: SETTLEMENT OF DIFFERENCES CONCERNING INDIAN LANDS.
speechtext:
Not quite. The commission was appointed in pursuance of an * agreement between the representatives of the Government of 'British Columbia and the representatives of the Government of Canada. The differences between the two Governments had lasted for a number of years; indeed, I think ever since British Columbia was a province. The two Governments by agreement undertook to appoint a commission composed of two representatives for British Columbia and two for the Dominion, the four so appointed to appoint a fifth, and the cost to be shared squally. The expense figures I have given are shared equally by the two. Governments. Perhaps I should very briefly state what the points of difference were. The British Columbia Government had contended that it, as distinct from the Governments of the other provinces, was entitled to a reversionary interest in all the Indian reserves in British Columbia; that is to say, if for any reason, whether by extinction of the tribe or by a decision to sell the reserves, or for any other cause, the land or any part thereof ceased to be used by the Indians, the Government of Canada was not entitled to sell that land' on any portion of it being surrendered and place the money in a trust fund for the benefit of the Indians, as is done in the ease of every other province, but that, that land upon so ceasing to be used by the Indians reverted to the province of British. Columbia. The administration of Indian affairs, if such a claim were to be conceded, would become not only very difficult but a tremendous burden upon the Dominion. That claim has not been conceded by the Government of Canada. The Government of British Columbia, by the terms of the Act of Union of 1874, bound itself to provide lands or reserves in that province adequate to the needs of the Indians, and the Government of Canada, on the other hand, bound itself to maintain a standard of Indian administration, equal in generosity, equal in

liberality towa'rds the Indians, to that maintained by British Columbia prior to Confederation. Clause 19 of the agreement, if I remember correctly-I do not know that I can express it fully; I have not the clause before me now-used words upon which British Columbia based its claim to this reversionary interest.
As time proceeded it became evident that certain reserves were larger than was necessary for the purposes of the Indians. That is true in every province. Scarcely a week passes without a surrender being made in some province of a portion of a reserve, the lands so surrendered being sold by the department and the proceeds going, according to the terms of surrender, to the trust fund,-some of them usually going to the Indians themselves direct. So this occurred in British Columbia. Reserves were found to be larger than necessary, and in some cases they were found to be too small. This, then, immediately brought to an acute point the question what was to be done with the reserves so in excess. We could not sell them, because if we did the money would not be ours, and we had no money with which to get new reserves.
I think I have indicated to the committee some of the difficulties that arose. It was determined by the two Governments that there should be a final end to this controversy. It was made more acute by the developments in relation to the Kitsil-ano reserve, which had become a very valuable property, to the business centre of the city of Vancouver; indeed, it was required by the Vancouver Harbour Commission in connection with harbour developments. That, then, became a fitting cause for the sale_ of that reserve and for the acquirement of some other land less valuable but more adapted to Indian habitation and to Indian pursuits. The property was valued at anything from half a million to a million and three-quarters. The Harbour Board had to have the property, but both Governments were claiming the proceeds, we, of course, claiming them only as trustees. There was not time,:-and furthermore there were other objections to doing so,-to have this question of reversionary title decided by' the courts. Consequently, an agreement was entered into and provision made therein whereby interim reports should be made, interim recommendations by the commission looking to the disposal of reserves or parts of reserves that might be immediately required for other purposes. Now, it was a term of that agreement, and embodied in the Orders in Council passed by the respective Governments subsequently adopting the agreement, that the agreement should be sympathetically received and acted upon by the two governments subject to such conditions or modifications as would be deemed reasonable. The effect was that virtually there was no agreement at all further than an agreement to have the matter investigated, and while that in itself might be worth while, it did not lead to^any finality. The Commission set to work and performed- on the whole, I think, very well-undoubtedly a very laborious task. Interim reports were made. One report was made with respect to this Kitsilano reserve, and that report was acted upon. As a result the Harbour Commissioners took possession of the Kitsilano reserve, and have possession of it to-day, but we are still in controversy as to what is to be' done with the money. Accordingly, the Harbour Board has not paid any money and there is no decision as to what they are going to pay or what is going to be done with the money when it is paid. A report was received in the early months of 1916 recommending certain cut-offs and certain new reserves, gnd the Government of Canada not long afterwards intimated its readiness to accept the report and to abide and be bound thereby. The report provided on the general and main issue that where land was found to be in excess of requirements, that excess might be sold and the proceeds equally divided between the two Governments, the Government of Canada to utilize the portion so received by it on behalf of the Indians for whom, of course, it was trustee. Now, the * Government of British Columbia did not deal with the report at all. They indulged in certain communications from time to time, it is true, but they have not yet intimated their willingness to accept. Indeed, we have at the present time no official communication-one was made and withdrawn-as to what the Government of British Columbia is prepared to do with regard to that report. But at the last session of the legislature of that province the Government took power to negotiate with the Dominion Government looking to the adoption of the report embodying modifications which were to result from the negotiations. There is no question in my mind that legislation is necessary to enable that to be done. That being the attitude and the action taken by the Government of British Columbia it seems desirable that we should be in the same position, because there will be no object in our negotiating with them

*without authority. They stand thSre with the authority given them by their legislature; it seems to me right and necessary that we have similar authority from ours. We have a list of the cut-offs recommended and also of the additions recommended; and the report is on the Table. This legislation is authority to negotiate and to make binding any agreement arrived at covering various details of these cut-offs and the disposition of the proceeds.

It is possible that the question of reversionary interest might be settled on a stated case. My information Is that an attempt was made some time ago by the legal departments of the two governments to come to terms on a stated case, but they could not agree on a stated case. A suggestion hhs been made again by the Attorney General of British Columbia looking to a stated case on two or three phases. They claim absolute ownership of the Kit-silano reserve. They claim reversionary interest and interest at law in all the other reserves. But in his communiction the Attorney General stated that the British Columbia Government were anxious to* settle the matter amicably if they could. I have replied to that' communication with a proposal which I hope will result in an amicable settlement of this question.
But even if such a settlement should be arrived at, that would not take care of the subjects sought to be taken care of by this Bill.
The question is,. what shall be cut off from the reserves. There are one thousand reserves in British Columbia alone, and they are all dealt with in the report. Even though the question of the reversionary interest were settled, we would still have to negotiate with the province as to just what cut-offs should be made from various reserves, what additions should, be made to otheis and what reserves should be added in the province. Consequently the legislation is necessary in any event even though we may have come to a stated case on the question of reversionary interest.

to presume that, because power is asked for the Governor in Council to fulfil every act, deed, matter or thing necessary for the carrying out of the said agreement between the Governments of the Dominion of Canada and the province of British Columbia according to its true intent. There

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
subsubtopic: SETTLEMENT OF DIFFERENCES CONCERNING INDIAN LANDS.
speechtext:
Yes.
Mr. DEVLIN- I do not wish to interfere in the affairs of British Columbia, but it seems to me-and I have had some experience in connection with the Indian Act-that this legislation in clause 3 of the present Bill is asked for independently of what may appear in the Indian Act. We are the custodians of the rights of the Indian, and the Government cannot take away from the Indians any of their reserves without first obtaining a surrender from the Indians concerned. The Government having obtained that surrender-I speak now from memory-the money goes to the credit of the Indians. If this Bill is passed, then it varies altogether the provisions of the Indian Act. I have in memory now a case in the constituency which I represent. There are two settlements, one of which is a very important settlement, at the other end of the county, called the village of Maniwaki. The land connecting the adjoining settlement, the River Desert, with the village of Maniwaki belongs to the Indian Reserve, and the river Desert runs right through that, and alongside of that is the main road w.hich is practically the only communication -between the two places. For years I applied to the Minister of Public Works of the former Government, not the present Government, and later to the Minister of Indian Affairs, to have that roadway protected by some kind of construction. The Public Works Department could not act-because this land was Indian land. This Government, I feel sure, would not be prepared to act possibly for the same reason, although I want to call the attention of the Minister of Indian Affairs to the fact that it is work that is abso-
10 p.m. lutely necessary for the preser-. vation of the Indian Reserve. It is also work that is absolutely necessary
i

to preserve a means of communication between the one place and the other. Upon this land that I speak of now in the immediate vicinity of the water, very few Indians reside; I think that right around there might be one family of Indians. ,And yet that land cannot be taken away from the Tribe. The Tribe still exists and the Tribe will not surrender. If this legislation is passed, of course, similar legislation could be applied as to Indian reserves in the province from wliicfi I come and with which I am more familiar.
I fail to see in what way, whilst the Indian Act remains, even in spite of clause 3 or any clause of the Bill, you are going to take away from the Indians vested rights. You may alter the sections of the Indian Act, but these are vested rights

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
subsubtopic: SETTLEMENT OF DIFFERENCES CONCERNING INDIAN LANDS.
speechtext: I know the reserve to -which the hon. member refers in the province of Quebec at Maniwaki, having been there, and 1 know the position of the road and river, It is quit? true that the Indian Department would be powerless to take from that reserve any portion of it without the formality of a previous surrender, and it. is quite true that in this case also of the British Columbia reserves, affected by the report of the commissioners, though we might agree on a settlement of this whole trouble, dating back almost to Confederation, we would be absolutely powerless to carry it out if even one band, for any reason, however capricious, were to say: We will not surrender these two acres -or whatever the area may be. It is only in most exceptional cases and for most extraordinary reasons that the Government, as the guardian of the Indians, should assert the right to take any land without the consent of the band. But for the life of me I do not know how we are ever going to settle this matter unless we do assert that right. We have no reason to apprehend especially that there will be the exercise of caprice or obstinacy on the part of these bands. It will be our endeavour in any event to secure surrenders, even though this clause passes. But surely it is only right that we should have the power to carry out this settlement, because the legislation is asked for only for the purpose of carrying it out, and otherwise w^ cannot administer Indian affairs in British Columbia. It is for the purpose of settlement that this commission was appointed, and in order .to make the settlement effective we must have the power in this clause. The reasons are extraordinary; the circumstances are most unusual and compelling, and on that account II decided to ask Parliament for this power in this special case.

speechtext: While I have no desire to see this Bill hurried through,. I desire to say a word or two in regard to the advisability of- proceeding. There -are more Indians in the constituency of Skeena than perhaps in -any other riding in Canada, -and I am the very last man who would wish to do an injustice to them. There are in British Columbia -a lot of reserves that have been held up for years, -such for instance as the Giltsalt Reserve. I may say that' there is a good deal of .mining up in the mountains and in the valley, and the whole development of the district is held up because the reserve cannot be de-alt-with. I would not wonder but that the leadef of the Opposition himself has received delegations on this very point. It has been in controversy-if you call this a controversy-for years and years; I cannot say how long, but I know the dispute dates back into a good part of the period of the Laurier Administration, if indeed it does not antedate that. maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
subsubtopic: SETTLEMENT OF DIFFERENCES CONCERNING INDIAN LANDS.
speechtext:
I think it is only fair to the gentlemen who are represented as
being agitators, to put on Hansard some of the arguments they present against the present Bill. They say:
1.	The Indian tribes of British Columbia have always claimed tribal ownership of their respective territories under ^aboriginal title and the Proclamation 'issued by King George Third in the year 1763.
2.	In the year 1875 by report of the then Minister of Justice of Canada adopted by the then Governor General of Canada in Council it was declared that the land claims of the Indian tribes of British Columbia are well founded and that those tribes are entitled to an interest in all the lands of that province.
3.	The then Government of the province of
British Columbia and succeeding governments of that province refused to recognize the land rights so declared, and proceeded to deal with the land's of British Columbia as the absolute property of the province notwithstanding the fact that in the year 1875 the then Land Act of the province had been disallowed upon the ground that its provisions ignored the land rights of the Indian tribes.	*
4.	The present position of the Indian land controversy which thus arose and has ever since continued is shown by the following extract from 'the statement of the Allied Tribes prepared at the request of the present Premier of British Columbia and presented to him on 13th December last:-
"By means of the direct and independent petition of the Nishga tribes we now have our case before His Majesty's Privy Council. We claim that we have a right to a hearing, a right which has now been made clear beyond any possibility of doubt. Sir Wilfrid Laurier, when Prime Minister, on behalf of Canada, met the Indian tribes of northern British Columbia, and promised without any condition whatever that the land controversy would be brought before the Judicial Committee. Moreover, the Duke.of Connaught, acting as His Majesty's representative in Canada, gave positive written assurances that if the Nishga tribe should not be willing to agree to the findings of the Royal Commission, His Majesty's Privy Council will consider the Nishga petition. In view of Sir Wilfrid Laurier's promise and the Duke of Connaught's assurances, both of which confirm what we regard as our ctear constitutional right, we confidently expect an early bearing of our case."
5.	By communication which on 27th May, 1918, the London agents of the Nishga tribe addressed to the then Lord President of His Majesty's Privy Council, it was submitted on behalf of all tribes allied1 in support of the Nishga petition, among other things as follows :

"They are unwilling to be bound by the agreement regarding reserves mentioned in the petition which was made in the year 1912 between the Government of Canada and the Government of British Columbia, as therein stated, 'as a final adjustment of all matters relating to Indian affairs in the province of British Columbia,' and under which the findings of the Royal Commission have been made. On the contrary, the allied tribes contend that both that agreement and the Order in Caunicil *adopting it which was passed on 27th November, 1912, are beyond the power of the Government of Canada."
3. Your petitioners therefore humbly pray that your honourable body do not read a second

time said Bill No. 13, until all matters above set out and related matters shall have been fully considered by your honourable body.
And your petitioners will ever pray.
Peter Calder, of Nishga tribe.
George Matheson, of Tsimpshian tribe.
Peter.R. Kelley, of Haida tribe.
Basil David, of Shuswap tribe.
All representing the Allied Indian Tribes of British Columbia.
Dated at Ottawa, the 23rd day of March in the year 19 2'0.
I have nothing to add.
