speechtext: It will be very clear to the hon. member now that what I said was 'correct. What these people claim-or rather what this man claims and what he got others to help him to claim-is that in 1874 the original Indian title was not extinguished, and he wants others to assist him to the foot of the Throne to argue out that question. Do hon. gentlemen really want to bring that question into the discussion of this Bill? Why? If that were the case we ought to cease the Indian administration altogether because we will have no Indian reserves at all.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
subsubtopic: SETTLEMENT OF DIFFERENCES CONCERNING INDIAN LANDS.
speechtext: Does my hon. friend deny that these men are true representatives of the Indian tribes?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
subsubtopic: SETTLEMENT OF DIFFERENCES CONCERNING INDIAN LANDS.
speechtext: Mr. O'Meara?

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
subsubtopic: SETTLEMENT OF DIFFERENCES CONCERNING INDIAN LANDS.
speechtext: No, these four gentlemen.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
subsubtopic: SETTLEMENT OF DIFFERENCES CONCERNING INDIAN LANDS.
speechtext:
No, of course they are not.	I understand there is no
Indian agent or missionary or any one who has anything to do with it who does not denounce the whole movement and denounce the men, or the man, at the head of it. I do not think the committee wall be well advised to make the representations they have presented a cause for interference with the regular course of parliamentary procedure. It seems to me that it would be giving it an importance away beyond what it deserves. If there is anything in it it is just in the same position after the Bill passes as before. There is nothing disturbed by this Bill.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
subsubtopic: SETTLEMENT OF DIFFERENCES CONCERNING INDIAN LANDS.
speechtext:
These Indians, I understand, are only, a minority, a lot of troublemakers according to the statement I hear from hon. gentlemen on the other side who seem to know about this matter. It is said that they only represent a small portion of the \uhole and that the majority of the Indians are' willing to submit to the report of the royal commission. Is my comprehension of the facts right? Is it true that these -men are a minority, that they are just a

few troublemakers who come before this House to oppose this legislation?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
subsubtopic: SETTLEMENT OF DIFFERENCES CONCERNING INDIAN LANDS.
speechtext: That part, I am satisfied, is right, I cannot make any statement as to the opinion of the majority of the Indians of British Columbia on the report of the commission. I cannot say that it can be said that the majority of them have any definite opinion on the matter. I do not know. If I had the deputy minister in front of me I might speak perhaps with more authority on a question of that sort, but I do stand by what I have said as to the authoritative or lack of authoritative character of the representations made through the instrumentality of Mr. O'Meara.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
subsubtopic: SETTLEMENT OF DIFFERENCES CONCERNING INDIAN LANDS.
speechtext: I would point out to the minister that the Indian Act provides all the machinery required for the surrender of this land and if these men are only a few troublemakers there should not be any difficulty because unanimity is not required. A tribe may reach a decision upon it and the majority decides whether the' surrender shall take place or not.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
subsubtopic: SETTLEMENT OF DIFFERENCES CONCERNING INDIAN LANDS.
speechtext: Oh, yes.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
subsubtopic: SETTLEMENT OF DIFFERENCES CONCERNING INDIAN LANDS.
speechtext:
The fact that you want to discard the Indian Act so as to reduce the area of these reservations is an indication to me that certain Indians are not getting a fair deal. They may be getting a fair deal but they are not getting the deal that they desire to have. If the Government were certain from the reports of their agents, or the investigations that have been made, that these men did not represent the feelings of the Indians, then, under the Indian Act, you have the power, where necessary, to get these tribes together and get them to surrender those parts of the reservations that you desire to acquire. The Government of British Columbia want a part of them and the Dominion Government are willing to make an agreement with the interested parties. Are we going to discard the contracts which we have made with these wards and under which we are bound to take care of their property and to look after them? I think that some consideration should be given to this matter before we proceed further. I see that one of the gentlemen who has signed this petition is the Rev. Mr. Kelley. Does the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Peck) know him? He is the Rev. P. R.
. Kelley, of Nanaimo.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
subsubtopic: SETTLEMENT OF DIFFERENCES CONCERNING INDIAN LANDS.
speechtext: I know most of the reverend gentlemen in my riding but I cannot say that I know Mr. Kelley. I never heard of him.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
subsubtopic: SETTLEMENT OF DIFFERENCES CONCERNING INDIAN LANDS.
speechtext:
I have the pleasure of knowing Mr. Kelley very well; I have heard from him in connection with another Bill which is before the House, iBill No. 14.
I am sure he is a gentleman well qualified to speak on these questions. He seems to know all that concerns the Indians of British Columbia.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
subsubtopic: SETTLEMENT OF DIFFERENCES CONCERNING INDIAN LANDS.
speechtext: What" I was saying when I was interrupted was this: No harm will be done by delay and we will have the opportunity of reading the papers and memoranda which have been prepared and thus of knowing exactly what we are doing when we vote upon this Bill, which brushes aside the Indian Act for the purpose of carrying out certain agreements. No time will be lost and we shall have the satisfaction on this side of knowing what the claims of these people are. We do not want to stop the passage of this legislation if it is necessary, and if the claims made are unfounded surely no exhaustive discussion will take place.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
subsubtopic: SETTLEMENT OF DIFFERENCES CONCERNING INDIAN LANDS.
speechtext: I do not want it to be thought for a moment that I wish to impose any hardship on the Indians of British Columbia; in fact, no member of the House will go as far as I am prepared to go in order to help them out. As far as the franchise is concerned, I wish to see the more advanced tribes get it, but I do not see that we are going to get anywhere unless you empower the Minister of the Interior to deal with this question. Unless you do that it will be possible for any tribe or any crest to hold up the Bill. Take the Eagle Crest consisting of only half a dozen. They can hold the settlement up unless the minister is empowered to deal with the matter.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
subsubtopic: SETTLEMENT OF DIFFERENCES CONCERNING INDIAN LANDS.
speechtext:
We are not trying" to kill this Bill. We merely want-on behalf of these people, who are in the minority, who are feeble and who ask for protection -a little time to study their grievances and to consider the question. I do not think this request should be refused.
Mr. MEIGIIEN; If hon. gentlemen opposite press for time to study the Bill further I am not going to ask the committee to report the Bill. I want, however, to bring this fact to their attention, especially to that of the hon. member for Three Rivers. Ninety-nine per cent of the Indians of British Columbia might look with favour upon the settlement and 'be satisfied with it, but unless this Bill goes through it might well be that the other one per cent could defeat its whole purpose. There might be some little tribe, in which there might not be twenty men who have a vote, but if those twenty men refused to surrender an acre and a half of their reserve

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
subsubtopic: SETTLEMENT OF DIFFERENCES CONCERNING INDIAN LANDS.
speechtext: I do not object to the Bill, I only want time to consider it.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
subsubtopic: SETTLEMENT OF DIFFERENCES CONCERNING INDIAN LANDS.
speechtext:
I am answering the
hon. gentleman's point. If those twenty men, with respect to an acre and a half of their reserves, say it shall not be surrendered no matter what happens, then the agreement we may come to goes by the board. It is not very hard for any one- at all events with some tribes-to get his way, if he goes about it in a skilful manner, with at least twenty persons. Consequently it seems to me necessary that if it is decided by us as trustees for the Indians, and we are acting for the Indians, that this' is a proper settlement of a long-standing controversy, surely it is right that we should put it -out of the power of any one who tries to influence the Indians, as well .as of a very small minority of Indians themselves, to totally defeat the whole settlement. I only want to point out that, if there was a petition presented to myself asking to be heard against this Bill on any ground that affected the legislation that would be one matter. But when people come and say " You have no title to Indian lands in British Columbia, they are still owned by the Indians and the descendants of the Indians of 1870," it does not seem to me that it is to be taken seriously as in any way affecting this legislation. That is the point I desire to make. On the ground that my hon. friends opposite wish to study the legislation in all its bearings I certainly will not press this (measure now. I therefore move the com-imittee rise and report progress and ask leave to sit again. * .
Progress reported.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
On the motion of Hon. Mr. Rowell (Minister of. Health) Bill No. 28 respecting Maple Products was read a second time and the House went into committee thereon, Mr. Boivin in the Chair.
On section 2-Manufacture and sale of adulterated maple sugar or syrup

Adulterated maple sugar or syrup defined-Use of word "maple" restricted to pure maple sugar or syrup.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext:
I should like to make an amendment to subsection 3. As hon. members will see, the language of this subsection-which is the language of the law as it now stands in the Adulteration Act- is so broad that it covers the use of the word "maple" in any connection practically, and some difficulties have arisen in the administration of the Act where the claim has been made that the word should not be used in relation to products having no relation to maple syrup whatever, such as the Maple Leaf Milling Company's brand of flour. It is difficult, however, to frame a definition that will just meet the case, and the Department of Justice has

suggested that the clause should be amended in this form:
by inserting at the beginning of the said subsection the following words: "Except with the consent of the Minister of Health."
I would therefore move that the clause be so amended.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext:
Ip the case of the .Maple Leaf Milling Company they would simply have to get consent?
i Mr. ROWELL: Yes; and in any similar case. One came to my attention during the past two or three months, where a firm had been selling a maple brand of biscuits, and had been doing so before this Act was passed. Their right to do it was challenged. Their product had no relation to maple syrup or maple sugar, but it was said they were violating the law.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext: Is it the Maple Biscuit Company?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext:
I think the Maple brand of biscuits manufactured by the McCormick Company of London.
Mr. -BUREAU:	Don't they claim that
they sweeten their biscuits with maple sugar?
Mr. ROWELL. Then they should not have permission under that clause, because unless it were pure maple sugar they should not use the term "maple."

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext: The minister instanced flour; that is not a product of maple sugar.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext: No; but my hon. friend will see that this subsection does not require that it shall be a product of maple sugar or syrup. The subsection really creates a monopoly in the use of the word " magpie," and it may be a serious question whether such was contemplated by the Act.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext: Will the minister explain subsection 2 of section 2? What is meant by being " up to standard " within the meaning of the Food and Drugs Act of 1920?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext: That Act prescribes a certain standard of purity, and the product must comply with that standard to be entitled to be considered pure maple sugar within the terms of this clause. That standard is fixed in order to protect those who are making maple syrup and maple sugar. A certain amount of maple syrup or maple sugar was being adulterated with other sweetening mixtures. The syrup or sugar must comply with a certain standard, or it cannot be sold as maple syrup or maple sugar. -

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext:
That is provided for in
subsection 3 of that clause. But what is the standard of maple syrup? May it be thinner or thicker, or is there any standard required under the Act?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext: The definition will come up when the other Act is before the House.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext: Is not subsection 1 of section 2, which says that " any article of food resembling maple syrup shall not be sold," rather a sweeping clause? If any food product resembles maple syrup, it seems to me it should be sold under its proper name.	-

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext:
My hon. friend will see that the latter part of that clause qualifies the language of the first two lines:
or being- an imitation of maple sugar or maple syrup, or which is composed partly of maple sugar or maple syrup, and which is not pure maple sugar or pure maple syrup.
That is the present law.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext: As that section now reads what my hon. friend has just said would apply. If the word "or" after " resembling " were changed to "and " it would meet the objection raised.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext:
Insert after " syrup
which is composed partly." That would be more grammatical.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext: I see no objection to the change being made, but this is the form in which the section was originally enacted and it has been in force for six years.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext: * If we may return to subsection 3, I do not know that I could suggest any better words than those proposed by the minister, and yet I think they are inadequate, as, if added, they will convey the impression that it is the purpose of the clause to allow the minister to consent to some of these adulterations. I know that that is not what is in his mind at all, but it leaves that impression, and he may find himself open to annoying applications of that nature. I am sorry that the Department of Justice has not been able to put some limitation on the consent to be given. I cannot, offhand, suggest the proper form which the amendment should take, but before the matter is finally disposed of I would like the minister to find some happier expression to make it clear that consent shall not be given in the case of any foodstuffs, but is to be given only in connection with the naming of an article which has no relation to the maple trade.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext: I suggest that the minister make a change in the language of the first section which will remove any doubt as to the legality of selling an article of food that may resemble maple syrup. If he will change the word " or " at the beginning of line 3 to " and," the point will be met.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext: I have no objection to making such an amendment. But the word " or " occurs twice in that line, and the meaning is quite different if you change the first and do not change the second.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext: Change the second and leave the first.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext: If you do that, the clause may be open to different construction.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext:
Change the second
" or "; then you provide that a man may sell a thing which is not maple sugar, though it resembles or imitates it, but he may not sell it if it is partly composed of maple sugar.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext: Why should a dealer not be permitted . to sell an imitation which is sold under its proper name, even if it contains no maple syrup? I do not see why he should be prevented from selling it simply because it resembles maple syrup. It may be syrup of some other kind, and a pure article of food.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext: Then some provision should be made that the article should be described by its proper name.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext: I agree.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext: That clause has been in the law for some time. I think it would be wise for the minister to consult his officials before making the change suggested. A slight change in the wording of an Act after it has been in operation for some years may materially affect it.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext: I know an article of food similar to maple sugar which is customarily on sale in confectionery stores. As this section now reads, it would be an offence to sell that article. I do not think that is the intention of the Act. The intention is to protect dealers against imitations of maple sugar. Under the Bill as it now stands it would be an offence to sell maple cream, for example, an article which is like maple sugar.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext: It is an oiffence to sell maple cream if it is not pure maple sugar.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext:
Under this Act it would be an offence to sell any candy that is at all like maple sugar.
Section stands.
Progress reported.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
On motion of Hon. Mr. Rowell (Minister of Health), Bill No. 29, respecting honey, was read the second time, and the House went into Committee thereon, Mr. Boivin in the chair.
On section 2-feeding bees with sugar:

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext: This is simply the re-enactment of clauses relating to this matter which have been eliminated from the present Adulteration Act.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext: Is there any change?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext: No change. The clauses are taken out of the Adulteration Act because in re-drafting and consolidating the law we think it desirable that where a monopoly is created it should be dealt with under a separate Act and not in the general Act respecting adulteration of foods.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext:
Section 2 provides as follows:
Feeding bees with sugar, except for the purpose of being consumed by them as food, or with glucose or any sweet substance-
And so on. But who is to go after the bees and see if they are fed with these different articles? Has the minister any official in his department who will follow the bees? 1 can assure him I had only one experience in going into an apiary; I found that there were more bees than I had reckoned upon, and I should not like to be an officer charged with the duty of going amongst them several times. The minister is putting on the statute book words, but he is not inserting any provision by which this law is to be carried out. Who is going to look after the bees?
Mr. ROWELL; If the Civil Service Commission advertise for some one to carry out this law, I shall not expect my hon. friend to be an applicant for the position.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext:
Clause 2
reads:
Feeding bees with sugar, except for the purpose of being consumed by them as food.
Can the minister suggest any other purpose that the bees would use the sugar for except for food?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext:
I do not profess to be
well versed in the art of caring for bees,

but the point is this. A certain amount of sugar is all right as food for the bees, and there is no objection to that; but if they are fed sugar for the purpose of making honey, a lower grade of honey is produced, not at all equal to the honey produced by the bees under normal conditions getting the honey from natural sources. That is the* object of the provision.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext: I take it that the Minister of Health is interested, not so much in the health of the bee, as in the product of the bee.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext: I should think the question of the health of the bee would come under the Department of Agriculture.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
Bill reported, read the third time and passed.

speechtext:
1.	How many members are there on the Wheat Board?

The Dominion Provincial Employment Service is endeavouring to secure the necessary farm labour to meet the needs for. spring work, and already more than 500 placements are being made on farms weekly. speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue

speechtext:
The Minister of Customs gives his decision in the matter respecting the seizure, as provided by section 177 of the Customs Act.
If the automobile be forfeited by the terms of such decision, it is disposed of in the manner provided by section 143 of the Customs Act, that is, either by public auction, or as the minister sees fit instead of being sold by public auction.

speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, it is essen-tian for the future national welfare of Canada that appropriate measures be taken by the Government to fit and prepare all immigrants of alien origin for assuming the duties and responsibilities of Canadian citizenship.
He said: Mr. Speaker, it is my belief that this is the first occasion in our history that the subject matter of this resolution has been formally discussed by this House- an evidence, perhaps, of the extreme disregard which we have had in the past of the important subject of the Canadianiza-tion of our alien population.
For many years we have been receiving large numbers of newcomers, representing practically every nationality and every known tongue, every variety of dress and embracing both sexes of all ages, from the babe in arms to the grandfather and the grandmother-this motley crowd speaking eighty-five languages and dialects and representing fifty-three nationalities. I need scarcely point out that such a condition has created a problem which, at the present day
 \
at least, cannot be ignored by this country.	,
Let us look for a moment at the number of people who have come to our shores to make Canada their home. In the ten years from 1906 to 1915 inclusive there arrived more than 2,500,000 who came ostensibly to make this land their home, some temporarily, many of them permanently. They came, I believe, nearly all actuated by one idea-to live under better, conditions than those which they had experienced in their home lands. But they knew nothing oi Canadian life, of Canadian laws, of Canadian customs; many of them knew nothing of Canadian civilization. About one-third of the two and one-half million were from the continent of Europe, and this element especially would be described by the words which I have just used. They, too, came to this country with no knowledge of our language or our history. Many of them had lived under conditions which would be absolutely repugnant to Canadian people, and many of them brought to this country and adopted here the very same conditions under which they had been living in the lands which they had left. So far as citizenship is concerned we have treated these people with utter neglect. We have been too busy building railways, canals, factories and other important public works. We have been thinking of the opening up of our country and the settlement of its vast areas. We have been interested in policies, many of them of national importance, having in view the material welfare of Canada, but we have given very little thought indeed to the citizenship of our country; to the necessity, the importance and the methods of receiving these newcomers into Canadian citizenship. Perhaps the war did something to wake us up from the lethargy into which we had fallen in this regard. It assisted us at least in seeing that the condition that had been produced in this country by the receiving of this vast army of foreign people might give rise to a menace; indeed evidences were forthcoming that in some sections of our land there was such a feeling as . would constitute a menace to the welfare of this country. Canada is a young nation, and if her future is to be what we all hope it will be and what we all believe it can be, it is absolutely necessary that this question of citizenship receive greater attention than it has in the past. After all, the people of Canada are Canada's greatest asset. But I must say that we have among our people a large element which are an undeveloped resource, a resource which should be the

subject of great care and thought. The future citizen of Canada must not be the result of chance; he must be created by influences set in motion by the present Canadian people. Professor Fairchild, of Yale University, in his book on immigration, says:
The recent rapid development of communication has made the ease of immigration so great that we have been overwhelmed by the resulting problems. The movement of millions of people from one region to another is a phenomenon of prodigious sociological import.
In that phenomenal movement Canada has been sharing, the magnitude of Canada's problem is in proportion to the number of people she has been receiving from that movement as compared with her resident population. Professor Fairchild was directing the attention of the American people to the problem which immigration had produced for that nation. Our problem may be better appreciated if we illustrate it by comparing it with that of the United States. The largest number of immigrants which arrived in the United States in any one year was 1,285,349 in 1907. That meant an addition of about 150 immigrants to each 10,000 of the resident population of the United States. Canada's largest immigration was in the year J913, when 402,432 people came to this country, representing an addition of 500 immigrants to each 10,000 of our population. So that the number of immigrants which Canada was asked to absorb in that year was about three and a half times as great as that which the United States was called upon to absorb in the year of its greatest immigration. Both countries have come to realize the necessity of a more careful selection of immigrants. But the United States has gone further than that; within the last five or six years they have organized a vast effort for the purpose of Americanizing their people-not only the foreigners who dome to their shores now, but even native-born Americans of foreign parentage, and perhaps some also of American parentage.
Last year Canada made certain amendments to its Immigration Act, the chief purpose of which amendments was to exclude from Canada undesirable citizens. I shall not take time to enumerate those amendments, but if it is important that this Parliament should by legislation in the form of an Immigration Act take all necessary precautions to exclude undesirable immigrants from our country, surely it is of even greater importance that we should endeavour to reduce to as small a number as possible the undesirables who are now in our midst.
I think that a man would not be unreasonably optimistic who would believe that in the very near future we shall have a large immigration to Canada. If I were to give my own opinion-which, of course, would not be of much value-I would venture to predict that by the year 1940 we shall have 20,000,000 people in Canada, the greater portion of which will be newcomers to our shores.
Let me direct the attention of the House to another phase of this question. During the twenty-year period from 1900 to 1919 there were received into Canada 3,311,498 immigrants, of whom 1,188,946 were British. 1,268,793 American born, and 853,039 from other countries, but all of non-English parentage. Let me put this in another waj:	1,188,946 were British-born and
2,121,832 were non-British. This means that in the past twenty years we have had to absorb a number equal to twenty-five per cent of our total population. Not only is the problem one of number, but we can well understand that while a country of limited population such as Canada is may successfully absorb a certain number, when the number exceeds that to a very large degree, it may become quite impossible for us to absorb and assimilate the new comers to our country.
Another phase of the situation which exists in Canada is brought out by the figures of the Canada Registration Board. Their report shows that on June 22, 1918, there were in Canada of males sixteen years of age and over, 2,656,548, of whom 561,650 were alien born, and of those so born only 200,580 had become naturalized, so that we had in this class of males 361,070 who still acknowledged allegiance to a foreign country. I think every one will admit that this is not a desirable condition to exist in our country; that people who come to our land, especially those who come intending to make Canada their home, should become part of our life, should become naturalized citizens and should put themselves in a position to take upon themselves all the responsibilities of citizenship in our country.
Another phase of the situation is shown by these figures. According to the census of 1916 taken in the three Western Provinces, we find that out of a total population of 1,240,374 there of those of ten years oi age and upwards, 102,425, or 8.3 per cent were unable to speak English. This included, of course, native-born as well as foreign-born, and they were distributed fairly equally throughout the three provinces, with 37,504 in Manitoba, 40,126 in

Saskatchewan, and 24,795 in Alberta. Oi the different nationalities there represented, the Ukrainians show the largest percentage who do not speak English, with a percentage of 39.8 of those ten years of age and over. Of the Austro-Hungarians 35 per cent did not speak English, of the Poles 27.2 per cent, and of the Russians 27.1 per cent. These aie the figures as regards inability to speak English; but there is a still further phase of the question which I wish to bring to the attention of the House, and that is the number of illiterates in our country. In the three Western Provinces, out of a population of 1,240,374 of ten years of age and over, 92,732 or 7J per cent were reported as illiterates, the foreign-born furnishing 62,559 or 67J per cent of these. Each province seems to have its sharp of this class. Manitoba with 32,978, or 8.1 per cent of its population of ten years of age and over; 'Saskatchewan with 36,021, or 7.7 per cent, while Alberta had 23,733, or 6.4 per cent, and Winnipeg alone had 4,642 unable to read or write. I do not refer to the Western Provinces with the intention of showing that they are any worse than other parts of Canada. I use these figures merely because I have them and they are more up to date than any other figures I have for the country. But if we look at the condition of Ontario as reported in the census of 1911, we shall find, when we consider the age of the province and the comparatively small number of its population that are foreign-born, that the condition there is even more deplorable than that of the Western Provinces. According to the census of 1911 there were in Ontario 147,225 who could neither read nor write.

Yes, that would be expected. But 6.5 per cent of the total population was in that class. There are in Ontario to-day large numbers of foreign-born residents, and it is estimated that one-fifth of the present population of Toronto is foreign-born. Even old conservative Quebec is not free from this same condition, because figures of at least two or three years ago showed that about 105,000 of the population of Montreal were foreign-born.
In all this I am not casting one word of reproach on the foreign-born. I am using
[Mr. Steeled
these figures simply to show the situation which exists in Canada to-day, and this situation, as I said, creates a problem which we cannot ignore. This condition of illiteracy, this condition of non-English speaking-and when I use the term "nonEnglish," I include with that the other official language " French;" but I may be pardoned if throughout my remarks to-day I use the term "non-English" as illustrating the condition which exists in the greater portion of Canada at least. The fact that we have so many illiterates so many who do not speak and are not learning to speak the English language, so many who apparently do not desire to become naturalized citizens, creates a problem which we must face, and so long as this condition exists in Canada we cannot have a unified country. IBut to remedy the situation we cannot trust to the happy-go-lucky methods of the past.
The solution of this problem involves not only the commercial prosperity of Canada, but even the safeguarding of our national life. Whatever policy is adopted in Canada should have for its sole object the making of Canadians who will be absolutely one hundred per cent Canadian in spirit. We should endeavour so to .assimilate this population that we shall have one common standard of nationhood. To all the foreign-born who comfe up to the standard of admission Canada extends a hand of welcome, but every immigrant should be made to understand that this is a British country, that while he may continue to love his homeland, which in many cases hap had a glorious history and demands the admiration of its people, while he must not necessarily give up the use of his own language, in this country Canada's methods of life must be maintained. The inferior civilization of the native lands of these people cannot be transplanted to this country, and they should be made to understand that our laws and institutions must be respected, that in future Canada will be their home, and that their duty and allegiance and responsibility is no longer to the land of their birth but to the land of their adoption.
Canada as a nation has a duty to the foreigner. While she has a duty to the foreigner she has perhaps an even more important duty to herself and her future. In my opinion there are three prime requisites in our methods of dealing with the foreigners who come to bur shores. First, we must fit them for industrial life. A very large proportion of the immigrants from southeastern Europe come here as un-

skilled labourers. They come largely for the purpose of making a little money, and when that is made they purpose returning to their own land where they have left their families to reside during their absence. They serve a good purpose in this country, without a doubt, hut even these temporary residents should be compelled to contribute their utmost while in Canada to the country's needs, not only by their labour, but by their mode of life and their influence as citizens. All our immigrants iwho are engaged in industrial life in this country, especially Europeans, should be compelled to observe our laws of health and of society, for otherwise our social organism will suffer. The illiterate, non-English foreignei provides a fertile field for anarchy, Bolshevism, and the many other "isms" and manias that are cursing the world to-day, and from which no one suffers more than the same common labourer of foreign birth. Just in proportion as we remove his illiteracy and teach him to read and speak the English language, and teach him proper methods of living, do we increase his value as a national asset, and increase his value to himself and his family. Men who cannot speak our language are generally condemned to the hardest kind of labour and the lowest wages, and they will generally be found in the lowest ranks of our industrial life. It is manifestly unfair that the labour of 'the low-living illiterate foreignei should enter into competition with that oi the Canadian; but it is much worse when conditions are such that Canadian laboui is driven to compete with that of the Asiatic or European foreigner. In the first case, the /condition of the foreign labourer may be raised to some extent towards that oi the Canadian, but in the second case the condition of the Canadian labourer is sure to be brought down lower, towards that ol the foreigner.
I said that by compelling the foreign labourer to live under Canadian conditions we will foe doing him a service. Employers of labour testify that as soon as the labourer can speak and understand English, that moment his earning power and usefulness is increased. Testimony is given by American employers of labour that a man who knows, speakjs, and reads the language by which he is surrounded is worth on an average five dollars per week more than before he acquired that knowledge.
The second requisite, to my mind, is to fit these people for naturalization. We define the terms upon which a foreigner can secure naturalization in this country. We say to these people: We desire you to
become naturalized subjects of His Majesty, and when you are able to comply with certain conditions you will be received into the Canadian family. We say further, by our actions, at least, that we disapprove of a refusal or neglect on the part of any newcomer to become a full Canadian citizen, and yet we put forward no effort to fit them for taking upon themselves the duties and responsibilities of citizenship. We make no effort in fact to acquaint them even with the requirements of the naturalization law, not to make them familiar with what we [DOT]expect them to do. If we say, as we do, that a peflson /seeking naturalization in this country must have a knowledge of English or French, it seems to me it is our bounden duty to give them an opportunity to learn either English or French. In the United-States a few years ago a concerted effort was made by Congress to remove some of these disabilities in respect of the foreigner, and to provide meanls whereby they could become familiar with the need and the methods of securing haturalization. The results were amazing. Let me give a few figures taken from United States records. In 1910, there were 222,264 applicants for naturalization, and in 1915, 354,132 4 p.m. -an increase of over fifty per cent.
In 1919 there were about 650,000 applicants for naturalization. There is no doubt that much of this increase was due to the efforts put forward to give the foreigner such conveniences and opportunities as would enable him to comply with the requirements of thfo naturalization law.
The third requirement, I think, is to fit these men for the franchise. One of the chief responsibilities laid upon the newly naturalized citizen is the exercise of the franchise. Canada, we delight to say, is a democratic country; we are a democratic people, but if we as a democratic people are going to govern ourselves in a democratic way, we must do so wisely.

The conditions which have existed in the past should not be allowed to exist in the Canada of the future and because slums existed in ancient cities and have existed in nearly all cities up to the present, is no reason at all why they should be allowed to exist in the cities of Canada. The homes of the foxeigners, their surroundings and the field of their labour, should be according to Canadian standards.

They should not be permitted to bring into this country the standards of life in the lands which they have left or to adopt these standards here and live according to them. They should be compelled to approach the Canadian standard. Not long ago, it is reported, a strike occurred among the foreign workmen in an American plant. They sought a conference with their employer and their demands were under three heads, as follows: They said they wanted a place to hang their hats and coats; they wanted a place to wash and they wanted an arrangement by which the foreman should stop kicking them. Whether that really occurred or not I cannot say but at all events it illustiates reasonably well, the conditions that exist in many of our labour fields in our country. The foreign labourer is not always properly treated and especially is he not properly treated by his own foreign employer.
But not only should the labourer of foreign birth be looked after; the foreign-born woman needs attention and all the more so now that in a few years at most she will probably be adding her voice to the solution of Canada's problems. She has been entirely ignored in the past and little or no provision has been made for her instruction-little or no thought given to her citizenship. These women will be the mothers of hundreds of thousands of boys and girls who will be brought up to be future Canadians. Statistics show that the foreign-born woman rears just about twice as many children as the native-born woman rears and if the old saying is true that the hand that rocks the cradle is the hand that rocks the world, we say that the hand that rocks the Canadian cradle should be the hand of a woman possessed of the Canadian spirit.
The foreigner should also be protected as far as possible from the exploiter and the-imposter. His ignorance of our language, laws, customs, institutions and business methods should not be taken advantage of by any person. Many of these people come from countries where the system of government is unlike that which exists here. In the homeland of many of these people government means tyranny, taxation and terror and it is easy for them to believe that all governments are the same and to become imbued with a feeling of opposition to all government. It is then that the agitator gets in his work and sows the seed which too often leads him to lose confidence not only in the Government but also in society, in the church and in his fellow men. Bol-

shevism and revolution are held up by the agitator as the only remedy. The man who comes under that influence cannot be expected to be a true Canadian; he is apt to lose the spirit.
Then there is the man 'who exploits the foreigner commercially, and robs his pocket, and the foreigner thus exploited -in apt to lose the Canadian spirit and to believe that all Canadians are equally dishonest. There was drawn to my attention a few months ago a case which illustrates this point effectively. In a certain part of the province of Ontario a middle aged man, who came from Germany a few years ago and has during his residence in this country proven himself an industrious well-behaved fellow, desired to become naturalized. He knew that lawyers are the men who are supposed to be able to advise on legal matters and he consulted a lawyer.

Can we expect that man to feel kindly towards Canadian institution? Now offenses of this kind are not confined to lawyers. That profession is responsible for quite sufficient we know; but even some of our judges in Canada to-day are receiving the applications of German and Austrian citizens, are passing upon them, and are recommending the applicants for naturalization, well knowing, or at least they should know, that no naturalization certificates can be granted that class of people. What is the result? The applications are sent on to Ottawa, but naturalization certificates are not forthcoming, and the man who has made application naturally desires to know why he is not receiving a certificate. Then the political exploiter comes in. " Oh," he says, " you cannot expect to get anything from that 52
Government at Ottawa." I am not making these remarks with any political significance at all because perhaps if any other government were in power the same story would be told. The result is that that man becomes an enemy not simply of the present Administration but of any Canadian Government. There is no doubt such a man has been badly used and I would call upon the Government to see that this practice among the lawyers and the judges of our country in deceiving German residents who are applying for naturalization, is stopped.
But perhaps the most dangerous exploiter is the political type, whether it be a person, or a newspaper or, as sometimes happens, the two combined. They plead the cause of the foreign born, appeal to their prejudices, stir up whatever racial feeling there may be, and in this way antagonize these people against prevailing Canadian conditions. They are constantly endeavouring to persuade foreign born that they are unjustly treated, that those in authority are their enemies, that their liberties are- being interfered with-that, in fact, 'Canada is more Prussian than Germany. I venture the opinion that a very large measure of the antagonism of the foreign-born to things that are Canadian is due to these two classes of people-the social agitator and the political exploiter. They are both imposters and future events will prove that they are, and have been, the worst enemies of the communities they are to-day professing to guide. Both these classes make their appeals in the name of British fair play knowing well that they are only doing so in order that they may, so far as they are able, destroy that same spirit of British fair play. The man or newspaper which seeks to excite the prejudice of the foreign-born at this time of our history against Canadian law in order that for selfish purposes he or it may claim to be the friend and protector of the alien, or the alien born, acts unworthily and is one of the chief instruments in destroying Canadian unity.
The Government to my mind should at this time set on foot a great movement for the Canadianization of the foreigner in our land. We owe this to the people who come among us, and we owe it to the nation itself. The future welfare of our nation is largely dependent on the ideals of its citizens. Canadianization is not only an intellectual process but it is closely associated with our economic, industrial, social and political progress and prosperity, and



it makes for the very life of Canada. The foreigner should be made to feel that he will get a square deal in Canada, but he should also be made to see that Canada must also get a square deal from him. He should be taught that his children have greater opportunities in Canada than anywhere else in the world, and that is so because of our resources, our laws, and our free institutions. I would go further and say that the foreigner as he lands in this country should be made to feel that he is here on probation, and that if he does not make good, back he will go in the course of time to the land he has left.
There have been rather extensive efforts made in this country along these lines by certain bodies who, however, are unable to co-operate and unite their efforts. Perhaps no organization in the country has made a greater and a more genuine effort to do something for the Canadian foreign born than the Daughters of the Empire. I am glad on this occasion to be able to say a word on behalf of that society, and to commend the splendid efforts that it has been making during recent years to bring under the influence of our Canadian life and spirit the young people of our country.
The Toronto Board of Trade have for several years been studying this matter and are bringing it to the attention of the authorities wherever it can be done. Our churches and our settlement workers have also taken the matter up, and our Western provinces are giving it very great consideration. I think that every person who looks into it feels that these agencies are unable to adequately handle the situation as it exists. Some paramount unifying body is needed which can induce all the existing, agencies to work in co-operation, and even then the task will be one that will be almost impossible to overtake. I would therefore urge the need and the wisdom of the Federal Government undertaking a thorough and extensive Canadianization programme which, with the aid of the provinces and the municipalities, will produce results which will materially promote the future unity and prosperity of our people. The task of preparing this army of foreign born people for a full and intelligent appreciation of the higher social, industrial and political life of Canada, and to produce within them a right point of view with respect to their relationship to the State, is difficult at the best. But if this mass of raw material now in our land is to be remodelled into good Canadian citizens, Canada must [Mr. Steeled
pay the price. This is a service we owe not only to the foreign-born and would-be Canadian citizens, but owe also as a matter of self-protection to the state.
And I bring this subject forward not with the thought of restricting the opportunities of the foreign-born nor of restraining them from making the best of their life in Canada, but rather for the purpose of enlarging their opportunities and of assisting them in securing their full part in the blessings and privileges and opportuities which Canada so lavishly possesses and which she offers so generously to her people.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to say a word or two in support of the resolution of my hon. friend (Mr. Steel) . I think the House will agree with me that he is to be commended for placing so much valuable information before us. The Canadianization of the foreign element is a question of interest to the people of the whole Dominion, and it will not be settled until it is properly settled. Doctor like, my hon. friend very carefully and, I think, very accurately diagnosed the disease and then proceeded to suggest many remedies that might be employed in order to ameliorate, if not cure, the disease. There are very many conditions, he said, which called for immediate action, if such action is at all possible.
Reference was also made to the question of the naturalization of our foreign element. Let me suggest one or two instances' in addition to those which have been already given. In 1918 the registration made of all males over sixteen years of age showed that there were 110,000 Austrians, of whom 70,000 still retained their nationality; 32,616 Italians, 27,000 of whom had not been naturalized; and 47,777 Chinese, of whom only 625 were naturalized. This is evidence that the foreign population is not here for the purpose of becoming Canadianized, but rather for the .purpose of making what money it can and, in the great majority of cases, returning to its native land to live in happiness and contentment. When that is so we have a right to consider what is the duty of Canada in connection with a solution of the problem.
The foreign element is responsible for very many of the unatisfactory conditions in the slum districts to which reference has been made. For instance, in 1907 in the Province of Ontario there were no fewet that 6,120 undesirable immigrants dealt with by the authorities, with this result: 1,51" patients were sent to hospitals for the insane, at a cost to the province of $227,550;

there were 4,314 prisoners in jail, which cost the province $61,329.23; and there were 289 prisoners in the central prison at a cost to the province of $25,425.80, making a total cost for those 6,120 persons-every one of whom had been brought into the province under the laws of the Dominion-$314,315.03 for that one year. Since that time many deportations have been made, and the Immigration laws have of course been improved, but notwithstanding that the undesirable element continues to flow into the larger cities, and it is a very conservative estimate to say that upwards of $3,500,000 has been expended upon this class of people during' the past twelve years. They are responsible for a very large proportion of the crime that exists in the country, and they are .also responsible for a great deal of the agitation that is disturbing the Dominion at the present time.
Following the conditions in Ontario, I might give you, Mr. Speaker, an example of what is happening in one of- the western provinces. A press despatch dated from Yorkton, Sask., April 8, 1919, is as follows:
Thirty criminal cases, including murder, incest, illegal shooting, assault, perjury, comprise the criminal docket of the Court of King's Bench which opened its sittings here this afternoon. Foreigners are involved in every one of the thirty cases.
The same conditions are brought out in the report of Mr. Perry, Commissioner of the Royal Northwest Mounted Police, which was tabled a few days ago. Speaking of the action of the foreign element in the West he says:
They have shown little appreciation of the Just and fair treatment meted out to them by the people of this country. They have shown themselves to follow and support the extremists who -play upon their ignorance and appeal to their national prejudices and sympathy for the Central Powers. Bolshevism finds a fertile field among them and is assiduously cultivated by the ardent agitator.
The assimilation of our large alien population is of the greatest importance and it demands wise and sympathetic action and constant attention.
Speaking of the literature that is being circulated, he says:
A -number of convictions have been secured but there is a flood of pernicious and mischievous literature not on the prohibited list. Under the cloak of freedom of thought and speech, this literature is being spread for the avowed purpose of overturning democratic government and destroying the foundation of civilization. Appeal is made to British fair play to protect them in their efforts to destroy British fair play.
In spite of these conditions a considerable number of our people are anxious to bring 52i
into Canada very large numbers of foreign-ersTn order chiefly that our farms and factories may be supplied with very much needed help. Important as it is that such help should be provided, I think it would be a very great mistake indeed if conditions were permitted to be created under which twenty or thirty millions of foreigners should be brought into -Canada in the next twenty years. We must have Canadians. We cannot Canadianize these people sufficiently fast to enable them to be assimilated as Canadians. So the greatest mistake we could make would be to bring in such a very large number of people. What we must do is to bring in picked people-men who are in sympathy with Canadian aims, and with its British institutions. If we do that we will succeed. If we proceed along the other line, I am convinced that we will have merely a population instead of a nation- we will be a house divided against itself.; and we have the strongest authority for the statement that such a house cannot stand.
That thinking people all over Canada are taking steps as I suggested a moment ago to meet and deal with this question is evidenced in many quarters. For instance, the president of the Board of Trade of Toronto, Mr. Kenneth J. Dunstan, at their annual meeting last January, made this statement:
Canada may expect large foreign immigration within the next few years and it is imperative that adequate steps be taken to teach not onlv the English language, but also the fundamental principles of our Government and our ideals of citizenship. It is intended to actively aid in the organization of a national movement in favour of a Canadianization policy, which will help the foreign-born and their children to appreciate our form of Government, our laws and their administration, and also to appreciate the responsibilities and duties which go with the privileges of such citizenship.
I think his statement will meet with a very ready response. Every campaign that has been carried on unitedly by our people has succeeded. That campaign, if inaugurated, will succeed in doing a very great service not only to the foreign element but in arousing the interests of our people to the necessities of the situation. To make such an effort successful there must be some backing from the Administration. Therefore I would suggest that the Government deport all foreigners found engaged in unlawful agitatioii and enforce the law to the letter against all citizens who are convicted of similar conduct.
The -Government should assist by substantial federal -grants the provincial author-

tise in the education of the children of foreigners. Such grants should be conditional upon the flag flying over every school, and every day there should be some exercises to emphasize the meaning and value of Canadian citizenship. Every newspaper printed in a foreign language should be required to print in English translations of all articles dealing with national Canadian questions. The Immigration Department should give special encouragement to immigrants from the old landis and from those countries whose people have shown a disposition to become Canadians. These suggestions are worthy of consideration by the Government and by the members of the House. The Government of the day and all those who have to do with the enactment of laws should have before them as faT as possible the old Gladstonian declaration to the effect that all Governments must pass legislation to make lit easy to do right and difficult to do wrong. To the extent that we follow that course we shall speedily succeed in creating a sound, united Canadian nationality.

Mr. Speaker, to my mind, this is one of the most important motions that has come before the House this year, because on the success or failure of our educational system depends the success or failure of ourselves as a nation. Education is to-day a matter of provincial jurisdiction, and rightly so. But to my mind the Government would be well advised to start a federal Department of Education for the purpose of bringing together the heads of the Departments of Education in the different provinces and formulating, if possible, some uniform plan. 'The curricula in the different provinces vary almost as much as the systems of education in some of the foregn countries. Pupils who move from one province to another find the systems so changed that they are sometimes put back two grades. If a Department of Education were established in Ottawa we could get these educational men together and bring about some uniformity in that regard. We could also correct a fault which is found in all provinces, and which I call the one-man system. Under our present educational system, every student who enters school and does not complete his course must struggle through the same routine as that which applies to the man who reaches the top. In fact, we are educating the graduate but not the multitudes who never become graduates. Of the thousands who enter our public schools, 
from fifty to seventy-five per cent never enter High School; of the thousands who enter High School very few pass on to the university, and of the thousands who enter university many never graduate. Our system is so- set that the multitude must struggle along the same route which is followed by the man who completely finishes his educational course. If we had a Department of Education at Ottawa, with the proper man at the head of it, we could start a system throughout Canada which would tend to develop in the body who leaves public school an idea of what kind of work he ought to engage in. Not one in a thousand men finish their careers in the line of work upon which they first started out; they stumble along from year to year and from job to job, and sometimes they fin-ally land in the job that the good Lord intended them -for. I -believe that we could establish a system under which we could develop in the boy *wh-o leaves school the tendency towards a particular line of work-his ability to -saw to a line; to use a square; to -weld a piece of iron; to use-in a simple way, perhaps-a surveyor's instrument; to keep books; and so on. In that way he has some idea or his parents have -some idea of what work he is best fitted to do. Our girls, too, would know more about the -work that God intended them to do.
Then, we have another difficulty which to my mind is worse th-an the one I have mentioned. Up to the age of six or seven years our children are told every day to go out and play; their whole education up to that time consists in what they get from play. But when they go to school they are put in a straight row of seats and if they attempt to move or to speak to their little companions on their right or left, they are immediately corrected. T-he strictness of our discipline takes the individuality from the child. It is true that we mu-st have discipline, but in our method o-f enforcing discipline we are taking away the child's individuality. I believe that these little children could siit around the school room in moveable seats and their education carried on in such a way as not to do away with all the benefit they have received through their play in the days before they started going to school. The child must know what discipline is, but he must still have that freedom, that opportunity for his love of play, that individuality, which -have been instilled into him up to the time when he fiist enter-s school. For these reasons I think that the Dominion Government would

be well advised to exercise some supervision over our educational system through a Department of Education at Ottawa.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the House and the country are indebted to the member for South Perth (Mr. Steele) for bringing to our attention a question which is, to my mind, of very great importance. The motion deals with something which this (Government should have taken up long ago. In the past the Governments of the day have been satisfied to bring people to Canada from Central Europe, set them in colonies, and leave them there. They have treated them about the same as we might treat imported horses or cattle which were brought here to perform agricultureal work and receive no further attention. The Governments of the past have failed to Tealize the necessity of Can-adianizing these people, -and on that account they deserve strong condemnation. But the leaders of these people who have been neglected by the -Government have in their own colonies carried out a policy of segregating their followers from -Canadian-born citizens for the purpose of exploiting them in elections and otherwise, -and the result has been very serious to the foreign-born population of our country. I understand that throughout the Northwest to-day you can find large numbers of people who have been in Canada many years, yet who do not sufficiently understand the English language to carry on business. This segregation of the foreigner from the native-born citizen of -Canada has enabled the foreigner's selfish leaders to develop prejudices that are very difficult to remove and (which aTe o-ften carried on to the second generation. Unless some steps are taken by this Government-steps that are beyond the reasonable responsibilities of Provincial Governments-this condition of affairs will not be improved with -any rapidity, and the state of things. which we find to-day will be perpetuated. So that the member for South Perth has made -a distinct contribution to the work of the session by bringing this matter forward. Most of the provinces have done something, but the Federal authority has entirely neglected its responsibilities- in this regard. The first really effective measures which have been -adopted in any part of Canada for Canadianizing the foreign-horn are to be credited to the Government of Manitoba, and the success that that Government has had in its new school legislation with respect to the Canadianizing of the foreigner warrants us in believing that similar measures
adopted in other provinces with assistance from this Government in other directions would produce the quickest and most important results. What Manitoba -has done is having its effect in the other provinces of western Canada, and it will not he very long before Saskatchewan -and Alberta will follow the example of Manitoba, because force of public sentiment will compel them to do so. Already those provinces have gone a considerable distance in that direction, and the Governments of those provinces are showing their sense of responsibility. In the United -States it has been recognized that the Americanizing of the people of foreign birth is a proper federal responsibility. That opinion rests on sound ground, and the Canadianizing of the foreigners of this country is likewise a federal responsibility. It is necessary and wise that the provinces should co-operate, in this work. The authority they -have in regard tc schools places the provincial power in a very strong position ot assist in this work; but I do not think that this Government has done its share; it has certainly never taken any initiative in inaugurating and carrying through a broad policy in this- direction.
The Canadianizing of the people of Canada i-s perhaps.one of the most important things that this Government has to do. It is fundamental in a new country like this that the people should understand our institutions; that they should learn our standards-of living and understand something of the fabric of our society. This country to-daj is in the making. If we allow those who have come to ns to go on as we have been allowing them to drift in the past, without proper instruction as to our institutions or the character and duties of our citizenship, and -if we add to them other hordes of foreigners Who may come to this land in the years that are approaching, we shall have no ground whatever to anticipate that we shall have anything like a unified country in this Dominion. Unless those hundreds of thousands who have come in and those who may come in aTe Canadianized, we shall have in this country a serious' situation, and with every year the problem will become more difficult of solution. Already this is a problem of very great magnitude in Canada. We have it in our large cities to a limited degree, but it i-s much more serious in the wide agricultural areas where the people are isolated and segregated into communities of their own race -and speech. And every year that passes adds to the difficulty of a final solution of this question.

In 'may sections of Western Canada the electors of foreign birth ate in control of local affairs; they exercise a great influence on provincial policies 'at the present time, and they form an ifnportant element in deciding the policies of the Dominion. It seems to me that it should be very plain to every man who has the power to think that the education and instruction of those people is one of 'the first and primary obligations of this Government. It is bad enough to have a big foreign population in a city, but there they have an environment that assists very materially in giving them information and instructing them in our principles of government. Their children go to public schools where they mix with children of British parentage; they are surrounded on every side by those who understand our institutions; they see the standards of living that have been set up, and little by little they are inevitably influenced thereby. But in those sections of the West where they are segregated into isolated colonies, they have none of this environment; they have extremely limited opportunities of studying Canadian ideals, and it is not surprising that they should be slow in acquiring anything like an adequate knowledge of the duties of Canadian citizenship. My judgment is that Federal aid should be given in generous measure for the purpose of instructing the adults of foreign nationalities who are in or who may come to this country, both in the language of the country and in the principles of citizenship of this country. This is a responsibility which rests primarily upon this Government' and upon this Parliament. When this work is added to that done by the schools conducted by the provincial authorities, it would be possible to have every member of a household of foreign birth being instructed at the same time in those things that make good Canadian citizens. In my limited association with foreigners in our city and elsewhere I have found that they show profound appreciation of the kindness of those who take an interest in their welfare. They are most responsive to kindly treatment, and they are quick to take instruction when it is offered to them by those who, they have reason to believe, are not serving any selfish purpose. But, unfortunately, so little interest has been displayed by the Dominion Government and such scant consideration has been shown by society at large to the problem of bringing the foreign-born citizen up to the standard set for the native-horn, that we have made very little progress in that direction. Progress has heen -made by the slow process of ex-
ample; and while I admit that it is potent, something more than that is necessary in order that results may be achieved in a short period of time.
This response to kindly treatment is illustrated in a very special and remarkable way in Manitoba. The Manitoba Government under the Premiership of the Hon. T. iC. Norris, has been able to convince the Galicians, Poles and other foreigners in that province that by insisting upon their children going to school, the Government is doing them a great kindness. It has taken a little while to convince them of that, but since the Act was passed three or four years ago the great majority of the Galicians and Poles and other foreigners in Manitoba have been brought to see that the measures enacted by the Provincial Government for the instruction of their children give them a better *chance to compete in every walk of life, add to their prosperity and help to (bring them up to the same level as the native-born in business and social intercourse. These people place a very high value upon this instruction, and the parents who are unable to converse in the language of the country take great pride in their *children being able to do so. They have found that by taking their children who have learnt the language of the country with them when they go to market or to the store, they make very much better progress in their dealings, and they are naturally proud that their children can take their part in ordinary conversation wherever they may happen to be. This is a most gratifying feature of the Canadian-izing efforts that have been put forward in the province of Manitoba, and it should encourage this Government to take this question under very careful advisement to determine just what steps can be taken by this Parliament to supplement what is being done by the provincial governments, particularly in the West, where the work has been done to the best advantage, and where it most needs to be done, because of the isolation in which many of these people live. The time has passed when this country can bring in Mennonites, Doukhobors, Galicians or any other class and after planting them down in a wide agricultural area, say to them: Now, we have no further interest in you. You cannot make a country in that way. The character of a country depends upon the character of its people, and if we leave these people to themselves we cannot expect to build up in Canada the kind of a country we are capable of building up by intelligent effort. I remember

a titne when even the British-born newcomer to Canada found himself isolated in this country, and in the city of Toronto we found it necessary to organize a league, which we called the British Welcome League. We had a building open to receive men and women of British birth the day they reached the city, and they found friends at once in the officers of the league who would advise them where to go, when to go, and what to do to get a start. That is what should be done with every man and woman of every family that comes to Canada, whether they be British or Galicians. It would start them off with the idea that they had come to a country where they were welcome. I hope that every pian, woman and child who comes to Canada in the future will be welcomed in that way, and will be instructed as rapidly and as fully as possible in the requirements of good citizenship. We must, of course, insist upon obedience to the laws of this -country, and that of course means that we must instruct the newcomers as to what the laws of the country are. We must teach them in the kindest and the most efficient way what they must do to perform their full duty beside the native-born citizens.
I agree with the mover of this resolution (Mr. iSteele) that in the future we must deal with our new citizens very differently from what we have done in the past. I believe this is a matter of self-preservation. I believe it is also a plain duty that we owe to those who come here to make their homes in this country. We in Canada have the greatest opportunity that has ever been given to any people since history began. My vision of Canada is that at the end of this century she will be one of the greatest nations in the world, one of the most populous, most powerful, and most prosperous nations in the world. Canada enjoys the finest climate that can be found anywhere, and advantages of soil and climate and natural resources that make it possible for us to build up in this country the most virile race that can be found in any part of the globe. But those who tcome to us not understanding our institutions must be instructed and educated and inspired with the high ideal of service to this .country as Canadian citizens, and it is the -bounden duty of this Government to take the initiative in this -work .
