speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for South Perth (Mr. 'Steele) deserves the congratulations of this House for bringing before us the subject matter of his resolution. I think
that is due him because primarily his resolution has to do with the social and mental and moral life of citizens, and indirectly with their economic welfare. It requires no argument to-day, I am sure, to prove that men are worth a great deal more than money, that boys are infinitely more valuable than business, and that girls are to be considered before goods,-in a word, that people are of vastly more significance than either their possessions or their -politics.
The resolution speaks of alien immigration, and the proper education of alien immigrants. The immigration question is not a new one, but, as has been pointed out, -any education looking towards citizenship ,on the part of these people, is practically a new thing so far as this and -5 p.m. other Parliaments of Canada are concerned. The war has taught us among other things that the quality and character of our citizenship has a great deal to do with the spirit that will be manifest when the nation is in danger- the spirit that is necessary for the perpetuation of our national life. In the closing years of the last century, and indeed until the war began, it would seem that the only consideration in immigration was the question of numbershow many can we induce to come to the Dominion of Canada? I think to-day we are not emphasizing quantity; the tendency is rather to emphasize quality.
In order to understand the matter -aright it -seems to m-e that we should be agreed at any rate upon one thing, namely, the viewpoint from which this -whole subject of immigration -should be -considered. In a word, what is the ultimate object in securing immigration -to this country? What have we really in mind? What ife the goal in view? In the last analysis we might agree that the national welfare -is the fundamental consideration and that any policy -that has to do with immigration -should have in view not sectional welfare or local interest but the national welfare and prosperity. If that be -so, and I think -possibly we could agree upon that, our aim in the securing of immigration will -become somewhat clearer. We will Tealiz-e that it is not nece-ss-ary to relieve the old nations of -any -surplus population which they may have. It may -do that and from their standpoint they will -certainly favour a policy which will relieve them of -their surplus population. They would like to have their -social problems solved but I claim it is not our business to undertake an immigration policy that

must remove it from the realm of sentiment and place it upon a big, broad, and national basis. As I see it, iSir, the question in the last analysis amounts to this:	Is British
Columbia to be maintained for a white Canadian citizenship, or is it to be held in reserve for an Oriental population? if the former is conceded then the influx of Orientals must be restricted; and another great question in that province to-day, coming to us from all kinds of organizations, is along the line " Shall we any longer permit land to be held in fee by the Oriental or shall he even be allowed to lease it?" I recognize the fact that the settlement of this question may involve somewhat serious international complications. Probably it does, but so far as our province is concerned the question is one which must be faced, and faced bravely and fearlessly, in the very immediate future, so that we in the far West may be able to make some provincial contribution to the Canadianiza-tion of our entile citizenship. At present there is no prospect whatever of our being able to do that if any large immigration on the part of settlers and residents from the Orient is permitted. Again I wish to say that I am exceedingly glad that the hon. gentleman (Mr. -Steele) has introduced this resolution which has primarily to do with the social, moral, and mental life of our coming citizenship, and I congratulate him upon his course.
Mr. JOHN W. EDWARDS (Frontenac): I do not intend to occupy more than a few minutes this afternoon, Mr. Speaker. I merely rise to add my commendation to that which has been already tendered to the member for South Perth (Mr. Steele) for his most interesting and instructive speech, and to say that I place myself in accord with his resolution. I shall refrain from making any extended remarks, for the reason that I have a motion on the order paper which I hope to bring up after the Easter recess, and which necessarily follows to some extent along the lines of the argument which has been advanced this afternoon. However, I did not want any hon. member to understand that I was withdrawing my motion, because it seems to me it is somewhat different from that now -before the House in proposing means to bring about the same ends which my hon. friend has in view. I shall therefore wait until that occasion to place before the House some arguments in favour of a Federal Bureau of Education, which I think is essential in the interests of the country.

(Mr. JOHN H. BURNHAM (West Peterborough) : Mr. -Speaker, this is probably the most important question that could be brought before the House of iwhat one might call " indirect nationality." I regret very much indeed, Sir, that the Opposition seems to take no interest in this important question.
Some hon. (MEMBERS: <Oh yes, we do.
-Mr. BURNHAM: The afternoon has worn itself away and the discussion seems to be drawing to a close, yet none of the oracles of wisdom on the other side of the House have ventured on this important question to make a remark which would be of the least benefit to the country at large. We expected something from them; perhaps we expected too much. They stand excused if they have not any ideas, but I did give them credit for having at least one idea on this important subject.
But what am I to say about the Farmers' Party? They seem to be absolutely oblivious of the whole matter. They represent primarily the West, but they have not even awakened to the fact that there is discussion proceeding on this subject. This is, to my mind, the saddest feature of all, and it shows that education in this country above all things must begin at home. Let us begin here in this House and educate hon. members who sit opposite us.up to the high possibilties of their station.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to continue the discussion of the resolution moved by the hon. member for South Perth (Mr. Steele) I desire to express my appreciation of its importance, and to give expression at the same time to two or three ideas that have been in my mind for a number of months. In the first place, while the problem of immigration is closely related to the resolution submitted to us, it is hardly contained in that resolution. It would seein that this resolution is an attempt to get at the problem of assimilation. It deals more particularly with the foreigners we already have in this country. With that in mind, is it not well for us to recognize the fact that we have a considerable body of foreign-born people in this country, and that these people may become a great liability, or a great asset? Much depends upon how we treat them, what we do with them, what we make it possible and necessary for them to do with themselves. I do not believe that we can (Canadianize a million and a half of foreign-born people by mere mechanical processes. If they are to live with us, we want to make it possible for them to become part of us. If we do not want them to live with us, the sooner we get rid of them the better. While, personally, I have fairly strong convictions with regard to the need of a rather severe immigration , policy, and while 3 am satisfied we should see to it that naturalization laws of a strict character are put into force, I am inclined to think that with regard to the better type of foreigner living in Canada we cannot coerce him into the possession of the Canadian spirit. We can show him with all seriousness, and in a very definite and positive way, what the laws of the land are; wa can explain to him the difference between our institutions and the institutions that he was glad to escape from on the other side of the Atlantic; but with it all, ' I am inclined to believe, we must in some way or other, as a nation,.as communities, and as individuals, endeavour to make use of a broader and a deeper socializing process than can be contained merely in legislation. All the legislation that we have in connection with the admission of foreign-born peoples I think I believe in, but now, what are we to do with those who are here? Has not the Federal Government some responsibilities in connection with the prob-

lem of initiating the foreign-born people into real Canadian citizenship? They brought these people to Canada. Surely this is more than a provincial problem. The fixed educational institutions of our country are provincial, that is, those that we call educational institutions; but 1 am inclined to think that the educational process is a much greater one than is usually considered to be linked up with, and the purpose of, the so-called public school. I believe, as every member of this House doubtless believes, that at the centre of the Canadianizing process for the foreigner there will always be the public schools; but there are other influences at work, and there should be still other influences, operating to the end that these men and women who have come to our shores may come to understand what Canada is, and what it is to become a Canadian. The hon. member for West Toronto (Mr. Hocken) urged, all too briefly I think, the importance of the education of the adult alien. Merely giving attention to the training of the child in the school will never enable us to overtake the problem that is on our hands. There are the grown-up boy and the grown-up girl, who will never go to school again and who have never gone to school in this country. There are the impressionable young man and young woman and there are perhaps a very few of the older foreigners who are susceptible to instruction along the lines that will make possible their understanding of the simple fundamentals of Canadian history, Canadian institutions, Canadian customs, Canadian laws and Canadian community life at its best. The details of any such programme certainly are not for us to consider here to-night, but I am yet to be convinced that it is impossible to help, especially in the cities, a larger number of the grown-ups by evening classes, and by the use of moving pictures of the kind that will make them understand. I have been informed on good authority that in our greatest city, the city of Montreal, out of a total foreign-born population of 105,000, only 6,000 are reached througlj social educational classes at the present time. Is it not possible also to reach the grown-up foreigner in rural Canada? The mothers are being reached in many western communities through instructors who go out at the direction of the Health Departments of the provinces. Mothers' clubs and similar groups have been organized with splendid results. But this does not of necessity make for Cana-[Mr. Wliidden.l
dian citizenship. It appeals to the mother, let us say; the teaching she gets makes it possible for her to conduct in a more modern way the little new home, so that there will be fewer deaths of young children in that home. But is there not possible this larger recognition of the opportunity-yes, of the necessity-that lies right at our hand at the present time of telling these people in such a way that they cannot mistake what it means to live in our country. I am interested in the double column printing of many articles in the non-English periodicals of Western Canada. I believe that for certain articles there should be in parallel columns an English translation, but I submit that merely legislating into the foreigner's press a translation is not sufficient to Canadianize him. I look upon their papers as a necessary evil for the time being. I think they should have them if they are conducted along right lines. I am of the opinion that some of them are not conducted along right lines because in some of them I have had the honour to be accused of being very much opposed to all foreigners in western Canada. But why could we not have the non-English press -the foreign press, if you will-of Canada publishing weekly or monthly articles in the language of the majority of the readers of these papers, conveying to the minds of these poor Canadians in some cases,- non-Canadians and new Canadians in a great many others-what is in the mind and in the heart of a sympathetic Canadian-born citizen who appreciates the foreigner in the land. Syndicate these articles if you will, in the less formal sense; let these people know, week after week and month after month, something of our past history; make it possible for these adults to read this in their own homes. They are not going to school. In the rural districts they will not go to the night schools, where there are night schools, for many weeks in the year at any rate. There are scores of different ways whereby we might touch for their betterment the lives of the foreigners who would be Canadians if we would give them all the opportunities that are possible.
I do not wish to convey the idea that I am among those who believe that all the foreign-born in Canada have the right spirit. Nor yet should any of us be so foolish as to think that all the foreign-born are not going to be good Canadians. There were some of the neutral aliens and some of the friendly aliens who were very far

from being with us. during the period of the war. We simply have to take them as we find them. Those who are the most impressionable we will teach in one way; those who are the least impressionable we will try to get at in another way; and those who are not impressionable at all should not be allowed to continue in Canada.
May I, before resuming my seat, illustrate what I mean by referring to a question asked, by a Ukrainian. Many of us think that Ukrainians and Ruthenians are pretty much the same. The young man to whom I refer insists that he is not willing to join a Ruthenian club but has become a charter member of a Ukrainian club. He understands the difference if we do not. This is the question that he put to me: " What do you Canadians think of us people anyway? " My answer was: " John, it depends very much on the Canadian who is doing the thinking and on the foreigner that he is thinking about." That has always been so and I suppose it will be so more or less to the end of the chapter. But I found in that man's mind, and in his heart too, questionings and desires that proved conclusively to me that he for one was anxious to know how to be a good Canadian. The first man to leave his work on the morning of armistice day, after he had secured permission, in order to get into the hall where there was to be a celebration, was this same Ukrainian.
But in Canadianizing him or any of his class are we to think tha't we cdn for one moment make Anglo-Canadians of them? Their viewpoint, their temperament, their disposition, their fibre, are different from ours. I do not want to see them hyphenated Canadians. I am not so much afraid of the word " Ukrainian-Canadian," as I am of the hyphen in the thing. It is the hyphen that is the menace, Mr. Speaker, and we must have none of it. But taking it for granted always that there will be a difference in the outlook and in the conception in regard to many things, is it not in the letter and in the spirit of this resolution, is it not in the heart and in the minds of the majority of the members of this House of Parliament, to make it more easily possible in future than it has been in the past to speed up the process whereby we can Kelp the best of these foreigners in our country to become intelligent and thoroughgoing Canadians? For the old people, they will always see some things differently from the Canadian-born. For the children who are in the schools now, and for the children who are yet to be
born, I think we can reasonably hope that they will become, if educated, if socialized, if assimilated in ways that are fair-that are strict, or exacting, if you please, but nevertheless fair, and consistent-a part of the very best sections of the body politic.
I believe in the resolution of the hon. member for South Perth.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is unfortunate that this resolution has come on in the absence of my hon. friend the Minister of Immigration and Colonization (Mr. Calder) whose duty it would have been, had he been present, to speak to the resolution from the standpoint of the Goyern-ment. It concerns a subject the administration of which until 1917 was under the Department of the Interior but has since passed under a separate organization and a separate minister.
The character of the immigration that has come to Canada in the last years is pretty well reflected in the census figures of 1911, but as to Western Canada is more closely reflected in the census of 1916. It is a matter of major consequence to this country that in these western provinces there lives to-day a population forty per cent ol which, speaking roughly,-much larger in Saskatchewan and smaller in Alberta and British Columbia-is non-Anglo-Saxon-born and very little relatively French-Canadian. To say that that percentage is not Anglo-Saxon-born is not to express the whole truth. A great proportion of the balance is of those born in the United States of_ America. These two classes of immigration have been so great that we find two of our western provinces to-day populated to the extent of virtually seventy per cent, and more in one case, by non-British born.
This is a consequence of the rapid development of the provinces; it could scarcely have been otherwise. Had those provinces waited for their growth until the overflow from the more populated regions of the East should have achieved that result, the growth would have been exceedingly slow, the development exceedingly tedious. On the whole a fairly useful class of citizens has come into that land. The emigration from countries who were the enemies of the British Empire was large and constituted, I should say, over half, much over half, of the non-Anglo-Saxon population. I have no comment to make on those references in the debate to the conduct of that portion of the population during the progress of the war.



we have not been as careful as we should have been to see that they lived in as healthful physical surroundings as were essential to their proper development.. But we have done something to educate them, and* some of our schools in Montreal are almost entirely attended by the boys and girls of these newcomers. And, Mr. Speaker, it makes one's belief in the innate goodness of humanity-in spite of the remarks made by the Minister of the Interior vVho has just taken his seat-to see how these people quickly respond to education. An old college friend of mine, a principal of one of our city schools, assured me that in these families one saw' a remarkable difference .from the eldest child to the youngest who had attended school, and that in the course of one short half a generation the improvement was most strongly marked.
Out in the West I cannot speak with any degree of authority, but I remember ah address delivered to this House last yeai by the hon. member for Centre Winnipeg (Mr. Andrews), if I mistake not, in which he said that in many places the folks out there had more or less shown the seamy side of the West rather than the best t the newcomer. The story which I once heard rather illustrates this point. A man was asked whether he was a Doukhobor, and he said, "Oh, no, me smoke, me drink, me swear-me aCanadian." I am lafiraid that very often it has been the seamy side of our life which we have shown to the newcomer.
Now, -Mr. Speaker, what do we need to do in order to make these people good Canadians? First of all, we have to give them an example of Canadianism; we have to be Canadians ourselves. We have to do less talking about the Empire and more talking about Canada. The member for Brandon (Mr. Whidden) made a very just and true observation when he said that if we attempted to make Anglo-Canadians out of these people we attempted an impossible task. The ideal we have to hold up before these people is the ideal of Canadianism. We should have our own flag in order that the children in the school-houses all over the country might learn to honour and salute the flag that belonged to us-jjust as Australia, New Zealand and the Union of South Africa have their own flags. It is not that we love the Union Jack less, but because we love the Canadian ensign more.
And the next thing we should show them is a Canadianism which is a kindly Canadianism. We want to get away from the spirit of bitterness and into that spirit which was so well exemplified by the Act-

ing Prime Minister (Sir George Foster) the other day in this House when he pleaded that we get together. We want to get away from that spirit exemplified so amply in the House to-night by the Minister of the Interior (Hoii. Mr. Meighen), one of whose purposes in intervening in a non-contentious debate is that of insulting the Opposition. We want to choose the better and leave the worst part. They are there, both before you; you will choose.
Next, if we want to have a good Canadian sentiment; if we want people to love our country, we must make our country lovely. That is something which Parliament cannot do, though it may help; something . which provincial- legislatures cannot do, though they may help. But it is something which individuals can do. After all, it is easy enough to talk high sentiment, but it is much harder to live in accordance with high ideals. We have to see to it that we who belong to the larger families of the Canadian people, we English-speaking folk and French-speaking folk, have the proper attitude toward each other as well as to these men and women who from other countries have come here to seek a larger freedom and better living conditions. We have to see to it that these people find Canada a kindly place to live in. We have to see to it that we regard them as our fellow-citizens, just as dear to us as our own folk, and to whom we shall extend the same even-handed justice . as we extend to our own folk. We have to see to it that our national thought runs along channels which will appeal to the newcomer and which will be as deep and as wide as humanity itself. We have to develop a broad and a generous spirit in Canada; and I believe we can do it.
I find myself in entire agreement with , the Minister of the Interior, when he suggests that it is unwise for the federal Government to collect from the Canadian people sums of money and then hand them over to the provinces to be expended. I would, as far as possible, put upon the provinces who have the responsibility for spending the money the onus of raising it. That, I believe, is sound economics, sound constitutional practice, something we should cleave to as far as possible. A great deal can be done by public bodies and by private agencies to bring together men and women of different races and different beliefs.
If a mistake has been made in the great West, it has been perhaps, in allowing groups of these people to settle together. Of course, there are two sides to the question. These people come to this country,

to them a foreign hind; they heard only a tongue which was foreign to their own, and it was natural that they should want to ' group together. Why, it is said that if two Scotchmen were left on a desert island they [DOT] very soon would form a Caledonian society. That spirit of clannishness is a natural spirit; it has its good side, though i( has also its dangerous side.
Work has been done among the new Canadians by many people in Canada. I hold in my hand a work by Mr. Alfred Fitzpatrick who has made up a book which is a partly historical, partly geographical, partly a pictorial way of teaching the English language. This shows that men are at work on this important matter.
After all, there is little that is controversial in this discussion. Appropriate measures should be taken,-I would rather say by " Government " than by " this Government," because, after all, this Government is only indirectly and in a very slight degree involved in the question of education, and it is of doubtful wisdom for us who have a very large field for our endeavours to trespass on the field occupied by the provinces. So, if it could be understood that this resolution is to be regarded as meaning " Government " rather than the federal Government, I believe I could give it my hearty support and approval.

Mr. Speaker, the resolution presented this afternoon opens up for consideration one of the most important questions, I think, that will come before Parliament this session. Not having been here during the afternoon I do not know what ground has been covered by preceding speakers, but at the risk of repeating some of the statements made during the afternoon I desire to express in a few words the view that I hold in regard to this importaant matter.
If anything of value is to grow out of this discussion we shall have to get down to particulars and apply the principles laid down in the resolution in some way that will bring practical results. The government of our country naturally divides itself into three different departments, municipal, provincial and federal
In the discussion of this question it would he well for us to keep in mind that each department of government makes its contribution to the building up of citizenship in those who are to live in this country. And as we bring people into this country expecting to make citizens of them, each of those departments of government must make a contribution towards the education of those prospective citizens. Hitherto, we 53}	,
have been, in a large measure at least, vague and indefinite in our method bring' ing in of the foreigner and in the invitation we extend to immigrants to come to our shores. We have sent out immigration officials to different countries of the world, and particularly to the old World, and our ambition has been to induce men and women to come to Canada. Our success has been measured by the numbers we have succeeded in bringing into this country, and we have put a financial value, per

haps, on the number in proportion to the largeness of that number; but we have not selected as carefully as we ought, and after they have been brought to our shores and have taken their place among us as citizens of this country, we have done worse than that; we seem to have treated them much as Topsy was" treated by her friends; we-have just left them to grow up. We have-paid very little attention to them after we have brought them here except perhaps at election time when, if we thought we could make a good Tory or a good Grit vote, we might interest ourselves sufficiently' to secure their naturalization and their' registration. But we have not approached the question with the idea, of placing before those foreigners as they come to our country, the responsibility of citizenship and the honour that should attach to the privilege of being a citizen of Canada. I was thinking about that the. other day and this incident came to my mind. There was a time in the history of the Christian church when conflict arose between the followers of Christ and some of the church officers with regard to the views they held on certain questions, and one of them was arraigned before a court for trial, lit was learned that he was a Roman by birth and when he appeared before the court, the officer -of the court said to him; "Art thou a Roman?" He replied in the affirmative: " With great price have I obtained this citizenship " said the officer. He felt that it was an honour to be a Roman citizen and he was prepared to pay a price for it; he was proud of his citizenship. We have failed on this point, in that we do not place before these people as we ought to the responsibility and the honour of citizenship in this country, and the privileges that go with that citizenship.
Canada is a confederacy and we have Dominion Day as the great day on which we celebrate Confederation. It seems to me that Confederation Day ought to afford us a great opportunity in connection with the development of citizenship, not only in the

children that are growing up, but in the foreigners that are coming to our land. If we would properly use that day, we could make it a day that would be educational in its value and influence along this line. I had in mind an arrangement something like this. It "is thought that perhaps we .should extend the terms of residence in this country before we would grant full citizenship to the foreigner who comes to our shores. We could use this terms of years in an educational way to great advantage to those foreigners. Upon reaching our shores, the immigrant makes a certain declaration and assumes certain responsibilities-declares his intentions. (Supposing we start in on the first Dominion Day after the immigrant reaches our shores by saying to him:	On Dominion Day, we shall expect you to appear with the multitude of the people who are gathered for celebration on that day, and one hour of the day of celebration programme shall be devoted to education on citizenship. Somebody should he present to speak on the flag and what it stands for; somebody else should be there to speak on the institution and laws of our land. Then I would say that an opportunity should be given to the candidate, after having heard those explanations, to declare himself publicly whether he desired to proceed further and at a later date, enter into citizenship in our country. A splendid opportunity would be given to lay all the advantages of Canadian citizenship before the immigrant and also to place before him the honour of becoming a Canadian citizen. I would follow that course until the first three years had passed, and then I would say to him: Now you have proven yourself worthy and we believe that the time has come when we can entrust you with part of the responsibility of citizenship. Government might be divided into three departments, viz: municipal, provincial and federal. You as a candidate having signified your desire of becoming a citizen; having lived amongst us so long, and during that time having proven yourself woithy. Therefore, we give you the first step towards citizenship in this country, and by this ceremony we publicly give you the right to vote in municipal affairs. In connection with this ceremony-I would explain all about our municipal institutions and laws, the privileges and the responsibilities connected with municipal life. After the expiration of the second term of years he would again appear before the properly constituted board and publicly be instructed with regard to the duties and [Mr. Henders.J
responsibilities of provincial citizenship. Having satisfied the board that he understood what was involved in such an examination and having publicly declared that he desired to proceed further, I would confer on him the right and responsibility'of a provincial voter. Then at the end of the term he would come up for full citizenship.
At that time I would have the 9 p.m. meaning of federal institutions, federal laws and federal responsibilities explained to him, and he would then publicly declare himself as to his desire to enter into full citizenship. If we adopted this course, we would not have so many mistakes made by these people afterwards, nor so many misunderstandings in regard to what it means to be a citizen' of our country. We w-ould have a citizenship that would be intelligent, that could not be played with, and that would be able to understand public questions as they came up from time to time. I am glad that the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Meighen) called attention to the fact that the Minister of Immigration and Colonization (Mr. Calder) is not here and I hope that, when definite action is taken he will be present to give us the benefit of his thinking along these lines. I believe the problem of what we are to do with the non-English and non-French speaking aliens who are coming to this country to assume citizenship will be solved by our taking them into bur confidence and explaining to them our institutions and our laws. Let us talk these matters over with them and mix more freely with them. Let us play with them more, let us sing with them more, and then we shall bring them to feel they are one with us, and I do not think we shall have any trouble in making them good citizens.

Mr. Speaker, the object of the resolution before us, to create and develop a better citizenship amongst the foreign-born in this country, is certainly to be commended, but that the responsibility should in a large measure devolve upon the federal Government, as is intimated in the resolution, is a conclusion with which I am unable to agree. The hon. member for South Perth (Mr. Steele) in introducing the resolution this afternoon drew attention to the fact that from 1906 to 1915 some two and a half million immigrants came to this country. Going into the figures a little more closely, I might point out that from 1910 to 1914, 1,662,025 immigrants came to this country, and of that number 1,270,000 and more came

from the British Isles and the United States.
Just here I wish to express my pleasure at the remarks made by the hon. member for Macdonald (Mr. Henders). He is really the first member of the House speaking to this resolution who has given us any constructive programme by which the object of the resolution might be attained. I also wish to say that notwithstanding the criticism that has been levelled at the hon. member for Maple Creek (Mr. Maharg) I know from experience that what he suggested this afternoon, that we should assimilate these people by getting them into community circles and clubs and making them feel they are at one with the citizens of the surrounding district, would go a long way towards establishing proper assimilation and promoting a good understanding and feeling amongst these people. It has been a gross error in the past that so little care has been taken in the proper examination of these people before they were admitted into this country. I do not mean a perfunctory examination at the border, possibly sometimes by an inexperienced or inefficient member of the Immigration or Health Department, but their whole record in their own country should have been closely inquired into before ever they were allowed to set foot on a steamer sailing for these shores. If we had taken that precaution in years gone by, instead of herding them here like so many cattle, we should not have had so much misery and suffering, nor so much of that element that has been a disturbing influence to our social and moral fabric. I can speak to some extent from experience on this question because in the country of Middlesex, and it was also done by our friends in the county of Lambton, in the year 1912 we organized a publicity association to bring immigrants to that district. We published a pamphlet of forty-eight pages, very nicely illustrated, describing farm and city life in that community, and we endeavoured to have only *honest statements made to these immigrants so that when they arrived they would find nothing misrepresented. We also sent over an immigration agent from the county whose duty it was to go into the rural communities in these different countries and personally select for farm life in this country men who had been trained to agriculture, men of character, good morals and of sound health. Farmers in the community from which I come were ready to advance the money to bring these men out, and when they did arrive we went one step further. After we were satisfied that these
men would fulfill the duties of citizenship in this country, we raised a fund and advanced money to them to enable them to bring their families out so that they could settle here and be happy and contented.
I do not at all doubt that the Minister of Immigration and Colonization (Mr. Calder) intends to make ample provision for a proper examination of every immigrant who is allowed to sail for this country, and that the intending immigrant's record will be known before he leaves his native country for his destination in Canada. This work devolves, I understand, not only on the Department of Immigration and Colonization, but to some extent also on the Department of Health, of which my hon. friend the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Rowell) has supervision. I saw not long ago in the Civil Service sheet that is sent out, advertisements calling for efficient and capable men to go to the border and to seaports to examine immigrants coming in; and here the old trouble comes up again. How are we going to get capable men for this work if we do not pay them the salary to which they are entitled? Colonel Amyot, the head of the Health Department, is a most capable and efficient man, and if he has at his disposal a sufficient sum to meet the requirements of proper supervision in this matter, I have no doubt that as regards the physical health of the immigrants we shall get a class of citizens whom we shall be glad to welcome. It is an old saying that an ounce of prevention is worth a pound of cure, and I do not know of any matter requiring our immediate consideration to which that saying is more applicable than the subject now under consideration. If we take proper precautions to guard against admitting undesirables into this country we shall get the kind of people we can welcome. I happened to pick up since dinner a pamphlet published in April by the Commission of Conservation ih which reference is made to the character of some of the immigrants who come to this country not long ago. It says:
Dr. C. IC Clarice, medical director, Canadian National Committee for Mental Hygiene, points out in the Toronto Globe of January 27, 1919, that out of nineteen girls introduced into Canada by one society, eighteen were mothers of illegitimate children-that was the case in one community. Out of four hundred admissions to fail in one western province, only 23 per cent were of Canadian birth. The Austrians contributed 33 per cent, although their normal proportion should have been 8 per cent. Of 266 cases of unmarried mothers, which passed through one Ontario hospital. 191 were feebleminded, 4 were insane, 42 were border-line cases, and only 26 were classified as normal.

In Manitoba and Ontario the proportion of unmarried mothers was but slightly over 25 per cent Canadian.
It is not necessary to refer to statistics; there can be multiplied a hundredfold and on every hand evidences that the type of immigrant we admitted to our shores in the past has been an injury to the moral and physical health of our people. I would just urge again that the Department of Health which exercises supervision over the admission of immigrants will see that only men of probity, efficiency and ability are entrusted with checking the inflow of immigration as it reaches our shores.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to offer just a word in closing this debate and to express my very great satisfaction at the interest that the subject has aroused in this House to-day. A few things have been said which I would like briefly to reply to. Emphasis has been laid on the question of this being a matter of education and, that being so, the federal Government should not interfere. It seems to me that it is not absolutely a question of education. 'The federal. Parliament decides what immigrants shall come into this country and it decides who shall be kept out of this country; we define what, each applicant for naturalization must comply with before he can become naturalized; and surely it will be inconsistent to take the ground that, when the federal Government has done all this, and with a perfect right, it should in no way whatever- take action in regard to training the newcomers to be intelligent citizens upon naturalization.
If we take the narrow view of education as we commonly speak of it, perhaps there [DOT]would be some strength in the argument; jbut if we take the wider view, that the diffusion of any and all knowledge is a process of education, where do we land ourselves? What could we do in our Agricultural Department in the way of sending out information to our farmers? Surely, that is educative. The federal Government does that. If we argue that this Canaddanizing of immigrants being a question of education we should not interfere, the reply must be that neither should we interfere with educating the farmer in proper methods ot farming. I. do not admit that at all. I believe that the federal Government is [DOT]doing a good work in the education of the farmers, and I believe it ought to be doing a good work in the education of foreigners for citizenship, not for the purpose of
[Mt. Glass/)
simply g-iving them an "education" as we [DOT] usually speak of it.
I do not know that I could entirely agree with the hon. member for Brome (Mr. Me-Master), when he expressed the opinion that a mistake had been made in the West in allowing the foreigners to group together. If we are going to continue to show the indifference towards foreigners that we have done in the past, I would be inclined to agree with him; but if we as a federal Government are going to take the interest in the foreigner that I think we ought to take, probably it would assist our efforts to Can-adianize him if those of a class are allowed to settle in groups. If that effort is made to Canadianize him it can be more effectively made when these foreigners are settled together and we can reach them through their own leaders, schools, churches and social organizations.
I do not think there would be any objection by the provinces to the federal Government taking part in this work. In fact, I noticed that when the National Conference on Character Education was held in Winnipeg last summer, most of the Western Provinces, if not all of them, and some of the Eastern Provinces were represented. That conference passed a very strong resolution calling upon the federal Government to assist with this work. I am not aware that any province made any objection to the passing of the resolution. I should think that the provinces would welcome the aid of the Government.. We know that in Saskatchewan last year 750 teachers were called for more than could be obtained. Do you pretend to say that the provinces would not be glad of the assistance of the federal authorities in providing teachers to assist foreign groups and communities in securing not only education through the public schools, but also education in oitizen-ship, civics and all other matters which are necessary in order to make them good Canadian citizens?
Some criticism was also offered that no constructive programme had been suggested except by the hon. member for Macdonald (Mr. Headers). I do not think that this is the stage for suggesting definite programmes. What we are concerned more about here to-day is to get this federal Parliament interested in the great question of Canadianizing the foreigner. When the interest of Parliament is secured there will be some way of deciding what method shall be adopted in order to give effect to the

expressed will of Parliament; definite methods will come later.
I was struck with one or two of the remarks made by the hon. member for Maple Creek (Mr. Maharg). He was glad to see, he said, the interest being taken in this matter by members opposite, referring, I presume, to the members on this side of the House. At that time the hon. member for Brome and no other member-on that side of the House had spoken; so I presume that the member for Maple Creek could feel like Pollyanna; he was glad also because of the interest that was being taken in the subject by members on the opposite side of the House, and he had two reasons for his gladness. But, in his succeeding remarks he expressed regret that this resolution had not been introduced three or four years ago.

I would like the members of this House to be given credit for being sincere when they discuss questions relating to the foreigner. I do not think it is at all necessary that the members of this
Parliament should be accused, every time that questions relating to the foreigner come up, of having ulterior motives in the discussion. Many of the questions relating to our foreign population are great national questions and fraught with the greatest im-.portance to the future of this country. While members on one side may differ from those on the other, and even members on each side may differ among themselves, as to what is the proper policy to pursue towards the foreigner, I should think we might each give credit to the other for being at least sincere in the ideas we entertain and the policies we advocate. I therefore trust that the word "suspicion" will be omitted when we are discussing' what our treatment of the foreigner should be. I know very well how easy it is to create suspicion in his mind. Very often all that is necessary is to tell him that the Parliament of Canada, or some one else, is looking upon him with suspicion. That is sufficient to develop in his mind suspicion of this body or that person. I am very glad indeed that this resolution has been accorded such a favourable reception, and that its presentation has led to such a wide and interesting discussion.	[DOT]

subsubtopic: MR. DUFF'S RESOLUTION IN FAVOUR OF IMMEDIATE DEVELOPMENT.
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, fish being a highly nutritious and palatable article of food, greater production is most desirable, and an the fisheries of *Canada are capable of much greater development, which can be best carried ou; by an aggressive policy on the part of the Fisheries Department of the Federal Government, in co-operation with the fishermen and others interested in this great industry, it is desirable that the Government take. immediate steps to formulate and put into effect a vigorous policy so that the fisheries of Canada may be prosecuted to the utmost possible extent.
He said: Mr. Speaker, this resolution is one which contains truths which are of vital importance to all Canada at the present time, fin view of the fact that the nations of the world are desperately in need of food products I feel that it is incumbent upon me at this time to endeavour to place before this House reasons why the Government should in every way possible develop one of the major and great industries of the country.
The fisheries, Mr. Speaker, is not a new industry. It is as old as the world itself.

If you will turn to the book of Genesis, you will find it says there in the 19th and 21st verses of the first chapter that "it was the evening and morning of the fourth day and God created great whales and every living creature that moveth, which the waters brought forth abundantly after their kind. And God blessed them saying 'Be fruitful and multiply and fill the waters of the sea.' " Again in the same book, when the flood was to be sent upon the earth, and Noah was warned thereof, and when he was told to take into the ark every clean beast by sevens and every unclean beast by two, including the animals of the earth and the fowls of the air, no mention was made of the fishes of the sea, I presume for the reason that the waters which were to cover the earth could not affect the fishes of the deep. But we also find that when the waters had subsided and the ark had rested on Mount Ararat, the same book says that God blessed Noah and his sons and said unto them "Be fruitful and multiply and replenish the earth." And he further said "And the fear of you and the dr.ead of you shall be upon every beast of the earth and upon every fowl of the air, upon all that moveth on the earth and upon all the fishes of the sea, into your hand are they delivered." So we see that in the olden times the fishes of the sea were put there for man's use.
Coming further down the ages, we .find in the New Testament that the Sea of Gallillee was a very prolific fishing ground and that when the Saviour of the earth desired disciples to do his bidding he went to the fishermen of the Sea of Gallillee and commanded them to follow him and he would make them fishers of men. We all remember that beautiful chapter in the gospel of St. John where Peter said unto his brother disciples "I go a fishing." They also said unto him, "We go with thee." We remember the story goes on to say that they entered into a ship and that night they caught nothing, but when the morning came the Master stood on the shore and said "Children, have ye any meat?" They answered him "No," and He said unto them "Cast the net on the right side of the ship and ye shall find." They cast therefore and now they were not able to draw it for the multitude of fishes."	*
The same is true to-day as it was then, that despite the quantities of fish taken from the sea and the sums of treasure derived therefrom, that if we cast our net on the right side of the ship we will bring it back filled with a multitude of fishes.

Coming to more modern times let me say, Mr. Speaker, that our fisheries have the distinction of being the only Canadian asset which was tendered even a passing notice by ancient historians, one of whom avers that five hundred years before Columbus started on his eventful voyage of discovery, Norwegian and Icelandic fishing fleets operated in the bays of Newfoundland and along the coast of Labrador, whilst by the recorded correspondence of diplomats and treaties drawn by French, American and British statesmen, it is made positively clear that as early as 1450 Portuguese and French fishermen pursued the codfish on the Grand Banks. John Cabot justifies this contention when in 1497 he reported to his Government that on arriving at Newfoundland he found foreign . fishermen operating in the waters surrounding that island.
As early as 1632, when Nova Scotia was under French rule, two cargoes of fish were shipped from Lunenburg county to Portugal, and whilst describing the fisheries of Acadia as they were in 1699, Villebun, the French historian wrote as follows:

"If rightly managed this Province is a Peru." If more be necessary to show the antiquity of this invaluable asset of Canada that more is set out in detail in an international record covering the negotiations between Great Britain and the United States, when they entered into their first fisheries treaty. It is a well known fact that for years the British Government spent large sums of money to retain the Atlantic fisheries and that for many years American and French had no rights there.
Coming, to the present age it is my desire to give facts and figures to show not only the value of the Canadian fisheries, but to give figures of the value of the fisheries of other countries so as to make comparison and to show what they are doing. I also intend to place on record some information which I have gathered fronl time to time as to what the other countries of the world are doing to encourage and help this great industry. My only regret is that I cannot devote sufficient time to properly give to you, Sir, and the.House, all the information which I have accumulated in many years of experience of this business. I have therefor to apologize not only to the House, but to the fishermen of Canada and the others with whom I have been closely connected during my whole lifetime.
I desire first to place on record some figures with regard to the fisheries of Canada and the various other countries of the world which place fishing in the forefront of their

industries. In giving those figures it will be noticed that most of them are for years previous to the war. My reason for doing this is that Great Britain and the countries adjacent to the North Sea were greatly handicapped in their fishery operations from 1914 to 1919, due as we all know to the [DOT] fact that these countries were engaged in the great struggle which convulsed Europe and the world.
The value of the fisheries of the whole Dominion of Canada for the three years, 1910, 1913 and 1917 is as follows: In 1910 the total value was $29,965,433; in 1913 it had increased to $33,207,748, and in 1917 the value had jumped to $52,312,044. The increase in value for the year 1917-and that also holds good for the three years previous for which I have not given figures,-was not due to the increased quantity of fish caught, but was entirely due to enhanced prices which were obtained during these years. Owing to the fact that other countries were not producing as much fish as usual, and owing to the further fact that all other commodities increased in value, prices of the different classes of fish also advanced in some cases 50 per cent,, in some 75 per cent and in others 100 per cent. If time permitted I would like to give detailed figures of the fisheries of the different provinces, but this would take too long and is not really necessary for my present purpose. However, I would like to give to the House a synopsis, first of the value of fisheries in Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Prince Edward Island and Quebec for certain years, and also the value of fisheries of Ontario, Western Canada and British Columbia.
For the eastern provinces the value of the fisheries in 1900 was $14,283,679; in 1910, $17,099,570; in 1913, $15,737,207 and in 1917, .$25,812,094. For Ontario and the western provinces, including British Columbia, the value in 1900 was $6,353,560; in 1910, $12,747,498; in 1913, $17,402,276 and in 1917, $26,432,549. The value for Eastern Canada as given for 1910 is probably over a million dollars too high, as it is well known . that the accuracy of the annual departmental report for that year of the dry cod returned was greatly doubted.
It should be remembered, Sir, in comparing the value of the Canadian fisheries with that of other countries that the Canadian value is given as the value of the product prepared for market, with all the expense of curing and packing added toil, In European countries and in the Atlantic coast districts of the United States the value quoted is the value of the fish as landed by the fishermen. Reckoned on the same basis as in Europe, therefore, the-value of our fish in 1917 for example would not be more than $34,500,000, and of course the value in other seasons would be relatively less than the value shown. The increased value, as I said before, during the war years is due to higher prices caused by the shortage of European supplies and is not due to development.
In comparison I would like to place on Hansard the following statistics and information with regard to the quantity and value of fish landed in the chief fishing countries of Europe, which will give an idea of the increase from 1907 to 1913, the year before the war.

Let me say here, in case I might miss it later, that one of the greatest competitors which the fish merchants or the fisheries of Canada have in their dry cod is Norway and Sweden,- or I might more truly say they had this competition previous to the war, as in the years previous to the great war Norwegian
great quantities and came into competition with Canadian Atlantic cod, which had to find a market in these places. Let me also say that this competition was very serious in view of the fact that the Norwegian people paid more attention to the curing and drying.of their fish than our Canadian fishermen did. I am pleased to say, however, that soon after the war started, when it. was practically impossible for the Scandinavians to send their fish across the

Atlantic, our merchants on the Atlantic coast, principally at Yarmouth, Lunenburg and Halifax, erected artificial dryers, and in these dryers they are able to hard-cure their fish for the Cuban and New York markets, with the result that Canadian Atlantic cod is practically to-day supplying the whole demand of those great markets to the south.
It will be noticed from what I have just given you, Mr. Speaker, that Great Britain's fisheries did not increase to the same extent proportionately as those of Norway. The reason for that is the very high state of development which has been already reached by the British fisheries, whilst those of continental Europe were in a backward state and their people had only awakened to the great asset which they had in the seas adjacent to their coast line. It is interesting to note here that most of the fish caught by the countries mentioned a few minutes ago were caught in that little strip of water called the North sea, and despite the fact that day after day and year after year the fisheries are prosecuted in this small body of water with the utmost vigour, yet the sea is still teeming with food for the nations. I might also say, Sir, that during the last two years, since the British people have built larger vessels, they go further afield, and to-day during some seasons of the year they are fishing as far north as Iceland and Greenland.
More than sixty per cent of the fish taken from the North sea consist of herring, fourteen per cent of haddock, and about eight per cent codfish. Of the herring taken from the North sea, more than fifty per cent are landed by British fishing vessels known as drifters-and let me say here that there is no good reason why our herring industry in Canada cannot be developed in the same way. At the present time our fishing for herring is done mostly by nets, anchored in the sea. It would be a good policy for the Government to give to the fishermen of the Atlantic coast the trawlers and drifters which were in service during the war and [DOT] which are now anchored and out of commission, so that they could further develop the herring fisheries by this method, a new method to Canada, but a method which has brought such great results to the fishing industry of Great Britain and other continental nations.
As an example of the growth of this industry in Great Britain, let us take the landings of herring at one port, that of Yarmouth, England. In 1890 there were landed at this port 575,640 cwts., and in 1913, 3,122,280 cwts. The neighbouring port
[Mr. Duff.l
of Lowestoft, where the landings were almost as great, shows a similar advance. Steam herring drifters were first introduced in 1900 and motor drifters in considerable numbers in 1910. The number of steam and motor drifters operated in 1913 from certain countries bordering on the North sea was as follows: Norway, 202; Germany, 65; Holland, 67; and Great Britain, 1,774. The greater proportion of such fish as cod, haddock, etc., landed in countries surrounding the North sea, excepting cod in Norway, is caught by steam trawlers, commonly called beam or otter trawlers. Steam trawlers were first used in the early eighties of the last century, and the number in operation in the Nox-th Sea countries in 1913 was as follows: Norway, 3; Denmark and Iceland, 24; Sweden, 58; Germany, 256; Holland, 158, and Great Britain, 1,677. These steam crafts use a large net which is dropped over the stern by the fishermen, and sinks to the bottom of the sea. The vessel keeps steaming ahead until such time as tlie skipper thinks or feels by the ropes attached to the net that he has a catch, when the steamer is stopped, the net hauled on board, and the fishes taken from it.
As an example of this branch of the fishing industry in Great Britain, let us look for a moment at what is being done at Grimsby, England. In 1890 the fish traffic amounted to 1,427,640 cwts, in 1910 to 2,576,820 cwts., and in 1913, 3,595,840 cwts. To appreciate Grimsby's huge fishing industry it has to be borne in mind that its fleet of steam trawlers in 1913 numbered 650, the value of which alone amounted to over $26,000,000. I might say here that within the last month I received from a young fishing captain from my own county, who is at present in Grimsby, England, learning the business of steam trawling, a number of photographs showing the city of Grimsby and the fishing fleet tied up at the docks. The photographs certainly picture a remarkable scene, as at the time the views were taken the fishermen were asking for better terms and consequently the great fleet was not in commission. I am glad to say that the fishermen and the fish merchants amicably settled their differences and that the Grimsby fleet is again plowing the North Sea. The landings of this fleet are xnostly ' consumed fresh throughout England, the number being so great that ten special fish trains are dispatched from Grimsby daily all the year round.	*
As is well known, Mr. Speaker, cod constitutes our main fishery in Eastern Can-

Now, for a few moments I will take you to the adjoining Dominion of Newfoundland, where the fisheries are the principal industry and where, perhaps, fishing is done more intensively, considering the population, than in any other part of the world 1 might, perhaps, be a little personal here, Mr. Speaker, and say that this is the country where I learned the difference between the different kinds of fish and where I received, my early training in the fish business.
As an illuminating example, the increase m the valuation in Newfoundland's staple fishery exports for the period ending June, .1918 and June, 1919, is worth noting. In 7 913 there was shipped from that country 1,821,306 dry quintals of cod valued at $18,829,560, and in 1919, 1,894,023, valued at $25,860,112. In 1918 there were shipped. 216-.048 barrels of herring, valued at $2 -067,697 and in 1919, 211,555 barrels valued at $2,429,403. In 1SJ08 there were shipped 4,327 tierces of salmon valued at $91,805
and in 1919, 4,111 tierces valued at $112,412. The Newfoundland fishermen do not confine their activities to the waters adjacent to the coast of Newfoundland. A migration of many fishermen and their families to the rock-bound coast of Labrador starts in the early days of June. There they fish until the month of October, when they again return to their homes in Newfoundland. I had the privilege of watching the fishermen on the coast of Labrador during two summers, catch and dry their product for market, and it was an experience which was of great value and which gave me an insight into the life and work of these people.
Another great fishing industry in the Dominion of Newfoundland is the seal fishing. The seal fishery has shown a decided drop for the last few years. The total catch for 1918 was 151,431 seals valued at $863,552 and in 1919 the total catch was 81,293, valued at $278,145. This is a decided decrease from previous years. I am told that only ten ships prosecuted this fishery in 1919 and only thirteen in 1918. This is a great falling off, Mr. Speaker, from the years I remember, when some 25 steamers left the city of St. Johns and the town of Harbor Grace on the eastern coast on March 10 and prosecuted this great industry. I had the privilege of spending two springs at the* seal fisheries. I saw about 250,000 seals on ice. at one time-an experience which only few in this v'orld have had, and one which I would not have missed for a great deal. A little seal fishing is carried on in Canada, but not very much. However, for a number of years a steamer has been leaving Halifax every spring for the purpose of engaging in the seal fishing business. For several years the "Harlaw," owned by J. A. Farquhar, prosecuted the seal fishing industry. During the last few years, the same firm have sent out the steamers "Seal" and "Sable." Fishermen on the Magdalen Islands and around the Cape Breton shore sometimes get a few seals, but as I say, the industry is riot very largely carried on so far as Canada is concerned.
The Newfoundland fisheries, in addition to finding employment for the Newfoundland people and providing food for numerous foreign countries, is also a great benefit to Canada. It is almost impossible to realize what would happen the great Lunenburg fleet, which operates from my owm county, if it were not for the fact that during the summer months the Newfound-

Then, a great many Canadian schooners manned by Canadian seamen-who by the way are some of the best in the world-are chartered by Newfoundland merchants to proceed to different ports in Newfoundland and there load codfish for Europe, West Indies or Brazil. I might say that throughout the whole of the war, vessels belonging to Nova Scotia were chartered to Newfoundland merchants and took the Newfoundland fishery catch to Europe in spite of the submarine menace.

The Alaskan fisheries, however, are developing rapidly. In 1917 there were 21,491 persons employed in the Alaskan fisheries, and the value of the product when prepaired for market amounted to $51,466,980. That was a record up to that time. But in the year 1918 a much higher record was established, when 31,213 persons were employed and the value of the product amounted 'to $59,154,859, which was a sum nearly eight times the purchase price of the territory fifty years ago.
The country which has perhaps shown more rapid progress in the years immediately preceding the war than any American or European country is that of Japan. For a number of years the Government of

Japan has sent its scientists and experts to the different fish producing centres where a great deal of valuable information with regard to our fisheries has been gleaned. This information, which no doubt is afterwards returned to the Government, has been taken advantage of by this wideawake little nation across the Pacific. In the year 1907 only one steam -trawler was operated out of Japan. In the following year there were two at work, in the next year thirteen, which was followed by 23 in 1910, 76 in 1911 and 110 in 1912; which shows conclusively that Japan is in earnest with regard to the development of her fisheries. The value of Japanese fisheries ran from $33,177,750 in 1908, to $45,063,250 in 1912, and to $48,295,250 in 1913. The disturbing feature with regard to the situation is that dry codfish from Japan has now definitely entered into competition with the product of Canada and the United States. The Japanese have studied the Canadian and United States markets and have given closer attention to the best methods of curing and handling the fish than 10 p.m. we have. In 1918, 40,000 cwts. of Japanese fish were brought into San Fransisco, and up to the end of October of last year 20,000 cwts. had been brought into Seattle, whilst as many more were on the way. This competition is a very serious menace to the dry fish trade of this continent, by reason of the fact that the cost of production is so much less in Japan on account of smaller wages and lower standards of living.
The Fishing Gazette of New York, which line a wide circulation and which represents a large fishing clientele, sounds a warning note about Japan codfish entering the American market. In its issue of November 22, 1919, it prints full particulars and gives reasons why Americans should wake up and endeavour to combat Japanese aggression.
I think this shows .conclusively that if we are to compete in the markets of the world with the fisheries of other nations we have to pursue a much more progressive policy than we have in the past.
