Now, Mr. Speaker, I would like, for a few minutes, to speak of what has been done in other countries to help this important industry. With the exception of the help given to the herring fisheries in Great Britain over 100 years ago in the shape of bounties on properly cured herring and some assistance to outlying poor districts in the shape of loans to secure boats and the building of piers and shelters, the great fishing industry of Great Britain has grown up practically without direct Government assistance. The reason for this is found in the fact that the business has been a highly organized one for such a long time that private capital has always been freely procurable for putting into practice advanced ideas and for developing the industry generally. As an instance, all the harbour, docks, and fish markets in Great Britain have been built either by private companies, such as railway companies, with a view to reaping an increased traffic or by city or town corporations who levy dues on the landings for maintenance purposes.
Just before the outbreak of the war, however, fishing vessels grew so much in size and number that the Government, through what is known as development commissioners, gave grants of money in aid of harbour extension works, especially at the smaller ports. But be it said to the credit of the British people that the greater part of the cost in each case is borne by the town or community by borrowing at a low rate of interest from the Government. Since the war, the development commissioners are assisting demobilized fishermen with loans to secure new motor fishing boats and to instal motors in existing boats, and trawlers and drifters are being made available to demobilized fishermen or groups of fishermen on very easy terms of payment. This is one way in which Canadian fishermen or Canadian young men can be eneouragd to go into the fishing business, namely, by the Government helping them in the manner just mentioned; and as there are a number of small steamers owned by the Government now out of commission, it would be good business to endeavour to induce fishermen to take them over and operate them. Both in England and in Scotland attention has been given to the education of. fishermen for a number of years. At several centres and in many of the public schools, courses of instruction in navigation, net making and mending, cooking and coopering, have been provided. I was very much interested in a booklet which came into my hands a few days ago and which is worth putting on Hansard; but as it is rather long, I will quote only a few paragraphs from it. This pamphlet was issued by the National Sea Fisheries Protection Association of London, and the first thing it says is that the fishermen of Great Britain catch 7,500,000,000 fish dinners each year. The next heading is:
Why we demand a Ministry of Fisheries.
The Prime Minister's .pledge. The Prime Minister has stated:-	,
"We must see that the national resources are developed to the full, and that the State renders all the assistance in its power for the attainment of that oblect."
Then it goes on to say:
Our fisheries are to-day the greatest of our potential national resources. Very few people realise this. But it is true. One hundredweight of fish will give a meal to 150 people. Before the war British fishermen caught more than 24 million hundredweight of fish a year (3,600,000,000 square meals). We exported ten and a half million hundredweight, and imported about three million hundredweight. The country consumed 16,500,000 hundredweight. The fishing industry provided:
2,400 million meals for Britons.
1,500 million meals for foreigners.
During the war our 5.0,000 best fishermen and 3,000 best fishing steamers were busy hunting mines and submarines. The old men and the boys and the unfit men in old fishing boats contiued to fish. They caught on the average 8,000,000 cwt. a year. The German Navy sank 672 fishing vessels, and killed1 416 men while they were catching this food for us. Many hundreds were wounded and taken prisoner. They never shirked their job. They1 often, fought and defeated U-boats.
It goes on to say:
On. our fisheries we depend :
(a)	For a supply of the finest seamen in the world.
(b)	For a supply of the most wholesome form of flesh food. In fact:
(a)	Without the fishermen we should not have been able to defeat the German U-boat in four years. Because no other seamen are trained from boyhood to hunt their prey under water.
(b)	We must now either eat fish or become (very largely) vegetarian. Why? Because even before the war (since 1900, in fact) the population of the world has grown more quickly than the beef herds. The population of the eleven chief cattle raising countries had risen by 20 per cent before the war; their herds had decreased 4 per cent. This shortage of beef will be much more marked after the war. In fact.

the development of the fisheries is as important a factor in the food problem as the development of agriculture.
There are a number of other important statements in this booklet which was published by the British Admiralty in November shortly after the armistice was signed, but I shall content myself by just quoting the statement on the cover:
Our Debt to Fishermen.
In all their varied work round the coasts of the United Kingdom, in the North Atlantic, on the African Coast, in all parts of the Mediterranean, and in Egyptian waters, the auxiliary patrol service have shown an adaptability and readiness both for hazardous deeds, and for steady arduous effort.
That is what the Admiralty says of the work the fishermen did during the war not only in catchipg fish, but on the patrol boats that operated in the North Sea. The same thing might be said of our Canadian fishermen. While, of course, they did not have to undergo the same risks as the British fishermen, not for one minute did they stop their *work on account of the German submarines when they were on this side of the, Atlantic.
Now let us see for a few minutes what Continental Europe has been doing to cultivate this great industry. In Norway a number of schools have been established and subsidized by the Government at suitable localities on the coast, where fishermen are instructed in navigation chiefly. Some attention has also been given to the instruction .of cooks for the larger fishing boats; to instruction in the use of motors on fishing boats. Also in three special schools instruction has been given in fishery legislation, fishworking, and the natural history of important sea fishes. Funds have been created at various times for provision of loans to fishermen, to aid them in obtaining large vessels for deep-sea fishing, and installing motor engines in sail boats. The funds were pooled in 1907 and amounted to $275,000. There is also a separate fund amounting to $50,000 for the provision of decked boats in Finmarken, the most northerly and poorest province of Norway. The Norwegian fishery is largely an inshore one, in sheltered waters. For that reason loans were not. extensively used to provide large vessels and steamers for deep-sea fishing; but for the inshore fisheries loans have been very freely used in securing larger boats with oil engines.
The deep-sea fisheries of Germany are carried on by steam trawlers and herring luggers and steamers. The vessels belong to joint stock companies. No particular

state aid had been given to trawling com-_ panies, but up to 1910 an annual bounty of $1,500 was paid to herring companies on each vessel buil-t and sent to the herring fishery. After that year, state aid took the form of a guarantee of 5 per cent dividend on the capital invested in the companies. In 1911 the Imperial Government voted $175,000 for the development of the herring fishery and the other deep-sea and inshore fisheries. In that year also the city of Hamburg voted an annual sum of $75,000 for three years to provide loans, under easy conditions, for the inshore fishermen of the lower Elbe, to enable them to purchase boats and gear of an improved type. In the Baltic, state aid was given in the form of a loan without interest for an amount up to three-fourths of the cost of a boat and engine.
In the matter of education, fishery schools or classes have been established since 1895 by the German Sea Fisheries Society, acting for the Government, on the following general lines: (1) That a school he set up in every fishing centre so long as the cost of instruction compared with the number of pupils is not too high; (2) Instruction to be free and all costs paid by the society; (3) Instruction to be arranged to suit the particular industry of the locality. In 1910 there were 23 such schools or centres. The instruction given consisted (1) of navigation and seamanship; (2) construction and use of marine motors; (3) the natural history of important sea fishes; (4) instruction on improved models of boats and vessels, improved fishing gear, preservation and handling of fish on board and on land.
If our fisheries department at Ottawa had arranged some years ago to carry out just such a programme, this would have done away with the difficulty we have today of getting certificated masters and mates to man our ships; as, had these schools been established in every large fishing centre, the fishermen when at home during the ivinter could have attended them and passed the necessary examinations. Lectures are also given once or twice a week during suitable seasons on all matters connected with the fisheries. Another feature of the educational facilities provided in both Norway and Germany is the fishery museum established at various centres, in which are displayed models of boats and vessels, and specimens of nets, traps and other fishing gear used not only in Norway, but in other countries as well. There are also collections dealing with the treatment and curing of fish, including models of

fish and smoke houses and the utensils used in curing and canning various kinds ot fish. Since the war, the Germans are striving to supply themselves with a greater proportion of the fish they consume. To that end companies have been and are being formed which aim at building and outfitting additions to the trawling fleet that will bring it up to 400 vessels at once, while fishing harbours are being extended and new ones planned. At Cuxhaven $1,750,000 is being spent in extending the fishing port, Large sums are also being spent in the same way at Hamburg, Altona and Geestemunda.
It should be noted that schools and lectures, whilst they are doing good for navigation, are not bringing about the desired improvement in the treatment of dried fish in Norway. However, we on this side must admit that Norway fish are far better cured than some of the fish caught on the Atlantic coast and make serious competition for us in the foreign markets. I might say that the best fish we have in Canada is the Gaspe cod, cured along the St. Lawrence shore.
The Government of Norway are evidently not satisfied, and recently they appointed' a commission to investigate and prepare a plan and finance proposals for state aid for teaching fishermen and curers the best methods of curing split fish,, and also to inquire and. report whether a system of official inspection and marking of the fish would be desirable.
Of all the European countries France gives the. greatest amount of financial aid for the development of the sea fisheries. The amount spent by the Government in 191 i was $1,125,000, and by the way this amount should be carefully noted and compared with the sum spent annually in Canada, as well as the different manner in which the amount is spent.
Of that sum $980,000 was expended as bounties for the encouragement of the deep sea fisheries, $90,000 was for equipment and $66,000 was spent on the product itself. The balance amounting to $145,239 was expended on the coast fisheries, on superintendence research work and experiments. Regarding the bounty granted to the French fisheries, it is to be noted that the bounty is paid per quintal and amounts to 10 francs or $2 on each quintal caught. We, in Canada, are paying our Atlantic coast fishermen, both deep sea and inshore, the paltry sum of ,$160,000 and the amount does not really come out of the Canadian people, as it is the interest on five and half million dollars paid by the United States Government some years ago for certain privileges which the
British Government on behalf of Canada gave them.
As a result of the aid which is given the French fleet it is fitted out and sent across the Atlantic and fishes on the Grand Banks of Newfoundland and the fishing banks off the island, of St. Pierre on Bank Quero and the Middle Ground. This French fleet has increased from 178 vessels in 1905 to 254 vessels in 1912, some of them being steam trawlers. A new policy has been adopted by the French Government lately, and as they cannot build sufficient ships themselves they have placed contracts in a number of shipyards in the. county of Lunenburg and in Queen's and Shelburne for the building of large numbers of wooden fishing vessels of 400 tons which will be used to prosecute the fisheries on the ' Grand Banks and will be manned by French fishermen. These ships come across the Atlantic in April and return in October and November. They have mother ships which lie at anchor in St. Pierre until the fishing vessels come in from the Banks to that port with their catches, which are put on board the mother ships, and when they are loaded they return to France, and the fishing vessels then again proceed to the fishing grounds. Their last trips are taken home in their own bottoms.

I have no fault to find with this large expenditure; in fact as long as we are obtaining good results and the farmers are being helped and more people are being encouraged to settle on the land I would not object to further expenditure.
In past years large amounts have been spent on agriculture, and it is also a fact that the provincial governments are helping the farmers in a great many ways by establishing colleges and experimental farms and doing a great deal of work necessary to promote a knowledge of agriculture. This Government has also granted $5,000 under the land settlement scheme, to each soldier who is willing to settle on land with which to purchase his land and also $2,500 to purchase the materials necessary to enable him to go on the farm. In addition to that they have established credits' whereby the farmers are enabled to sell their products to foreign lands. If I am rightly informed credits to the amount of $300,000,000 have been established by this Government in aid of agriculture.
It will be remembered that a few years ago the Government voted a lump sum of $10,000,000 towards the encouragement , of agriculture and I might here say that a smaller special grant should have long ago been voted towards fisheries to help in their development. Most of the expenditure on fisheries at the present time is for salaries, patrol service and hatcheries and there is very little of this amount spent in either scientific or practical work for the encouragement and development of the great industry.

Sonie years ago the Government built two dogfish plants, one in the eastern end of the province of Nova Scotia at Canso and one at Cape Sable Island. Two or three years ago the Fisheries Department decided to abandon the work of exterminating the dogfish pest and sold the plants. This was a great mistake, as instead of selling the two plants already established, it should have been the policy of the Government to place additional plants along the coast of Nova Scotia and give a bounty to the fishermen to exterminate the pest which interfers with their work during the summer season. It is quite true that these plants did not pay their expenses or make any money for the Government, but it is not usual for plants' erected for the assistance of the people of the country in any industry to pay dividends or interest on the investment. But I will say this, that if these plants had been kept going for the last two or three years, owing to the prices which would have been received for the oil and the fertilizer, the Government would have received a handsome profit on the investment, and with proper business management, these plants could also have taken care of a large quantity of the offall and by-products of the fisheries.
In the March, 1919, issue of the Canadian Fishermen, several recommendations were put forward for the reconstruction and development of the Canadian fishing industry. Many of the recommendations will necessitate the expenditure of a good deal more money, and as money is a somewhat scarce .commodity and rather hard to secure in these days, the question should be first considered of turning the amount at present voted for fisheries administration to better use.
It should be clear to any one who intelligently studies the departmental blue books -and the more they are studied, the clearer becomes the fact-that a . large sum of money is positively wasted annually on the artificial propagation of fish. Especially so in view of the much larger sum spent in the shape of salaries and travelling expenses for the maintenance of an army of outside officers, numbering nearly 1,000, besides 40 permanent and 18 hired patrol boats with their crew's, whose main duty is police work,
i.	e., enforcing the observance of close seasons and other restrictive measures for the protection, chiefly, of the very kinds of fish that are artificially propagated at such enormous expense in our numerous hatcheries-. Any sane man is bound to conclude, if he looks at the thing below the surface,

that either the enormous expenditure on fish protection, or that on fish breeding, should be largely reduced. There is neither room nor necessity for both expenditures on a large scale at the same time. With such a huge output of fish fry from the hatcheries, the protection afforded by close seasons, and the elaborate system of licensing and controlling in vogue, one would naturally expect our fisheries to have been showing, years ago, a very greatly increased annual production. But what has actually occurred? The lobster fishery we know is barely holding its own, notwithstanding the output of hundreds of millions of fry from the hatcheries annually, especially in the last ten years; and now all the lobster hatcheries have been closed up as useless.
The Fraser river as a producer of salmon on the Pacific is played out, notwithstanding artificial propagation of millions of fry annually, mainly as a result of over-fishing by Americans at sea and in Puget Sound, and can never be restored except by the proper regulation of the means of capture and the season for fishing in salt *water on both sides of the international line. The artificial propagation of a species of fish like the Pacific salmon, which has to be maintained in such enormous numbers to keep the canning industry going, as a means of restoring this fishery, is about as futile as pouring a bucket of water into the Pacific ocean with a view' to swelling it a little.
A glance at page 102 of the Census of Industry, Part 3, Fisheries Statistics for 1917, shows clearly that the. total quantity of salmon canned in British Columbia from year to year is being maintained by the very kinds, such as pinks and chums, that are propogated artifically in very small quantities; while the sockeye, the kind that is produced in the hatcheries in enormous quantities, has been decreasing.
Leaving out the Fraser river altogether, and taking the figures for the rivers in the north, that are far removed from the destructive operations of American trap fishermen, we find convincing proof for the statement just made. In round figures, the blue books show that the weight of salmon carried by rail and steamboat in Scotland, the produce of Scottish salmon fisheries, prior to the war, was 40,000 cwts. annually. There are only two small private hatcheries for salmon in the whole of Scotland. Both are maintained by the proprietors of the rivers on which they are located, with a view to increasing the salmon supply therein. Neither of these rivers, however, has showrr any better results than those that have been without hatcheries. In fact I believe one of the two hatcheries was closed recently. The superintendent of Scottish salmon fisheries, who is an expert in his line, said in 1916: "We in this country do not rely on artificial hatcheries for the upkeep of the stock of salmon. We have magnificent natural spawning grounds in our Scottish rivers and we prefer to rely upon the process of nature for the replenishment of the stock."
The point is this: The few comparatively small Scottish rivers, without the aid of hatcheries, maintain a yearly production of salmon rather greater than that of the whole Atlantic coast . of Canada from the Bay of Fundy to the Labrador, with its many huge natural salmon rivers into which are dumped annually the output of no less than sixteen hatcheries.
What of the Great Lakes? Eight hatcheries in the province of Ontario have been turning out many millions of whitefish ami pickerel fry annually for a number of years.

In the United States artificial propagation of fish has been conducted on a great scale for many years. Yet Canada relatively has been doing far more than the United States in this line. In 1913 Canada had 61 main and subsidiary hatcheries, while the United States had not any more. But, as the United States authorities do not regularly collect statistics as to the catches of the various kinds of fish throughout the country, they cannot determine the results of their fish cultural work. As proof of this, let me quote the Commissioner of Fisheries at Washington, who, in a recent report, says:
The Bureau has given greater attention to the collection of fishery statistics which afford the only reliable basis for determining the condition of the fisheries, and indicating the need for and results of fish cultural work.
Even in the United States, however, where fish culture has been looked upon as a kind [DOT]of fetish, its value is now being questioned.

In the report of the Bureau of Fisheries for 1916 the following occurs:
In some sections an almost idolatrous faith in the efficiency of artificial culture of fish for replenishing the ravages of man and animals is manifested, and nothing has done more harm than the prevalence of such an idea. While it is an exceedingly difficult thing to prove, the consensus of opinion is that artificial culture does considerable good, yet the very fact that this cannot be conclusively proven ought to be a warning not to put blind faith in it. The best way in which to conserve the fisheries of the coast is by enacting and enforcing laws, making a close season, under which a certain proportion of the salmon runs will be enabled to reach the spawning beds. If this is done there can be no question of the perpetuation of the industry.
This good advice from Washington, Sir, should be followed by our officials.
The report of the Bureau of Fisheries for 1919 intimates that lobster hatching in the United States has practically been abandoned.
The great development of the fisheries of Norway is sometimes quoted as an example to this country, but the Norwegians place no reliance on artificial propagation of fish and do not waste money on it. One small hatchery, and no more, has been in existence at Flodevig since 1882 for hatching and distributing cod along the nearby coast. It is supported in part only by government funds. Its practical usefulness was so frequently called in question owing to the difficulty of proving any beneficial effects from it, that a commission was appointed in 1910 to investigate and report as to whether it should be continued. The commission consisted of scientists, a majority of whom, largely from a scientific view point, recommended its continuance. No one, however, believes it is of any benefit to the fisheries, and no doubt if practical men had been on the commission they would have recommended its abandonment.
The sum spent for the protection of the fisheries in Canada, in the shape of salaries to fishery officers and the maintenance of patrol boats is a huge one. According to the blue books it amounted to over $400,000 in 1913. That, for negative work, is surely much too much. But when to that large sum is added $400,000 more for artificial fish breeding in that year, without the slightest visible sign of the supplies being increased thereby, the thing to any one capable of understanding the 'figures dealing therewith assumes something of the character of a scandal. Perhaps no one in particular is to blame for this condition. It has evidently grown up under the system of administration past and present, which has blundered along guided by impracticable theorists. If 54|
the bull were now taken by the horns, so to speak, and the artificial propagation of fish and police work reduced, to their fitting place in the scheme of reconstruction, hundreds of thousands of dollars would be available for more useful' and necessary work without Parliament being asked for an increased vote.
Amongst more useful work might be classed the maintenance of a completely equipped steamer, like the "Michael Sars" of Norway, for scientific investigation of all kinds at sea bearing on the fisheries; also the establishment of what may be called fishery museums or schools at centres on both coasts and inland, in which models of all modern fishing crafts and appliances used throughout the fishing world would be on view, together with models of modern fish-curing, smoking, and canning establishments and the implements used therein. To such museums or schools fishermen and those directly concerned might be taken periodically to listen to lectures on and explanations of the various exhibits, by duly qualified experts, and to witness practical demonstrations in fish-curing and barrel making.
Money would be well spent in periodically sending a duly qualified expert or experts to cured-fish consuming centres abroad^ to study their desires and report to the trade. The money spent in the shape of bounties, amounting annually to $160,000, should be increased. Under the present system of distribution, the owner of a boat under 13 ft. keel gets $1; a boat fisherman gets about $4; owners of vessels of from 10 to 80 tons get $1 per ton, and those of vessels over 80 tons get $80 and vessel fishermen about $6.50. The aggregate sum paid is large, but the amount in each case so small as to make the avowed intention of the Act, namely " to encourage the development of the sea fisheries and the building of fishing vessels," a huge joke. How far, for instance, would an $80 bounty, which is the limit, go on a vessel costing say $30,000? A decent sum would help shipbuilding as well as fisheries. How much encouragement for the building of bigger and better crafts is therein the payment of $10 or $20 to the owners of small vessels of 10 to 20 tons, of which there are a great many on all parts of the coast? The other payments to boat owners and to vessel and boat fishermen are simply doles and can not be looked upon as encouraging the development of the fisheries.
Then money should be spent on improving the quality and consequently the value of all cured fish, by setting up a standard

of quality and paying a substantial bounty on all fish and packages found after proper inspection, up to that standard. No amount of lecturing and demonstrating could compare with this as a means of encouraging and developing our fisheries.
It is not for lack of money being spent by the Canadian Government on Canadian fisheries that they are not progressing as they should. It is rather due to the money being wrongly expended. The total expenditure on fisheries services in Canada in the year 1913 (all such expenditures were of course more or less curtailed during the war years) amounted to $1,229,518, including the bounty. Now, we have seen that the expenditure of France, which spends more on its fisheries than any other European country; amounted in the year 1911, to not more than $1,125,000. But, whereas Canada on the one hand spent over $800,000 of the total on superintendence, policing and fish breeding, and only $160,000 on bounties, France on the other hand, spent $980,000 on bounties for the encouragement of its deep sea fisheries and only $ 145)000 on superintendence, research work and experiments. These comparisons are very striking and should lead to a call for radical and sweeping changes in Canada.
There is not much hope for real practical assistance being given, however, as long as the administration of the fisheries services of Canada remain as at present, both inside and outside, almost entirely with a few notable exceptions in the hands of men who may be good clerks, but are, through lack of a working acquaintance with the industry, incapable of sizing up its l'eal needs or of directing any practical efforts towards its development.
The further development of our fisheries is dependent upon several things:
1.	An increased demand for fish at home.
2.	An increased demand for our cured fish abroad.
3.	Increased production. -
4.	Utilization of all by-products.
5.	A fisheries department, manned by practical business men, and scientific experts.
6.	Sufficient moneys to carry on necessary development.
The first can be brought about only by supplying the consuming public with real fresh fish in the shortest possible time after it is taken from the water.* The quality of such fish would be their own best advertisement and would very quickly lead to greater consumption. No amount of lecturing nor of newspaper or other advertising will induce people to continue the use of fish or

to increase their purchasing when as at present, they frequently find them so long out of the water as to fill the house with an offensive odour when being cooked. This was made clear in the evidence of inland dealers at the inquiry in 1916, as to the spread in prices. In Ontario the chief demand is for lake fish, because if its much fresher condition when offered for sale.
Sea fish can never be delivered in prime condition in the interior markets of Canada until a refrigerator or chilled car is made available on express trains, for all sizes of shipments; not once a week or three times a week, but every day of the week. The trade is not of sufficient volume at present to warrant the provision of such a daily car at a rate that would make it possible for shippers to make full use of its without assistance. But if adequate financial aid were provided by the Government for the operation of a daily refrigerator express car service, concurrently with a publicity campaign, the business would very quickly grow large enough to justify special express facilities without governmental aid. Until some such plan is adopted I have not much hope of seeing a great expansion of our fresh and semi-fresh fish traffic. It will, of course, be more expensive than the method of subsidizing fish shipments hitherto in force, but the importance of the industry and the results that are bound to follow are sufficient justification for any increased expenditure for a limited period.
The second is, perhaps of more importance than the first, for this reason: that the export trade in cured fish brings money out of the pocket of the foreigner and puts it into that of the Canadian, whereas the home trade in fresh fish largely consists of a transference of money from the pocket of one Canadian into that of another Canadian. Like the first, the second can only be secured by improving the quality of the product. Especially is this so in view oi the efforts of other countries to increase their output of cod and other salt fish to markets which are common to all fish-producing countries.
Efforts to persuade fishermen and curers by mere lectures or by written articles are not sufficient to bring the required improvement. That method is too slow. While waiting the results from such efforts we may wake some day soon to the fact that our competitors, by giving more attention to this quesiton of quality, have ousted us from the very markets we hitherto had looked upon as peculiarly ours. Such action as will be more quickly effective is therefore necessary. Here again the Government

should come to the rescue with financial assistance for a time.
A standard should be established for all cured fish, and after adequate inspection. If necessary the Government should appoint cullers in all the principal buying sections of the country and pay them so much per quintal for culling fish of different qualities. There should also be paid on each of the various units of quality which conform to the fixed standard a sum sufficient to encourage fishermen and eurers to turn out standard products. After a few years of such encouragement, with rigid inspection, followed by instruction where necessary, our salt fish producers would undoubtedly find themselves in a position to meet all competition unaided.
With an increasing demand for fish at home and abroad would come a demand for increased production. To meet such a demand individual fishermen or groups oi fishermen should be encouraged and assisted ' financially in securing such crafts as may be deemed most suitable. This is no more than the governments of other countries have been and are doing to advance their fisheries. To this end a fund should be created from which loans-not gifts-at low rates of interest could be made to approved persons or groups of persons to enable them to buy or build approved fishing crafts of all sizes.
While this suggestion is applicable in some measure to the Pacific coast, it applies mainly to the Atlantic where a much greater number of people are engaged and a much smaller sum is earned by their labour, which is performed under more severe conditions. The salmon fishery has been pretty well exploited and developed on the Pacific, and now that the salmon canning monopoly in the shape of protecting canners by limiting the number of cannery licenses has been ended recently, the provision of loans to white fishermen who are British subjects to enable them to secure boats for the halibut fishery-fully half the quantity of halibut landed at Prince Rupert is landed by American vessels-and the salmon fishery is perhaps the most effective way in which to help forward the Pacific fisheries. The increased production is bound to follow if the fishermen are encouraged to prosecute the industry. For the large fleet of trawlers which operate from Lunenburg county and proceed to the different banks where they fish from March to October, one or more hospital ships should be provided, so that fishermen will know that if they get sick they can be properly looked after.
Then to encourage men to engage in this industry, a scheme of state insurance, both life and accident, should be inaugurated. It would not cost a great deal of money to insure the fishermen during each season for an amount from $1,000 to $5,000, so that in [DOT] case any of them lose their lives during the voyage their families would be looked after. If you will look into the statistics you will find that although their calling is a very hazardous one, yet the fatalities are a small percentage of the number of. men engaged in the industry.
I also think that some state provision either of insurance or otherwise, should be-made for men who get hurt and also for those who, after serving a certain number of years have to give up fishing, either on account of ill health or old age.
Bait freezers should be established at not' only different parts of the Nova Scotia coast,, say at Lunenburg, North Sydney and northern Cape Breton or Prince Edward Island, but also at three or four important places in Newfoundland, as during certain seasons of the year bait is scarce and our vessels have to lay sometimes from one to four weeks waiting for bait. If these freezers were established and bait put in them from the previous season the fishing fleet would not be delayed and consequently would catch a great deal more fish. Last year, notwithstanding the handicap under which the fishermfen laboured, the fleet caught some 30,000,000 pounds of fish. Had they been able to get bait, and get it without waiting for it, they would have caught at least fifty per cent more than they did.
The fishermen should also be encouraged by having a lower tariff on all they eat and wear in their homes, and what they use either in the building or outfitting of small boats or large vessels should come into the country free of duty. They have to go into the open market to sell their product and take what they can get for it, and to properly encourage them they should be allowed to purchase anything they require without the barrier of a protective tariff.
The by-products of the fish should be taken care of. Plants should be erected to take care of the heads, guts, skins and other offal of the fishes. This would serve a twofold purpose, as fertilizer for the farms could be made from the bones and offal, oil would be extracted from the livers of the fish, and glue made from the skins. The Government would therefore kill two birds with one stone.
We also need in this country a new fisheries organization. The present department

'at Ottawa is ashamed to be known as the Fisheries Department, as a few years ago they changed the name of that department from "Marine and Fisheries" to "Marine and Naval Affairs." Why this was done passes all understanding, as the fisheries is of sufficient importance to be designated by the proper title. Looking over the Routine Proceedings and Orders of the Day, I notice a resolution under the name of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries. This resolution states that it is necessary to amend a certain part of the Canada Shipping Act relating to the inspection of hulls, boilers and machinery of vessels. It is quite right that that resolution should be under the name of the Minister of Marine, but I cannot see what the Fisheries Department has to do with the inspection of boilers. Immediately below that resolution there is another standing in the name of the Minister of the Naval Service, and having to do with a proposed amendment to the Fish Inspection Act regarding pickled herring, ale-wives, and mackerel. Now, I do not know whether they are going to supply pickled herring, ale-wives and mackerel to the Canadian Navy, but it certainly seems ridiculous for a resolution of that kind to be in the name of the Minister of the Naval Service.
What we want is a new lock, stock and barrel in thit department, with practical men in e1 arge, and until we get this we cannot expect very much to be done to encourage or oromote this great industry.
Some money should be spent to enour'.gf the immigration of fishermen to this country. I think I am safe in saying that I could pick from the Lunenburg fishing fleet at least one thousand men who are capable of taking charge of fishing vessels, although at the present time they are fishing in dories from other vessels, but I feel quite confident that if the Government would encourage the immigration of capable fishermen to this country these men would be able to get vessels of their own, which would greatly enlarge the present fishing fleet. If the Government would provide the men, I feel quite confident that the people of Nova Scotia, especially the people of my own county, would see that vessels aTe built and the fleet enlarged.
I trust, Mr. Speaker, that my remarks will not fall upon barren ground, but that the Government will take steps to encourage the proper development of this great industry. The men who are prosecuting it at the present time are not only the salt of the earth, but they are the salts of the sea. Their calling is an arduous one; they risk

their lives every hour of the day and every day of the year; they are brave and daring and are not daunted either by the winds or the waves or by storms or fogs. Such men as these who go down to the sea in ships and do business on the great waters should receive every consideration and every encouragement from the Government of this country.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, While I do not agree with a great many of the conclusions of the member for Lunenburg (Mr. Duff) I think that we owe him a great deal for introducing this question into the House and that we must, respect his great grasp of the' fishery situation. When I have occasion again to speak on this subject, I purpose proving that the minister who is at the head of the Fisheries Department (Mr. Ballantyne) is doing a great deal, in our part of the country at least, to develop the very principles for which my hon. friend stands. My hon. friend speaks of the Atlantic fisheries; 1 speak of the Pacific fisheries, and I will say this, that of all the Ministers of Fisheries we have had there ha.s been no other minister who has at all approached the Minister of Fisheries of this Government in regard to his policy in developing the fisheries of British Columbia. I came from a fishing country, namely, the province of New Brunswick, and I live in a fishing country, in northern British Columbia, one of the greatest fisheries in the world, and I certainly look on fish as one of the most delicious products. The whole question in regard to its production and also in regard to it from an appetising standpoint, is very interesting. At this hour of the night, however, I do not think that our hardworking members of Parliament who labour for the very large sum of $2,500 a year, should be delayed in order to discuss this subject.

I am going to do that in two or three minutes. I hope this debate will be resumed at an early date. If it is not, I mean to take up the subject, which is very controversial and bitter in British Columbia, of the destruction of the cannery monopoly. I have taken <a part in that question and I am deeply interested in it. I wish to prove, in my humble way, to the Parliament. of this country that the minister has proved himself to be the strongest minister we have, had in regard to that question and that he has not hesi-

tated to play the part of a strong and disinterested man in destroying the cannery monopoly. I see some of my hon. friends opposite smile, and, I presume, in derision, because they were the people who introduced this cannery monopoly which has been the cause of so much trouble in our province.
I want to speak of the question of the returned soldier. I have been an advocate of the policy that the Government should assist in establishing the returned soldier in the fishing business. I can say honestly that I think ithe minister and his officials are quite in sympathy with that policy, and I commend that to' the consideration of the House. If you can re-establish men in farming, while I realize that you cannot re-establish them in every walk in life, there is one business in which you can re-establish them, and that is the fishing business. Therefore, I hope this debate will be resumed at an early date, and if it is not, I purpose taking up the whole question of the salmon fisheries of British Columbia in a most interesting and entertaining manner. I move the adjournment of the debate.
